93077.q: What can you find out by running a slow pointer and a pointer twice as fast through a linked list?
a: Whether the list contains a cycle
Whether the list contains duplicate values
How big the largest element is
93077.e: If there is a cycle, the fast pointer eventually catches up with the slow one. The method comes from Robert Floyd and is called “tortoise and hare”.
93077.m: If a fast and a slow pointer meet, the list contains a cycle.

93078.q: What disadvantage does a linked list have compared with an array in terms of memory?
93078.e: Each node stores at least one pointer as well as the data. With small data elements, this extra need is significant.
93078.m: Linked lists need extra memory for their pointers.

93079.q: Which principle does a stack work by?
93079.e: LIFO stands for “Last In, First Out”. What was put on last is taken off first.
93079.m: A stack gives back the element put on last first.

93080.q: What is the operation called that puts an element on top of a stack?
93080.e: push puts a new element on top of the stack. It is then the topmost element.
93080.m: With push you put an element on the stack.

93081.q: What is the operation called that removes and returns the top element of a stack?
93081.e: pop takes the top element off the stack. After that, the element that was second from the top is on top.
93081.m: With pop you take the top element off the stack.

93082.q: The numbers 1, 2 and 3 are put one after another on an empty stack. What does a pop then give?
93082.e: The 3 was put on last and is therefore on top. A stack always gives back the top element.
93082.m: A pop always gives the element put on last.

93083.q: Where does a running program store the return addresses when functions are called?
93083.e: Each function call puts a frame with the return address and local variables on the call stack. When the function returns, this frame is removed again.
93083.m: Function calls are managed on the call stack.

93084.q: What is the value of the expression “3 4 + 2 *” in reverse Polish notation?
93084.e: With a stack: put 3 and 4 on, + gives 7, then put 2 on, * gives 7 · 2 = 14.
93084.m: Expressions in reverse Polish notation are worked out with a stack.

93085.q: For which task do you typically use a stack?
a: Checking that brackets are correctly matched
Shortest routes in a road network
93085.e: Each opening bracket is put on the stack, and each closing bracket must match the top one. If the stack is empty at the end, the brackets are correct.
93085.m: A stack can check whether brackets are closed correctly.

93086.q: Which operation gives the top element of a stack without removing it?
93086.e: peek only looks at the top of the stack. pop, by contrast, would remove the element.
93086.m: With peek you look at the top element without taking it away.

93087.q: Which principle does a queue work by?
93087.e: FIFO stands for “First In, First Out”. Whoever joined the queue first is also served first.
93087.m: In a queue, the element added first comes out first.

93088.q: What is the operation called that adds an element to the back of a queue?
93088.e: enqueue adds an element at the end. dequeue, by contrast, takes out the front element.
93088.m: With enqueue you add an element to a queue.

93089.q: A, B and C are added to an empty queue. Which element does the first dequeue give?
93089.e: A was added first and is therefore at the front. A queue always gives out the front element.
93089.m: A dequeue gives the element that has been waiting longest.

93090.q: With which structure can a queue of fixed size be put into an array efficiently?
93090.e: In a ring buffer, the start and end pointers move in a circle through the array. That way nothing has to be moved when an element is taken out.
93090.m: A ring buffer implements a queue without moving the elements.

93091.q: Which graph algorithm uses a queue to visit nodes level by level?
93091.e: Breadth-first search adds discovered neighbours to the back and processes them in that order. That way nearby nodes are visited before distant ones.
93091.m: Breadth-first search works with a queue.

93092.q: With which data structure is a priority queue usually implemented efficiently?
93092.e: A binary heap gives the element with the highest priority in O(1) and inserts in O(log n). That is faster than an unsorted array.
93092.m: Priority queues are usually implemented with a heap.

93093.q: What is a queue called in which you can add and remove elements at both ends?
93093.e: Deque stands for “double-ended queue”. It combines the abilities of a stack and a queue.
93093.m: A deque allows adding and removing at both ends.

93094.q: Which everyday computer task typically works with a queue?
a: The undo function in an editor
The back button in a browser
93094.e: Print jobs are printed in the order they arrive. The undo function and the back button, by contrast, work with a stack.
93094.m: Print jobs are handled one after another from a queue.

93095.q: What is the maximum number of child nodes a node in a binary tree may have?
93095.e: “Binary” means two. Each node has at most one left and one right child.
93095.m: In a binary tree, each node has at most two children.

93096.q: How many nodes does a binary tree with 4 levels have if all its levels are completely full?
93096.e: The levels hold 1, 2, 4 and 8 nodes. Together that is 2⁴ minus 1 = 15 nodes.
93096.m: A full binary tree with k levels has 2 to the power of k minus 1 nodes.

93097.q: In a binary search tree, where are the keys that are smaller than a node's key?
93097.e: In a binary search tree, smaller keys are on the left and larger keys on the right. That way you can rule out one half at each step of a search.
93097.m: In a binary search tree, smaller keys are on the left.

93098.q: Which traversal order gives the keys of a binary search tree sorted in ascending order?
93098.e: Inorder first visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree. Because of the search tree property, this gives the sorted order.
93098.m: An inorder traversal outputs a binary search tree in sorted order.

93099.q: What is the running time of searching in an unbalanced binary search tree in the worst case?
93099.e: If you insert the keys in sorted order, the tree degenerates into a chain. Then in the worst case you have to check all n nodes.
93099.m: A degenerate search tree is no faster than a list.

93100.q: What is special about an AVL tree?
a: It keeps itself balanced through rotations when inserting
Each node has exactly three children
It stores values only in the root
It may only contain numbers up to 255
93100.e: An AVL tree is a binary search tree that balances its height with rotations after every insertion or deletion. This keeps searching fast. It is named after Adelson-Velsky and Landis (1962).

93101.q: What do you call a node in a tree that has no children?
93101.e: Nodes without successors are called leaves. The root, by contrast, is the only node without a parent node.
93101.m: A node without children is called a leaf.

93102.q: In which order does a preorder traversal visit a binary tree?
93102.e: In preorder, the current node is processed before its subtrees. Then come the left and the right subtree.
93102.m: Preorder processes the root first and then the subtrees.

93103.q: What is the minimum number of levels a binary tree with 1,000 nodes needs?
93103.e: 9 levels hold at most 2⁹ minus 1 = 511 nodes, 10 levels at most 1,023. So at least 10 levels are needed.
93103.m: The minimum height of a binary tree grows logarithmically with the number of nodes.

93104.q: What is the average running time of searching in a hash table?
93104.e: The hash function directly calculates where a key is stored. With a good spread, only a few comparisons are needed.
93104.m: Hash tables find entries in constant time on average.

93105.q: What is it called when two different keys get the same hash value?
93105.e: Since there are usually far more possible keys than places, collisions cannot be avoided. A hash table therefore needs a strategy to resolve them.
93105.m: If two keys have the same hash value, a collision occurs.

93106.q: What is the collision resolution called in which each table slot keeps a list of all entries that have landed there?
93106.e: In chaining (separate chaining), colliding entries hang in a list at the same slot. In probing, by contrast, you look for another free slot.
93106.m: In chaining, each slot collects its entries in a list.

93107.q: What is the open addressing method called that simply checks the next slot when there is a collision?
93107.e: In linear probing, you check the following slots one by one until you find a free one. Entries can bunch together into clusters this way.
93107.m: Linear probing looks for the next free slot when there is a collision.

93108.q: A hash table has 100 slots and contains 75 entries. What is the load factor?
93108.e: The load factor is the number of entries divided by the number of slots: 75 / 100 = 0.75.
93108.m: The load factor shows how full a hash table is.

93109.q: The hash function is h(k) = k mod 7. In which slot does the key 23 go?
93109.e: 23 divided by 7 is 3 remainder 2. The remainder 2 is the hash value.
93109.m: In the division method, the hash value is the remainder of the division.

93110.q: Which built-in Python data type is implemented internally as a hash table?
93110.e: A dict assigns values to keys and uses the keys' hash values to do so. That is why keys must be hashable.
93110.m: A Python dict is a hash table.

93111.q: What running time can searching in a hash table have in the worst case?
93111.e: If all keys land in the same slot, you have to search through all entries. A bad hash function can ruin performance like this.
93111.m: In the worst case, a hash table is as slow as a list.

93112.q: What is the average running time of quicksort?
93112.e: On average the pivot splits the list into roughly two halves. There are then about log n levels, each with linear effort.
93112.m: Quicksort sorts in n log n steps on average.

93113.q: With which input does the worst case occur if quicksort always takes the first element as the pivot?
a: With data that are already sorted
With an even number of elements
93113.e: With sorted data, the first element is always the smallest. The split is then as uneven as possible.
93113.m: Sorted input is especially bad for quicksort with the first element as pivot.

93114.q: Which property does the usual version of quicksort lack?
93114.e: When splitting, equal keys can lose their original order. Such a method is called not stable.
93114.m: Quicksort in its usual form is not stable.

93115.q: Which principle does quicksort work by?
93115.e: Quicksort splits the list around a pivot into smaller and larger values and sorts both parts further recursively.
93115.m: Quicksort breaks the problem down recursively into smaller parts.

93116.e: John von Neumann described the method in 1945. That makes it one of the oldest sorting algorithms for computers.
93116.m: Mergesort goes back to John von Neumann.

93117.q: Is mergesort a stable sorting method?
a: Yes, equal keys keep their order
93117.e: When merging, if there is a tie you take the element from the left sublist. That way the original order of equal keys is kept.
93117.m: Mergesort is a stable sorting method.

93118.q: How much extra memory does mergesort usually need when sorting an array?
93118.e: When merging, a helper array of the same size is needed. This is the main disadvantage compared with quicksort.
93118.m: Mergesort needs a linear amount of extra memory for arrays.

93119.q: What is the maximum number of comparisons needed to merge two sorted lists of 4 elements each?
93119.e: Each comparison places one element in the result list. As soon as one list is empty, the rest is added without comparing; this gives at most 4 + 4 minus 1 = 7 comparisons.
93119.m: Two sorted lists of lengths m and n are merged with at most m plus n minus 1 comparisons.

93120.q: How many times do you have to halve a list of 1,024 elements until only single elements are left?
93120.e: 2¹⁰ = 1,024. After 10 halvings, each sublist has length 1.
93120.m: The recursion depth of mergesort is the base-2 logarithm of n.

93121.q: Which task is mergesort particularly well suited to?
a: Sorting very large files on storage media
93121.e: Mergesort only reads the sublists in order. That is why it is suitable for external sorting, when the data do not fit into main memory.
93121.m: Mergesort is ideal for external sorting of large amounts of data.

93122.q: Which sorting algorithm in the Python standard library combines mergesort with insertion sort?
93122.e: Timsort was developed for Python by Tim Peters in 2002. It takes advantage of sections in the data that are already sorted.
93122.m: Python sorts with Timsort, a mix of mergesort and insertion sort.

93123.q: In which year did Dijkstra publish his shortest path algorithm?
93123.e: Dijkstra designed the algorithm in 1956 and published it in 1959 in the journal “Numerische Mathematik”.
93123.m: Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm appeared in 1959.

93124.q: Which algorithm finds shortest paths even with negative edge weights?
93124.e: The Bellman-Ford algorithm checks all edges repeatedly. It is slower than Dijkstra but also detects negative cycles.
93124.m: With negative weights you use the Bellman-Ford algorithm.

93125.q: In Dijkstra's algorithm, which data structure efficiently gives the node with the smallest provisional distance?
93125.e: At each step, the open node with the smallest distance is chosen. A priority queue gives exactly this minimum quickly.
93125.m: Dijkstra chooses the next node with a priority queue.

93126.q: Edges: A-B 4, A-C 1, C-B 2, B-D 1, C-D 5. How long is the shortest path from A to D?
93126.e: The path A-C-B-D has length 1 + 2 + 1 = 4. A-B-D gives 5 and A-C-D gives 6.
93126.m: The shortest path is not always the one with the fewest edges.

93127.q: Which internet routing protocol calculates routes with Dijkstra's algorithm?
93127.e: OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) is a link-state protocol. Each router uses it to calculate the shortest routes in the network.
93127.m: OSPF uses Dijkstra's algorithm for routing.

93128.q: Which important computer science award did Edsger Dijkstra receive in 1972?
93128.e: Dijkstra received the Turing Award in 1972, among other things for basic contributions to programming and to the language ALGOL. The prize is considered the highest award in computer science.
93128.m: Dijkstra was honoured with the Turing Award in 1972.

93129.q: Roughly how does the running time of an O(n²) algorithm change when n doubles?
a: It becomes eight times as long
93129.e: With quadratic growth, (2n)² = 4n². So the running time becomes about four times as long.
93129.m: With quadratic running time, doubling the input quadruples the effort.

93130.q: After which mathematician is Landau notation named?
93130.e: The German number theorist Edmund Landau made big O notation well known. Paul Bachmann had introduced it in 1894.
93130.m: Landau notation is named after Edmund Landau.

93131.q: Which class does the function 3n² + 5n + 7 belong to?
93131.e: In big O notation, only the fastest-growing term counts, and constant factors are dropped. What remains is n².
93131.m: In Landau notation, only the dominant term counts.

93132.q: Which of these functions grows fastest for large n?
93132.e: Exponential growth beats every polynomial. Even for n = 20, 2ⁿ is more than a million, but n³ is only 8,000.

93133.q: What does big O notation, such as O(n²), tell you about an algorithm?
a: How fast the effort grows at most with the input size
The exact running time in seconds
The number of lines of code
The space used on the hard disk
93133.e: Big O notation is an upper bound for growth. Constant factors and the speed of the computer play no role.
93133.m: Big O notation describes how fast the effort grows at most.

93135.e: The US mathematician Richard Bellman introduced the term in the 1950s. He used the method for optimisation problems.
93135.m: Richard Bellman coined the term dynamic programming.

93136.q: Which property of a problem does dynamic programming mainly take advantage of?
93136.e: If the same sub-problems come up several times, you solve them only once and store the result. That way you avoid doing the same work twice.
93136.m: Dynamic programming solves each sub-problem only once.

93137.q: What is storing function results that have already been calculated called?
93137.e: In memoisation, a function remembers its results in a table. When it is called again with the same arguments, it gives the stored value.
93137.m: Memoisation stores results so they do not have to be calculated again.

93138.q: What is the running time of calculating the n-th Fibonacci number with a table from the bottom up?
93138.e: Each Fibonacci number is calculated exactly once from the two before it. Naive recursion, by contrast, needs an exponential number of calls.
93138.m: With dynamic programming you calculate Fibonacci numbers in linear time.

93139.q: What is the Levenshtein distance between “cat” and “hat”?
93139.e: You only need to replace the “c” with an “h”. One replacement counts as one operation.
93139.m: The Levenshtein distance counts the minimum number of changes needed between two words.

93140.q: Why is the knapsack problem often solved with dynamic programming rather than by trying out all combinations?
a: With n items there would be 2 to the power of n combinations
Trying things out always gives wrong results
There is only ever one single combination
93140.e: Each item can be taken or not, which gives 2 to the power of n possibilities. With 50 items that is over a quadrillion. A table of partial solutions is much faster.

93141.q: What is the principle called that an optimal solution consists of optimal solutions to its sub-problems?
93141.e: The principle of optimality is the basis of dynamic programming. Only if it holds may you put partial solutions together.
93141.m: Without optimal substructure, dynamic programming does not work.

93142.q: How many paths are there along the lines of a grid of 3 by 3 squares from top left to bottom right if you may only go right or down?
93142.e: You make 3 steps to the right and 3 down, so 6 steps. The number of arrangements is 6! / (3! · 3!) = 20; with a table you add the values from above and from the left each time.
93142.m: Grid paths are counted with a table in which each square is the sum of the one above and the one to the left.

93143.q: Which strategy does a greedy algorithm follow?
a: The locally best choice at each step
93143.e: A greedy algorithm always goes for the option that is best at that moment. Earlier decisions are never undone.
93143.m: A greedy algorithm always picks what is best right now.

93144.q: How many coins does a greedy algorithm give for 3.70 francs using Swiss coins?
93144.e: It always takes the biggest coin that fits: 2 francs, 1 franc, 50 centimes, 20 centimes. That is 4 coins.
93144.m: When giving change, the greedy algorithm always takes the biggest coin that fits.

93145.q: With coins of 1, 3 and 4, you have to pay 6 units. How many coins does a greedy algorithm choose?
93145.e: Greedy first takes 4, then 1 twice, so 3 coins. Two coins of 3 would be optimal.
93145.m: A greedy algorithm does not always find the optimal solution.

93146.q: Which problem does Kruskal's greedy algorithm solve?
93146.e: Kruskal takes the edges in ascending order of weight and adds them if no cycle is formed. This creates a spanning tree with the minimum total weight.
93146.m: Kruskal greedily builds a minimum spanning tree.

93147.q: Which compression method greedily builds a code tree by always combining the two rarest characters?
93147.e: In Huffman coding, frequent characters get short codes and rare characters long ones. Here the greedy strategy provably gives an optimal prefix code.
93147.m: Huffman codes come from greedily combining rare characters.

93148.q: In which knapsack problem does a greedy algorithm based on value per weight always give the optimum?
93148.e: If you may divide items, you fill the knapsack with the best value per weight first. In the 0/1 problem, by contrast, this strategy can fail.
93148.m: In the fractional knapsack problem, the greedy choice is optimal.

93149.q: What is the greedy heuristic for the travelling salesman problem that always picks the nearest unvisited city called?
93149.e: The nearest neighbour heuristic is fast but often does not give the shortest round trip. It shows that greedy decisions can only be an approximation.
93149.m: The nearest neighbour heuristic is fast but not always optimal.

93150.q: Which greedy rule selects the largest possible number of non-overlapping appointments?
a: Always the appointment that ends earliest
Always the appointment that starts earliest
93150.e: Choosing the appointment that ends earliest leaves the most time for further appointments. It can be proved that this rule is always optimal.
93150.m: In interval scheduling, you greedily choose the earliest end time.

93151.q: Which choice of pivot lowers the risk of quicksort's worst case with nearly sorted data?
a: Median of the first, middle and last element
93151.e: The median of three candidates is usually close to the middle of the values. This makes the sublists more balanced.
93151.m: The median-of-three rule makes quicksort more robust.

93152.q: In quicksort, what is the element called at which the list is split into smaller and larger values?
93152.e: All values smaller than the pivot go to the left and all larger ones to the right. Then both parts are sorted further in the same way.
93152.m: In quicksort, the pivot splits the list.

93153.q: Quicksort splits the list 7, 3, 9, 1, 5, 2 using the pivot 3. How many elements end up to the left of the pivot?
93153.e: All values smaller than 3 end up on the left. Those are 1 and 2, so two elements.
93153.m: After splitting, only smaller values are to the left of the pivot.

93154.q: What advantage does a randomly chosen pivot bring in quicksort?
a: No particular input is always unfavourable
The running time is always linear
93154.e: With a random pivot, the running time no longer depends on the order of the input. The expected running time is O(n log n) for every input.
93154.m: A random pivot protects quicksort against deliberately unfavourable input.

93155.q: What do you get when you merge the sorted lists 1, 4, 7 and 2, 3, 9?
93155.e: You compare the front elements of both lists each time and take the smaller one. This creates a single sorted list.
93155.m: When merging, you always take the smaller of the two front elements.

93156.q: Which algorithm extends Dijkstra with an estimate of the remaining distance to the goal?
93156.e: A* prefers nodes that, according to a heuristic, are closer to the goal. If the estimate is never too large, A* still finds the shortest path.
93156.m: A* is Dijkstra with an estimate of the goal.

93157.q: What is the running time of Dijkstra's algorithm if the minimum is searched for in a simple array each time (V nodes)?
93157.e: For each of the V nodes, the whole array is searched for the minimum. That gives V times V steps.
93157.m: Without a heap, Dijkstra needs quadratic time in the number of nodes.

93158.q: Which running time class does trying out all orders of n cities have?
93158.e: For n cities there are n! possible orders. With just 20 cities that is more than 2 quintillion.

93159.q: Which greedy algorithm builds a minimum spanning tree edge by edge from a starting node?
93159.e: Prim always adds the cheapest edge that connects the tree so far with a new node. That way the tree grows from a starting point.
93159.m: Prim grows a minimum spanning tree from a starting node.

93160.q: What happens when a hash table is rehashed?
a: The table is enlarged and all entries are redistributed
The hash function is kept secret
93160.e: If the load factor becomes too large, a bigger table is created. Each entry gets a new place there using the hash function.
93160.m: In rehashing, a full hash table is enlarged.

93161.q: What is the running time of two nested loops that each run over all n elements?
93161.e: The inner loop runs n times for each of the n passes of the outer loop. That gives n · n steps.
93161.m: Two nested loops over n elements give quadratic running time.

93162.q: In which order does the programming language C store a two-dimensional array in memory?
93162.e: C stores multi-dimensional arrays row by row (row-major order). Fortran, by contrast, stores them column by column.
93162.m: In C the rows of a two-dimensional array lie one after another in memory.

93163.e: There are many varieties of apple. Their skin can be red, yellow, green or a mix.
93163.m: Apples can be red, yellow or green.

93164.q: Which canton has lots of apple trees and is therefore jokingly called “Mostindien”?
93164.e: There are especially many apple trees in Thurgau. Because a lot of apple juice and cider (Most) is made there, it is jokingly called “Mostindien”.

93165.q: What is the soft purée made from cooked apples called?
93165.e: You cook pieces of apple until soft and mash them. This makes apple sauce.
93165.m: Apple sauce is made from cooked apples.

93166.q: Why does a cut apple turn brown after a while?
a: Because air gets to the flesh
93166.e: Substances in the flesh react with the air. This creates the brown colour.

93167.q: What can you drizzle on apple slices so they do not turn brown so quickly?
93167.e: Lemon juice slows down the browning. This keeps the slices pale for longer.
93167.m: Lemon juice keeps apple slices pale.

93168.q: What happens to an apple if you put it in a bucket of water?
93168.e: An apple contains a lot of air between its cells. That is why it is lighter than water and floats.

93169.q: Who usually lives in an apple with a “worm” in it?
93169.e: The “worm” in the apple is actually the caterpillar of a small moth. It eats its way through the flesh.
93169.m: The worm in the apple is actually a caterpillar.

93170.q: In the legend, which fruit did William Tell shoot from his son's head?
93170.e: In the legend, Tell had to shoot an apple from the head of his son Walter with his crossbow. He hit it.
93170.m: William Tell shot an apple from his son's head.

93171.q: Which insects mainly pollinate the flowers of apple trees?
93171.e: Bees fly from flower to flower and carry the pollen with them. This is the only way lots of apples can grow.

93172.q: What shape is a typical pear?
a: Fat at the bottom, narrow at the top
93172.e: A pear is rounded at the bottom and gets narrower towards the stalk at the top. That makes it easy to recognise.
93172.m: A pear is fat at the bottom and narrow at the top.

93173.q: Which canton is known for its Williams pears?
93173.e: Lots of Williams pears grow in sunny Valais. They are very juicy and smell strongly.
93173.m: Valais is known for Williams pears.

93175.q: Which fruit is the pear closely related to?
93175.e: Pears and apples belong to the same plant family, the rose family. Both grow on trees here.
93175.m: Pears and apples are close relatives.

93176.q: Which group of fruit does the pear belong to, because it has a core inside?
93176.e: Fruits with a core and small pips are called pome fruits. The quince, for example, is one too.
93176.m: The pear is a pome fruit.

93177.q: What happens to a hard pear if it lies in the kitchen for a few days?
93177.e: Pears keep ripening after they are picked. That is why they get soft and sweet in the kitchen.

93178.q: Why do some pears feel a bit gritty when you eat them?
a: Because of sand in the skin
Because of sugar on the skin
93178.e: In the flesh of the pear there are tiny hard cells. They are called stone cells, and you can feel them when you chew.
93178.m: Small stone cells make pears a bit gritty.

93179.q: What is a Swiss bake with a filling of dried pears called?
93179.e: Birnbrot has a dark, sweet filling of dried pears. It is eaten especially in winter.

93180.q: How do cherries often hang on the tree?
a: On the trunk without a stalk
93180.e: Cherries have long stalks. Often two or more cherries hang together.

93181.q: What are the cherries that taste sour and often go into cakes called?
93181.e: Sour cherries are less sweet. That is why people like to bake or cook with them.
93181.m: Sour cherries are good for baking.

93182.q: In which season are cherries ripe here?
93182.e: Here, cherries ripen in about June and July. They are among the first fruits of summer.

93183.q: Which group of fruit does the cherry belong to?
93183.e: Fruits with a single hard stone in the middle are called stone fruits.
93183.m: The cherry is a stone fruit.

93184.q: What often happens to ripe cherries when there is a lot of rain?
93184.e: Ripe cherries soak up water when it rains. Then their skin gets too tight and splits.
93184.m: Lots of rain makes ripe cherries split.

93185.q: What is a little bag of cherry stones used for?
93185.e: You warm the bag in the oven. The stones give off the warmth for a long time, for example when you have a tummy ache.
93185.m: A cherry stone bag stays warm for a long time.

93186.q: What colour are ripe sweet cherries usually?
93186.e: Most sweet cherries turn dark red as they ripen. But there are also lighter varieties.
93186.m: Ripe sweet cherries are usually dark red.

93187.q: What is the wood of the cherry tree often used for?
93187.e: Cherry wood is reddish with a lovely grain. Carpenters like to make furniture from it.
93187.m: Beautiful furniture is made from cherry wood.

93188.q: What colour is the skin of a ripe plum (Zwetschge)?
93188.e: Ripe Zwetschge plums are dark blue to purple. Unripe ones are still green.
93188.m: Ripe Zwetschge plums are dark blue.

93189.q: What is the white coating that you can wipe off a plum?
93189.e: The plum makes a thin layer of wax itself. It protects the fruit from drying out.
93189.m: The white coating on plums is natural wax.

93191.q: What does the stone of a Zwetschge plum look like?
93191.e: The stone of the Zwetschge plum is hard, flat and long. It comes away easily from the flesh.
93191.m: The Zwetschge stone is flat and long.

93193.q: When are Zwetschge plums ripe here?
93193.e: Zwetschge plums ripen in about August and September. Then there are lots of plum tarts.
93193.m: Zwetschge plums are ripe in late summer.

93194.e: Dried plums are sweet and keep for a long time. They are called prunes.

93195.q: What colour is the flesh of a Zwetschge plum?
93195.e: On the outside the plum is blue, on the inside it is yellowish to greenish.

93197.q: In which canton do most Swiss apricots grow?
93197.e: Valais is sunny and dry. Almost all of Switzerland's apricots grow there.
93197.m: Most Swiss apricots come from Valais.

93198.q: What colour is a ripe apricot?
93198.e: Ripe apricots are orange and often have red cheeks.

93199.q: What does the skin of an apricot feel like?
93199.e: The apricot has fine, short hairs on its skin. That is why it feels velvety.

93200.q: Which jam is inside a Sachertorte?
93200.e: The Sachertorte is a chocolate cake from Vienna. Between the cake and the icing there is apricot jam.

93201.q: Why are apricot blossoms often in danger in spring?
a: They flower early and can freeze
93201.e: Apricot trees flower very early in the year. If there is still frost then, the blossoms can freeze.
93201.m: Frost is dangerous for early apricot blossoms.

93202.q: Which bigger fruit looks similar to the apricot?
93202.e: Peaches and apricots are related. The peach is usually bigger and juicier.
93202.m: The peach is a big relative of the apricot.

93203.q: When are most apricots harvested in Valais?
93203.e: Apricots need lots of summer sun. Most of them are picked in July and August.
93203.m: Apricots are harvested in high summer.

93204.q: Should you eat the bitter kernels inside an apricot stone?
93204.e: Bitter apricot kernels contain a substance that can form poison in the body. That is why you do not eat them.
93204.m: Do not eat bitter apricot kernels.

93205.q: What colour is a ripe strawberry?
93205.e: Unripe strawberries are green or white. When ripe they are bright red.

a: On low plants close to the ground
On vines up the wall of the house
93206.e: The strawberry plant is small and stays close to the ground. The fruits often lie almost on the soil.
93206.m: Strawberries grow close to the ground.

93207.q: Why do people put straw under strawberry plants?
a: So the fruits stay clean and dry
So birds can build nests there
93207.e: On the straw, the strawberries do not lie on damp soil. That way they rot less and stay clean.
93207.m: Straw keeps strawberries clean and dry.

93208.q: What are the small wild strawberries at the edge of the forest called?
93208.e: Wild strawberries are much smaller than garden strawberries. But they taste very aromatic.
93208.m: Wild strawberries are small and grow wild.

93209.q: When are most strawberries harvested outdoors here?
93209.e: Swiss strawberries are mainly available in May, June and July. That is strawberry season.
93209.m: Strawberry season is in early summer.

93210.e: The strawberry plant has small white flowers with a yellow centre. Later they turn into the fruits.

93211.q: For plant scientists, is the strawberry a true berry?
93211.e: For plant scientists, the strawberry is an aggregate fruit with lots of tiny nuts. Only in everyday life do we call it a berry.
93211.m: The strawberry is not really a true berry.

93212.q: Do green strawberries still turn red and sweet after picking?
a: No, they hardly ripen any more
93212.e: Strawberries only ripen properly on the plant. That is why you only pick them when they are completely red.
93212.m: Only pick strawberries when they are ripe.

93213.q: Which animals like to nibble strawberries in the garden?
93213.e: Slugs and snails crawl to the strawberries at night and eat holes in them. That is why gardeners protect the plants.
93213.m: Slugs and snails like eating strawberries.

93214.e: Ripe raspberries are usually bright red. That shows you can pick them.

93215.q: What does a freshly picked raspberry look like inside?
a: It is full of juice like a balloon
93215.e: When you pick it, the little cone stays on the plant. That is why the raspberry has a hole inside.
93215.m: A picked raspberry is hollow inside.

93216.q: What is a raspberry made of?
93216.e: A raspberry is made up of lots of tiny little fruits. Each one has a tiny seed.
93216.m: A raspberry is made of lots of tiny little balls.

93217.q: What does the raspberry bush have on its canes?
93217.e: Raspberry canes have lots of small, fine prickles. But they prick less than those of the blackberry.

93218.q: Why are raspberries only put carefully into small punnets?
a: They are soft and squash easily
93218.e: Raspberries are very delicate. In big heaps, the ones at the bottom would get squashed.
93218.m: Raspberries are delicate and squash easily.

93219.q: When do most raspberries ripen here?
93219.e: Most raspberries are ripe in summer. Some varieties keep fruiting into autumn.

93220.q: What can you make from dried raspberry leaves?
93220.e: You can dry raspberry leaves and pour hot water over them. This makes a mild tea.
93220.m: You can make tea from raspberry leaves.

93221.e: There are raspberry varieties with yellow fruits. They often taste especially mild.

93222.e: Redcurrants are the best known. But there are also black and white varieties.
93222.m: Currants come in red, black and white.

93223.q: How do currants hang on the bush?
a: One by one on long stalks
93223.e: Lots of small currants hang one behind the other on a thin stalk. It looks like a small bunch of grapes.

93226.e: Redcurrants are juicy but quite sour. Many people eat them with a little sugar.

93227.q: What is another name for the blackcurrant?
93227.e: The blackcurrant is also called cassis. Syrup and jam are made from it.
93227.m: The blackcurrant is also called cassis.

93228.q: Which vitamin is found in large amounts in blackcurrants?
93228.e: Blackcurrants contain a particularly large amount of vitamin C. Even more than lemons.
93228.m: Blackcurrants have lots of vitamin C.

93229.q: What can you use to strip currants easily off their stalks?
93229.e: You pull the bunch through the prongs of a fork. The berries fall off and the stalks are left over.
93229.m: You can strip currants off with a fork.

93230.q: What happens to your tongue and teeth if you eat lots of wild bilberries?
93230.e: Wild bilberries have a strong blue colouring. It stains your mouth, tongue and fingers.
93230.m: Wild bilberries turn your tongue blue.

93232.q: What colour is the inside of a wild bilberry?
93232.e: In the wild bilberry, the flesh is also dark. Large cultivated blueberries are pale inside.
93232.m: Wild bilberries are dark inside too.

93233.q: Where do the large blueberries from the shop originally come from?
93233.e: The large cultivated blueberries were bred from a species from North America. They grow on tall bushes.
93233.m: Large cultivated blueberries come from North America.

93234.q: Which large forest bird likes to eat bilberries in summer?
93234.e: The capercaillie lives in mountain forests with lots of bilberry bushes. It eats the berries and the leaves.

93235.q: Roughly how big is a wild bilberry?
93235.e: Wild bilberries are small, about half a centimetre. That is why picking them takes patience.
93235.m: Wild bilberries are as small as peas.

93236.q: Which tool did people use in the past to pick lots of bilberries quickly?
93236.e: A berry comb has lots of prongs. You use it to strip the berries off the little bushes.
93236.m: A berry comb makes picking bilberries faster.

93237.q: When are wild bilberries ripe here?
93237.e: Wild bilberries ripen in about July and August. In the mountains, a little later.
93237.m: Wild bilberries are ripe in high summer.

93238.q: What colours can ripe gooseberries be?
93238.e: Depending on the variety, ripe gooseberries are green, yellow or red.
93238.m: Gooseberries can be green, yellow or red.

93239.q: What can you often see through the skin of a gooseberry?
93239.e: The skin of the gooseberry is almost see-through. You can see pale lines running from top to bottom.
93239.m: Gooseberries have fine stripes under the skin.

93240.q: Roughly how big is a gooseberry?
93240.e: Gooseberries are about the size of marbles. That makes them bigger than many other berries.
93240.m: A gooseberry is about the size of a marble.

93241.q: Which berry is the gooseberry closely related to?
93241.e: Both belong to the same plant genus. Their bushes and leaves look similar.
93241.m: Gooseberries and currants are close relatives.

93242.q: What do unripe gooseberries taste like?
93242.e: Unripe gooseberries are hard and sour. Ripe ones are softer and sweeter.

93243.q: What do some gooseberries have on their skin?
a: A layer of wax like candles
93243.e: In some varieties, the skin is covered with fine hairs. Other varieties are completely smooth.

93244.q: How do gooseberries hang on the bush?
93244.e: Gooseberries mostly hang one by one or in pairs on the twigs. They do not form long bunches.
93244.m: Gooseberries mostly hang one by one.

93245.q: What are gooseberries often used for in the kitchen?
93245.e: Gooseberries taste fresh and a little sour. That is why they go well in cakes and jam.
93245.m: Gooseberries are good for cakes and jam.

93246.q: What colour is a ripe quince?
93246.e: Ripe quinces are a bright golden yellow. Unripe ones are still green.

a: No, raw they are very hard
93247.e: Raw quinces are hard and tart. Only when cooked do they become soft and delicious.

93248.q: What is often made from quinces?
93248.e: Quinces contain a lot of pectin. That is why their juice sets nicely when cooked, making jelly.
93248.m: Quinces are often made into jelly.

93249.q: What does a quince have on its skin?
93249.e: The quince is covered with a soft fuzz. You rub it off with a cloth before cooking.
93249.m: Rub the fuzz off the quince before cooking.

93250.q: What are ripe quinces known for?
93250.e: Ripe quinces have a strong, lovely scent. A few quinces can make a whole room smell nice.

93251.q: Which two shapes of quince are there?
93251.e: Some quinces are round like an apple, others long like a pear. That is why they are called apple quinces and pear quinces.
93251.m: There are apple quinces and pear quinces.

93252.q: What are small sweet cubes made from cooked quinces called in Switzerland?
93252.e: For Quittenpästli, quince purée is cooked down thickly with sugar. Then it is cut into cubes and rolled in sugar.
93252.m: Quittenpästli are a sweet Swiss speciality.

93253.e: Quinces ripen late in the year, usually in October. They are picked before the first frost.

93254.e: There are pale green grapes and dark blue grapes. The dark ones often look almost black.
93254.m: Grapes are usually green or blue.

93255.e: Grapes are dried in the sun or in the oven. They become small, wrinkly and sweet.

93257.e: Varieties have been bred that have no pips or almost none. They are popular for eating.

93258.q: Where do people in Switzerland like to plant vines?
93258.e: Vines need lots of sun and warmth. On slopes they get an especially large amount of sunlight.
93258.m: Vines like to grow on sunny slopes.

93259.q: Which wine-growing area on Lake Geneva is a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
93259.e: In Lavaux, the vineyard terraces rise steeply from Lake Geneva. They have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007.
93259.m: The Lavaux vineyard terraces are World Heritage.

93260.q: Which juice is pressed from grapes?
93260.e: To make grape juice, fresh grapes are pressed. It is sweet and can be pale or dark.
93260.m: Grape juice is pressed from grapes.

93261.q: What is a single small fruit in a bunch of grapes called?
93261.e: A bunch of grapes is made of lots of single berries. They sit on small stalks.
93261.m: A bunch of grapes is made of lots of berries.

93263.q: What is the bottom part of a light bulb that you screw into the lamp called?
93263.e: At the bottom, a light bulb has a metal base with a thread. You screw it into the lamp's socket.
93263.m: You screw the base of the light bulb into the lamp.

93264.q: Which metal is the filament in a light bulb usually made of?
93264.e: Tungsten only melts at over 3400 degrees. That is why it can stand the great heat in a light bulb.
93264.m: The filament is usually made of tungsten.

93265.q: Why should you not touch a light bulb that is switched on?
93265.e: A light bulb gives off a lot of heat. You can burn your fingers on it.
93265.m: A light bulb that is on is hot.

93266.q: What does a light bulb turn most of its electricity into?
93266.e: Only a small part of the electricity becomes light, and most of it becomes heat. That is why it uses a lot of energy.
93266.m: A light bulb makes more heat than light.

93267.q: Which lamps mostly replace the old light bulbs today?
93267.e: LED lamps use much less electricity for the same amount of light. They also last much longer.

93268.q: What is the outer shell of a light bulb made of?
93268.e: The filament sits inside a glass shell. The glass lets the light through and protects the filament.
93268.m: The shell of a light bulb is made of glass.

93269.q: What did people use for light at home before there was electric light?
93269.e: In the past, people needed flames for light, for example candles, oil lamps or gas lamps. Electric light only came later.
93269.m: In the past, fire gave the light in the home.

93270.q: Where is the vegetable drawer in a fridge usually?
93270.e: The vegetable drawer is usually a drawer right at the bottom. It is not quite so cold there, and vegetables stay fresh.
93270.m: Vegetables go right at the bottom of the fridge.

93271.q: What is the very cold part where ice cream stays hard called?
93271.e: In the freezer it is about minus 18 degrees. Ice cream, peas and fish fingers freeze there.
93271.m: Ice cream belongs in the freezer.

93272.q: Why does food not go off so quickly in the fridge?
a: Germs grow more slowly in the cold
The light kills all the germs
The air in there is salty
The food is cooked in there
93272.e: Tiny living things such as bacteria multiply only slowly in the cold. That is why food goes off later.
93272.m: Cold slows down the germs in food.

93273.q: Where did people keep food cool in the past, before there were fridges?
a: At the window in the sun
93273.e: It is cool in the cellar even in summer. Some people also had an ice cellar with blocks of ice from the winter.
93273.m: In the past, the cellar was the fridge.

93274.q: What happens if you leave the fridge door open for a long time?
93274.e: With the door open, cold air flows out and warm air flows in. The fridge then has to use more electricity.
93274.m: You should close the fridge door quickly.

93275.q: What was used to cool food before there were electric fridges?
93275.e: In winter people sawed ice out of frozen lakes and stored it in ice cellars. With it they cooled food and drinks all year round.
93275.m: In the past, people cooled things with natural ice.

93276.q: Where does a fridge usually give off heat?
a: On the floor in front of it
93276.e: The fridge takes heat out of its inside. It usually gives it off into the kitchen through a grille at the back.
93276.m: A fridge gives off heat at the back.

93277.q: What should you not put into the fridge while it is hot?
a: A pan of freshly cooked soup
93277.e: Hot food warms up the fridge, and it then uses a lot of electricity. You let it cool down a little first.
93277.m: You let hot food cool down first.

93278.q: Where does the dust go in a vacuum cleaner?
93278.e: The dust is collected in a dust bag or a container. When it is full, you empty it or change it.
93278.m: The dust ends up in the dust bag.

93279.e: An electric motor turns a fan that sucks in the air. That is why a vacuum cleaner needs electricity.
93279.m: A motor makes the vacuum cleaner suck.

93280.q: What did people clean the floor with before the vacuum cleaner existed?
a: A broom and a carpet beater
93280.e: In the past, people swept the floor with a broom. Carpets were hung up outside and the dust was beaten out of them.
93280.m: In the past, people cleaned with a broom and a carpet beater.

93281.q: Which country did Hubert Cecil Booth, who built a large vacuum cleaner in 1901, come from?
93281.e: Hubert Cecil Booth was an English engineer. His first vacuum cleaner was so big that it was pulled through the streets by horses.
93281.m: An early vacuum cleaner came from England.

93283.q: What do you need to clear off the floor before you vacuum?
93283.e: Otherwise small things like Lego bricks would be sucked up. They can get stuck in the vacuum cleaner.
93283.m: Before vacuuming, you tidy away small things.

93284.q: Why does a vacuum cleaner have a filter?
a: So the dust does not blow out again
93284.e: The air goes back out of the vacuum cleaner. The filter holds back the fine dust as it does.
93284.m: The filter keeps the dust inside the vacuum cleaner.

93285.q: What is a small cordless vacuum cleaner that you hold in your hand called?
93285.e: A handheld vacuum cleaner has a rechargeable battery instead of a cable. You use it to quickly suck up crumbs from the table or in the car.
93285.m: A handheld vacuum cleaner has a rechargeable battery.

93286.q: What is the part of the washing machine that turns with the washing called?
93286.e: The washing lies in a drum. The drum turns and moves the washing about in the water.
93286.m: The washing turns in the drum.

93287.q: What do you put in the washing machine to get the washing clean?
93287.e: Washing powder loosens dirt and stains. Together with water and movement, the washing gets clean.
93287.m: Washing powder makes the washing clean.

93288.q: What does the washing machine do during the spin cycle?
a: It turns fast and forces the water out
93288.e: During the spin, the drum turns very fast. This squeezes a lot of water out of the washing.
93288.m: During the spin, the water is flung out.

93289.q: What did people use to wash clothes by hand in the past?
93289.e: People rubbed the wet washing with soap on a ridged washboard. It was hard work.
93289.m: In the past, people washed on a washboard.

93290.q: What is the shared room for washing in many Swiss blocks of flats called?
93290.e: In many Swiss blocks of flats, everyone shares a laundry room. A washing rota sets out who may wash when.
93290.m: Many Swiss buildings have a shared laundry room.

93291.q: Why do you sort the washing before washing it?
a: So colour does not run onto light clothes
93291.e: New red or dark clothes can lose colour. A white T-shirt can then turn pink.
93291.m: Light and dark washing are washed separately.

93292.q: Which machine dries the washing with warm air after it has been washed?
93292.e: In Switzerland a tumble dryer is often just called a “Tumbler”. It turns the wet washing in warm air.
93292.m: The tumble dryer dries the washing.

93293.q: What does a label with a number in a tub of water on a piece of clothing show?
a: How hot you may wash it
93293.e: The symbol with the tub shows the highest washing temperature in degrees. If it says 30, you wash at 30 degrees at most.
93293.m: The label shows the washing temperature.

93294.q: What do you do with a toaster?
93294.e: In the toaster, slices of bread get hot. They turn brown and crispy.

93295.q: What gets hot in the toaster so that the bread toasts?
93295.e: There are heating wires in the toaster. The electricity makes them so hot that they glow red.

93296.q: What is the toasted bread from the toaster called?
93296.e: Bread that has been toasted is called toast. The German language has borrowed this word from English.

93297.q: What happens if you leave the bread in the toaster for too long?
93297.e: The longer the bread toasts, the darker it gets. In the end it burns and tastes bitter.
93297.m: Bread toasted for too long burns.

93298.q: What does a modern toaster do when the bread is ready?
93298.e: A spring pushes the bread up as soon as the time is up. The American Charles Strite invented this pop-up toaster around 1919.
93298.m: The toaster pops up the finished bread.

93299.q: Why must you never poke around in a toaster with a fork?
a: You can get an electric shock
93299.e: There are live wires inside the toaster. A metal fork conducts electricity, and that is dangerous.
93299.m: Metal does not belong in a toaster.

93300.q: What is the dial on many toasters for?
a: It sets how brown the bread gets
It chooses the type of bread
93300.e: With the dial you set the toasting time. A higher setting makes the bread darker.
93300.m: The dial decides how brown the toast gets.

93301.q: What collects at the bottom of the toaster and should be emptied now and then?
93301.e: When you toast, crumbs fall to the bottom. Many toasters have a crumb tray for them.

93302.q: What do you need a zip for?
93302.e: A zip closes jackets, trousers and bags in one pull. That is quicker than lots of buttons.

93303.q: What are the small parts of a zip that fit into each other called?
93303.e: A zip has two rows of small teeth. When you close it, they fit into each other like fingers.
93303.m: The teeth fit into each other.

93304.q: What is the part of a zip that you pull up and down called?
93304.e: The slider brings the teeth together or pulls them apart. It often has a small tab for pulling.
93304.m: You pull the slider up and down.

93305.q: What does the slider do when you close a zip?
a: It presses the teeth of both sides into each other
It glues the two sides together
It sews the two sides together
93305.e: The small teeth on both sides hook into each other. The slider brings them together so that they hold firmly.
93305.m: The slider fits the teeth of the zip into each other.

93306.q: What can the teeth of a zip be made of?
93306.e: On jeans, the teeth are often made of metal. On sports jackets, they are often made of plastic.
93306.m: Zips are made of metal or plastic.

93307.q: What did clothes often have instead of a zip, before zips existed?
93307.e: In the past, clothes were almost always fastened with buttons or hooks. Velcro and magnetic fasteners were invented much later.
93307.m: In the past, clothes mostly had buttons.

93308.q: Which zip comes completely apart at the bottom?
a: The one on a pair of trousers
The one on a pencil case
93308.e: On a jacket you can open the zip completely. That way you can take the jacket off like a coat.
93308.m: A jacket zip can be opened completely.

93309.q: What helps when a zip gets stuck?
a: Rubbing a pencil over the teeth
93309.e: The graphite rubbed off the pencil lead works like a lubricant. Then the slider glides more easily.
93309.m: Pencil graphite makes a zip run smoothly.

93310.q: What stops you pricking yourself on a safety pin?
93310.e: The point of the pin sits in a small cap. That way you do not prick yourself.

93311.q: What did Walter Hunt bend the first safety pin out of in 1849?
93311.e: The American Walter Hunt bent the safety pin out of a single piece of wire and had it protected by a patent in 1849.
93311.m: A safety pin is made of a bent wire.

93312.q: What is a safety pin bent out of?
93312.e: A safety pin is a piece of wire. It is bent into a spring, a pin and a clasp.
93312.m: A safety pin is made of wire.

93313.q: What does a safety pin have at the bend so that it springs back?
93313.e: At the bend, the wire is wound into a round loop. This spring presses the pin into the cap.
93313.m: A loop of wire makes the pin springy.

93314.q: What is a safety pin often used for in sport?
a: To pin on your race number
93314.e: In a race you wear a number on your shirt. It is fastened with safety pins.
93314.m: Race numbers are pinned on with safety pins.

93315.q: What can you quickly fix with a safety pin?
a: Trousers with a button torn off
93315.e: If a button is missing, a safety pin holds the fabric together. It is a quick emergency fix.
93315.m: A safety pin is good for quick repairs.

93316.q: What were safety pins often used for with babies in the past?
93316.e: In the past, babies had nappies made of cloth. A large safety pin held them together without pricking the baby.
93316.m: In the past, cloth nappies were fastened with safety pins.

93317.q: Why is the safety pin called that?
a: Because its point is safely covered
Because it is made of gold
93317.e: On a normal pin the point is free. On a safety pin it is covered, so it is safer.
93317.m: The safety pin hides its point.

93318.q: What do you need a paper clip for?
a: To hold sheets of paper together
93318.e: A paper clip holds a few sheets of paper together. You can take it off again without damaging the paper.
93318.m: A paper clip holds sheets together.

93319.q: What is a simple paper clip made of?
93319.e: A paper clip is a piece of wire bent into loops. The wire is springy and clamps the paper tight.
93319.m: A paper clip is a bent wire.

93320.q: What is the advantage of a paper clip compared with a stapler?
a: The paper does not get holes
93320.e: A stapler pushes staples through the paper. A paper clip only clamps it and leaves no holes.
93320.m: A paper clip makes no holes in the paper.

93321.q: How many sheets does a small paper clip hold together well?
93321.e: A small paper clip only clamps a few sheets. For lots of sheets you need a large clip or a folder.
93321.m: A small paper clip holds a few sheets.

93322.q: What happens if you keep bending a paper clip open and shut?
93322.e: When wire is bent back and forth many times, it gets tired at that spot. At some point it breaks there.
93322.m: Wire that is bent too often breaks.

93323.q: What fun thing can you make with lots of paper clips?
93323.e: Paper clips can be hooked into each other. This makes a long chain.
93323.m: Paper clips can be joined into a chain.

93324.q: What attracts a steel paper clip?
93324.e: Many paper clips are made of steel. Steel contains iron, and iron is attracted by a magnet.
93324.m: A magnet attracts steel paper clips.

93325.q: Where are paper clips often kept?
93325.e: Paper clips are small and easily get lost. That is why they are kept in a small box or tin.
93325.m: Paper clips are kept in a box.

93326.q: Roughly how long should you brush your teeth for?
93326.e: In two to three minutes you can clean all your teeth well. An egg timer or a song helps you keep time.
93326.m: Brushing your teeth takes about two to three minutes.

93327.q: After roughly how many months should you change your toothbrush?
93327.e: Over time the bristles get bent and clean less well. That is why you take a new one about every three months.
93327.m: You need a new toothbrush about every three months.

93328.q: What are the many fine hairs on a toothbrush called?
93328.e: The bristles rub the plaque off the teeth. Today they are mostly made of nylon, a type of plastic.
93328.m: The hairs of a toothbrush are called bristles.

93329.q: In which country were there toothbrushes with bristles more than 1000 years ago?
93329.e: In China, more than 1000 years ago, there were already brushes with a handle made of bamboo or bone. They are thought of as early toothbrushes.
93329.m: There was an early toothbrush in China.

93330.q: What were the bristles often made of in the past?
93330.e: In the past, people used stiff hairs from pigs. Nylon bristles have existed since about 1938.
93330.m: Toothbrushes used to be made with animal hair.

93331.q: What do you put on your toothbrush?
93331.e: Toothpaste helps with cleaning. It often contains fluoride, which strengthens the teeth.

93332.q: What does an electric toothbrush do by itself?
93332.e: A small motor turns or shakes the brush head. You just guide it from tooth to tooth.
93332.m: An electric toothbrush moves by itself.

93333.q: What is the lead of a pencil made of?
93333.e: Despite its name, there is no lead in a pencil. The lead is made of graphite and clay.
93333.m: There is no real lead in a pencil.

93334.q: What is the outer case of a wooden pencil usually made of?
93334.e: The lead sits in a case made of wood, often cedar. The wood is easy to sharpen.
93334.m: A pencil has a wooden case.

93335.q: What does HB on a pencil mean?
93335.e: H stands for hard and B for black, which means soft. An HB pencil lies right in between.
93335.m: HB stands for a medium hard pencil.

93336.q: What is the advantage of a pencil compared with a ballpoint pen?
a: You can rub out what you write
It writes in lots of colours
93336.e: Graphite only sits loosely on the paper. That is why you can remove it again with a rubber.
93336.m: Pencil writing can be rubbed out.

93337.q: What is the lead of a modern pencil made of?
93337.e: Despite its name, a pencil contains no lead. The lead is made of graphite mixed with clay. People used to think graphite was a kind of lead ore.
93337.m: Pencil leads are made of graphite and clay, not lead.

93338.q: What shape is a pencil often, so that it does not roll off the table?
93338.e: Many pencils have six edges. That way they do not roll away so easily and sit well in your hand.
93338.m: A hexagonal pencil does not roll away so easily.

93339.e: A rubber rubs the bits of graphite off the paper. That is how pencil marks disappear.
93339.m: A rubber gets rid of pencil marks.

93340.q: What were the first rubbers made from?
93340.e: The sap of the rubber tree turns into rubber. Around 1770, people noticed that it could rub out pencil.
93340.m: The first rubbers were made of tree sap.

93341.q: What did people use to rub out pencil before there were rubbers?
93341.e: In the past, people rubbed out pencil marks with soft bread. It worked, but it was crumbly.
93341.m: In the past, people rubbed things out with bread.

93342.q: What is left lying on the paper after rubbing out?
93342.e: When you rub, some rubber comes off. It rolls up with the graphite into small crumbs.

93343.q: Where is there a small rubber on some pencils?
a: In the middle of the wood
93343.e: Many pencils have a rubber at the end in a metal sleeve. This was already patented in 1858.
93343.m: Some pencils have a rubber at the top.

93344.q: Why can a normal rubber hardly remove ballpoint pen?
a: The ink soaks into the paper
93344.e: Ballpoint ink soaks into the paper fibres. Pencil, on the other hand, only stays on top of the paper.
93344.m: Ballpoint ink can hardly be rubbed out.

93345.q: What are most rubbers made of today?
93345.e: Today many rubbers are made of plastic such as vinyl. They rub out cleanly and smudge very little.
93345.m: Modern rubbers are made of plastic.

93346.q: Where does the word “erase” come from?
a: From a Latin word for scratching
From an English word for red
From a French word for bread
From an Italian word for rubber
93346.e: “Erase” comes from Latin and goes back to the word “radere”, which means to scratch or scrape. In the past, people scratched mistakes away with a knife.

93347.e: Tesa film is a thin, see-through tape with glue on one side. You use it to stick paper.
93347.m: Tesa film is a see-through sticky tape.

93348.q: On how many sides does normal sticky tape stick?
93348.e: Normal sticky tape only sticks on one side. But there is also double-sided tape.
93348.m: Normal sticky tape only sticks on one side.

93349.q: How is sticky tape usually stored?
93349.e: The tape is wound round a core. You pull off a piece and tear or cut it off.
93349.m: Sticky tape is wound onto a roll.

93350.q: What is sharp on a sticky tape dispenser?
93350.e: The dispenser has a jagged edge made of metal or plastic. You tear the tape off against it.
93350.m: You tear the tape off on the dispenser.

93351.q: In which German city did the company Beiersdorf bring out Tesa film in the 1930s?
93351.e: The company Beiersdorf from Hamburg brought out the see-through Tesa film in the 1930s. Later the name was used for many kinds of sticky tape.

93352.q: What do you often use to close wrapping paper when wrapping a present?
93352.e: A few strips of sticky tape hold the wrapping paper together. That way the present stays well wrapped.
93352.m: You stick wrapping paper down with sticky tape.

93353.q: What is sticky tape good for?
a: Mending a torn sheet of paper
93353.e: A tear in paper can be closed with a strip of sticky tape. Then the sheet holds together again.
93353.m: You mend paper with sticky tape.

93354.q: What is a wide brown tape for sealing cardboard boxes called?
93354.e: Parcel tape is wide and strong. You use it to seal boxes for a house move or for the post.
93354.m: Boxes are sealed with parcel tape.

93355.q: What often happens when you pull sticky tape off a poster on the wall?
a: A bit of paint or paper tears off with it
93355.e: The glue holds tight to the surface. When you pull it off, it can tear paint off the wall or paper with it.
93355.m: Sticky tape can tear things off when you pull it away.

93356.q: What is the part of the ear you can see on the outside of your head called?
93356.e: The outer ear is the part of the ear you can see. All the other parts are hidden inside the head.
93356.m: You can see the outer ear on the outside of your head.

93357.q: What is the outer ear for?
93357.e: The outer ear is shaped like a funnel. It collects sounds and guides them into the ear.
93357.m: The outer ear collects sounds like a funnel.

93358.q: What do people often do with their hand to hear better?
a: Hold it in front of the eyes
93358.e: A cupped hand behind the ear makes the outer ear bigger. That way it catches more sound.
93358.m: A hand behind the ear helps you hear.

93359.q: What is the soft lower part of the outer ear called?
93359.e: The earlobe has no cartilage, so it is soft. Many people wear earrings there.

93360.q: What makes the outer ear firm but bendy?
93360.e: There is cartilage in the outer ear. It is firmer than skin, but you can bend it.
93360.m: Cartilage makes the outer ear bendy.

93361.q: Which animal can turn its ears in different directions?
93361.e: Cats have lots of muscles in their ears. They turn their ears towards a sound.
93361.m: A cat can turn its ears.

93362.q: How many ears does a person have?
93362.e: People have one ear on each side of the head. With two ears you can tell better where a sound comes from.
93362.m: With two ears you can hear where a sound comes from.

93363.q: Which animal has especially big ears that it also uses to cool down?
93363.e: African elephants have huge ears. By flapping their ears they cool their blood.
93363.m: Elephants cool down with their ears.

93364.q: Which animals have no outer ears, only hidden ear openings on the head?
93364.e: Birds have no outer ears. Their ear openings are on the sides of the head under the feathers.

93365.q: Can a small hole in the eardrum heal again?
a: Yes, it often heals by itself
Only with a plaster on the outside
Only if you drink lots of milk
93365.e: The eardrum can often close small tears by itself within a few weeks. Even so, a doctor should look at the ear.
93365.m: A small hole in the eardrum often heals by itself.

93366.q: Why is the eardrum called that?
a: It vibrates like the skin of a drum
It is made of animal skin
It is round like a ball
93366.e: A drum has a tight skin stretched over the top. The eardrum is stretched in a similar way and vibrates.
93366.m: The eardrum is stretched like the skin of a drum.

93367.q: What can a very loud bang do to the eardrum?
93367.e: A very strong bang can injure the eardrum. It can get a small hole.
93367.m: A strong bang can injure the eardrum.

93368.q: What are the three tiny bones behind the eardrum called?
93368.e: The three ear bones are named after tools. They pass the vibrations of the eardrum further inside.
93368.m: Behind the eardrum are the hammer, anvil and stirrup.

93369.q: What should you never do right next to another child's ear?
93369.e: A loud shout right next to the ear is very strong. It can hurt and damage the ear.
93369.m: Never shout right into someone's ear.

a: At the end of the ear canal
On the outside of the outer ear
93370.e: The eardrum separates the ear canal from the middle ear. You cannot see it from the outside.
93370.m: The eardrum separates the ear canal from the middle ear.

93371.q: What do you often feel in your ears when a plane is landing?
93371.e: When landing, the air pressure changes. This presses on the eardrum until the pressure evens out again.
93371.m: On a plane your ears often feel pressure.

93372.q: What helps against the pressure in your ears on a plane?
93372.e: When you swallow and chew, a little air flows into the middle ear. That evens out the pressure.
93372.m: Swallowing evens out the pressure in your ears.

93373.q: What is an ear doctor more exactly called?
93373.e: The ears, nose and throat are connected inside. That is why an ear, nose and throat doctor looks after all three.
93373.m: For your ears you go to an ear, nose and throat doctor.

93374.q: What is the yellowish, sticky stuff in the ear canal called?
93374.e: A waxy substance forms in the ear canal. It is called earwax.
93374.m: Earwax forms in the ear canal.

a: It protects the ear from dirt
93375.e: Earwax traps dust and tiny particles. It also keeps the skin in the ear canal soft.

93376.q: Why should you not push cotton buds deep into your ear?
a: They push the earwax further in
93376.e: A cotton bud pushes earwax inwards. It can form a plug or injure the ear.
93376.m: Cotton buds do not belong deep in the ear.

93377.q: How does earwax normally get out of the ear?
a: You have to scrape it out every day
93377.e: The ear cleans itself. The earwax slowly moves to the opening of the ear canal.

93378.q: What is the right way to clean your ears?
a: Poke a pencil into the ear
93378.e: It is enough to clean the outer ear and the entrance of the ear with a flannel. Deep inside the ear needs no cleaning.
93378.m: You only wash the outside part of the ear.

93379.q: What can happen if too much earwax blocks the ear?
93379.e: A plug of earwax can block the ear canal. Then sounds reach the eardrum less well.
93379.m: Too much earwax can muffle your hearing.

93380.q: Who is best at removing a hard plug of earwax?
93380.e: A doctor can remove the plug safely with water or small instruments. That way the ear is not injured.
93380.m: A doctor removes a plug of earwax.

93381.q: What can the doctor put into the ear to make hard earwax soft?
93381.e: Ear drops soften hard earwax. Afterwards it can come out more easily or be rinsed out.
93381.m: Ear drops make hard earwax soft.

93382.e: A jet plane taking off is extremely loud close up. That can damage your ears.
93382.m: A plane taking off is very loud.

93383.e: Rustling leaves are a very quiet sound. The other sounds are much louder.
93383.m: Rustling leaves are a quiet sound.

93384.q: What can music that is too loud in headphones do over time?
93384.e: Very loud sounds can destroy the tiny hearing cells in the inner ear. They do not grow back.
93384.m: Music that is too loud harms your ears.

93385.q: What can you sometimes hear in your ear after a very loud concert?
93385.e: After a lot of noise, your ear sometimes rings or hisses. That is a warning sign that it was too loud.
93385.m: Ringing in the ear warns of too much noise.

93386.q: What is the part of the inner ear that looks like a snail shell called?
93386.e: The cochlea is coiled like a snail shell. Inside it are the hearing cells that report sounds to the brain.
93386.m: The hearing cells sit in the cochlea.

93387.q: Where does a person notice what they hear?
93387.e: The ears pick up the sounds. Only the brain understands what you hear, for example a word or a song.
93387.m: The brain understands what the ears hear.

93388.q: Which symbol is often used for the volume on a mobile phone?
93388.e: A small loudspeaker symbol shows the volume. With the buttons you make it louder or quieter.
93388.m: The loudspeaker symbol stands for the volume.

93389.q: Who often wears ear protection at work?
93389.e: A pneumatic drill is very loud. Ear protection keeps the ears from being damaged.
93389.m: For loud work you wear ear protection.

93390.q: When should children wear ear protection?
93390.e: Fireworks bang very loudly, for example on 1 August. Children's ears are especially sensitive.
93390.m: At fireworks you protect children's ears.

93391.e: Ear protection muffles sound before it reaches the ear. So less noise gets in.

93392.q: During which hobby do many people in Switzerland wear ear protection?
93392.e: A shot is a very loud bang. That is why shooters at the shooting range wear ear protection.
93392.m: When shooting, you protect your ears.

93393.q: What is good for your ears at a loud party if you have no ear protection?
a: Going to a quiet place now and then
Standing right next to the speakers
Turning the music up even louder
93393.e: Breaks in a quiet place let your ears recover. That way they are under less strain.
93393.m: Breaks from noise are good for your ears.

93394.q: Apart from ear protection, what else is good for your ears in a loud place?
93394.e: The further you are from the source of the noise, the quieter it gets. That is why you do not stand right in front of the speakers.
93394.m: Distance from the noise protects your ears.

93395.q: Which animal has no ear protection but hears fireworks especially well and is often frightened?
93395.e: Dogs hear much better than people. That is why the bangs of fireworks often scare them a lot.
93395.m: Dogs are often frightened by fireworks.

93396.q: What does a hearing aid do?
93396.e: A hearing aid picks up sounds and plays them louder into the ear. That way people who are hard of hearing hear better.
93396.m: A hearing aid makes sounds louder.

93397.q: Where do you wear a hearing aid?
93397.e: Many hearing aids sit behind the ear. Others are so small that they fit in the ear canal.
93397.m: You wear a hearing aid on or in the ear.

93398.q: What does a hearing aid need to work?
93398.e: A hearing aid is a small electrical device. It needs power from a battery or a rechargeable battery.
93398.m: A hearing aid runs on power from a battery.

93399.q: Which part of a hearing aid picks up the sounds?
93399.e: A tiny microphone catches the sounds. The device makes them louder and passes them on through a small loudspeaker.
93399.m: A microphone in the hearing aid catches the sounds.

93400.q: Who often needs a hearing aid?
a: People who do not hear well
People who do not see well
93400.e: People who are hard of hearing find it difficult to follow conversations. A hearing aid helps them.
93400.m: People who are hard of hearing often wear a hearing aid.

93401.q: What did people use before there were electric hearing aids?
93401.e: An ear trumpet is a funnel that you hold to your ear. It collects sound and guides it into the ear.
93401.m: In the past, an ear trumpet helped people hear.

93402.q: What should you not do with a hearing aid?
a: Take it out in the evening
93402.e: Most hearing aids are electrical devices and cannot take much water. That is why you take them out to shower.
93402.m: You take the hearing aid out before showering.

93403.q: Which specialist fits a hearing aid?
93403.e: Audiologists test your hearing and set up the hearing aid to suit you. That way you hear well with it.
93403.m: An audiologist sets up the hearing aid.

93404.q: Where in Switzerland do you often hear an echo?
93404.e: If you shout towards a rock face, the shout comes back. That is why there is often an echo in the Alps.
93404.m: In the mountains you often hear an echo.

93405.q: What is needed for an echo to happen?
93405.e: The sound has to bounce off something hard, for example rock. The wall must be far enough away for you to hear the shout separately.
93405.m: An echo needs a hard, distant wall.

93406.q: Which animal finds its way in the dark using echoes?
93406.e: Bats make very high sounds. From the echoes they can tell where obstacles and insects are.
93406.m: Bats find their way using echoes.

93407.q: Why do you hear the echo a little later than your own shout?
a: The sound needs time to travel
The wall only calls back later
93407.e: Sound is fast, but not endlessly fast. It needs time to reach the wall and come back.
93407.m: Sound needs time to travel to the wall.

93408.q: When does an echo come back to you faster?
a: When the rock face is closer
When the rock face is further away
When you shout in a deeper voice
93408.e: The sound has to travel to the wall and back. If the wall is close, the path is short and the echo comes back faster.
93408.m: The closer the wall, the faster the echo comes back.

93409.q: Which sea animal also uses echoes to find its way?
93409.e: Dolphins make clicking sounds. The echoes show them where fish and rocks are.
93409.m: Dolphins find their way with echoes.

93410.q: Where indoors do you often hear sound ringing out like an echo?
a: In a room full of cushions
93410.e: In an empty hall, sound bounces off the hard walls. Soft things would swallow the sound.

93411.q: What do you do when you whisper?
93411.e: When you whisper, you speak without your voice, only with your breath. That is why it is very quiet.

93412.q: Where do people often whisper so as not to disturb others?
93412.e: In a library, people want to read in peace. That is why you speak quietly there.

93413.q: What is the game called where a word is whispered from ear to ear?
93413.e: In Telephone, each child whispers the word into the next child's ear. At the end, something completely different often comes out.

93414.q: What does not vibrate when you whisper, unlike when you speak normally?
93414.e: When you speak normally, the vocal cords in your throat vibrate. When you whisper they stay still, and only the air rushes.
93414.m: When you whisper, the vocal cords do not vibrate.

93415.q: What do you often hold in front of your mouth when you whisper a secret to someone?
93415.e: With your hand next to your mouth, you direct the whisper to the ear. That way the others see and hear less of it.
93415.m: When whispering to someone, you often hold your hand in front of your mouth.

93416.q: Why do you whisper something into someone's ear?
a: So that others do not hear it
So that the ear gets warm
93416.e: A secret is meant for only one person to hear. That is why you whisper it close to the ear.
93416.m: You whisper a secret into someone's ear.

93417.q: When do people often whisper at home?
a: When calling someone from far away
93417.e: A sleeping baby should not wake up. That is why people speak quietly.
93417.m: Next to a sleeping baby, you whisper.

93418.q: What helps if you want to hear someone whispering in a noisy room?
93418.e: Quiet sounds get even quieter with distance. Very close up, you understand a whisper better.
93418.m: You can only understand a whisper from close up.

93419.q: What is a common cause of earache in children?
93419.e: In children, the middle ear often gets inflamed. That hurts and often comes after a cold.
93419.m: A middle ear infection often causes earache.

93420.q: After which illness do children often get earache?
93420.e: With a cold, germs can travel from the nose to the ear. Then the ear gets inflamed.
93420.m: After a cold, the ears often hurt.

93421.q: What should you do if your ear hurts a lot or you also have a fever?
a: Push a cotton bud deep inside
93421.e: Bad earache with a fever should be looked at by a doctor. They can find out what is wrong.
93421.m: With bad earache you go to the doctor.

93422.q: What does the doctor use to look into the ear?
a: A small light with a funnel
93422.e: The instrument is called an otoscope. It has a light and a small funnel so you can see as far as the eardrum.
93422.m: You look into the ear with an otoscope.

93423.q: What can often cause earache after swimming?
a: Water that stays in the ear canal
93423.e: If water stays in the ear canal for a long time, the skin gets soft. Then germs can cause an infection.
93423.m: Water in the ear can lead to an infection.

93424.q: What protects your ears in a cold wind?
93424.e: A cold wind can make your ears hurt. A hat or a headband keeps your ears warm.
93424.m: A hat protects your ears from the cold.

93425.q: What do you do if your ear hurts?
a: Pour cold water into your ear
93425.e: Sharp things can injure the ear canal or the eardrum. If it hurts, leave your ear alone and tell a grown-up who will take you to the doctor.
93425.m: Sharp objects never belong in the ear.

93426.q: What helps if your ears feel pressure when travelling up a mountain?
a: Holding your breath for a long time
93426.e: A thin tube connects the ear with the throat. When you swallow or yawn it opens, the air pressure evens out and the pressure stops.
93426.m: Swallowing helps when your ears feel pressure.

93427.q: What do you use to speak in sign language?
93427.e: In sign language you show words with your hands, face and body. You see the language instead of hearing it.
93427.m: Sign language is spoken with the hands and face.

93428.e: Deaf people cannot hear spoken language. With sign language they can talk with each other easily.
93428.m: Deaf people often use sign language.

93429.q: How many sign languages are there in Switzerland?
93429.e: In Switzerland there is a Swiss German, a French and an Italian sign language. They belong to the language regions.
93429.m: There are three sign languages in Switzerland.

93430.q: Is there only one sign language in the whole world?
93430.e: Just like spoken languages, there are many different sign languages. Each country usually has its own.
