94006.e: NP stands for nondeterministic polynomial. Equivalently: for every yes instance there is a certificate that can be checked efficiently.
94006.m: For NP problems, a solution can be checked quickly.

94007.q: What prize money has the Clay Mathematics Institute offered for solving the P versus NP problem?
94007.e: The P versus NP problem is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems chosen by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000. A million dollars is offered for each.
94007.m: P versus NP is a Millennium Problem with a million dollars in prize money.

94008.q: Which inclusion between P and NP has been proved?
a: P is a subset of NP
NP is a subset of P
P and NP do not overlap
94008.e: What you can solve efficiently you can also check efficiently: you simply solve it again. The only open question is whether the inclusion is strict.
94008.m: Every problem in P is also in NP.

94009.q: Which problem was provably placed in P in 2002 by the AKS algorithm?
94009.e: Agrawal, Kayal and Saxena found a deterministic polynomial-time test of whether a number is prime. Breaking a number down into prime factors, by contrast, is still not known to be efficient.
94009.m: Since the AKS algorithm, prime tests are provably in P.

94010.q: What would be a far-reaching consequence if P equalled NP and a fast algorithm were found in practice?
a: Many of today's encryption methods would be unsafe
Computers would no longer need electricity
The halting problem would be solvable
All programs would be free of errors
94010.e: Finding a secret key is often an NP problem, because a candidate can be checked quickly. An efficient algorithm for NP would make such methods open to attack.
94010.m: P equals NP could lead to attacks on many encryption methods.

94011.q: What does the N in the complexity class NP stand for?
94011.e: NP means “nondeterministic polynomial”. It does not mean “not polynomial”, because all problems in P are also in NP.

94012.q: What do most experts suspect about the P versus NP problem?
a: P is not equal to NP
94012.e: In surveys of researchers, a large majority believe P is not equal to NP. But this has still not been proved (as of 2026).
94012.m: Most experts suspect that P is not equal to NP.

94013.q: Which problem was the first to be proved NP-complete, in 1971?
94013.e: Stephen Cook proved in 1971 that SAT is NP-complete, and Leonid Levin did something similar independently. The result is called the Cook-Levin theorem.
94013.m: SAT was the first problem proved to be NP-complete.

94014.q: Which two conditions must an NP-complete problem meet?
a: It is in NP and every NP problem can be reduced to it in polynomial time
It is in P and undecidable
It has exponential running time and is not in NP
94014.e: NP-hard means that every NP problem can be reduced to it in polynomial time. If it also belongs to NP, the problem is NP-complete.
94014.m: An NP-complete problem is in NP and NP-hard at the same time.

94015.q: What do people often do in practice when a problem is NP-complete?
a: Use approximation methods to find a good, but not necessarily the best, solution
Solve it with a simple formula
94015.e: With large inputs, the best solution usually cannot be found in a reasonable time. Heuristics quickly give very good solutions, for example in route planning.
94015.m: For NP-complete problems, good approximate solutions often help.

94016.q: Which of these problems is NP-complete in its general form?
a: Solving a generalised sudoku of any size
Finding the largest number in a list
Finding the shortest route between two places
94016.e: For sudokus with n² by n² cells, no efficient way of solving them is known; the problem is NP-complete. Sorting, maximum and shortest routes, by contrast, can be calculated quickly.

94017.q: What would follow if a polynomial-time algorithm were found for a single NP-complete problem?
a: Only this problem would be in P
The halting problem would be solvable
94017.e: Every NP problem can be reduced in polynomial time to an NP-complete problem. So a fast algorithm for it would solve all NP problems quickly.
94017.m: A fast algorithm for one NP-complete problem would prove P equals NP.

94018.q: How does the effort of the best known algorithms for NP-complete problems grow with input size in the worst case?
94018.e: No algorithm with polynomial running time is known for any NP-complete problem. Even a few extra elements can multiply the effort.
94018.m: For NP-complete problems, only exponentially growing algorithms are known.

94019.q: What is the knapsack problem about?
a: Choosing items with the greatest total value without going over a weight limit
Building a knapsack as light as possible
Finding the shortest route with luggage
94019.e: Each item has a weight and a value. Finding the best selection is NP-complete as a decision problem.
94019.m: In the knapsack problem you look for the most valuable selection under a weight limit.

94020.q: Which decision problem on graphs is NP-complete?
a: Is there a cycle that visits every node exactly once?
Is there a path between two nodes?
Can the graph be coloured with two colours?
Is there a cycle that uses every edge exactly once?
94020.e: The Hamiltonian cycle problem is NP-complete. Reachability, two-colourability and Eulerian cycles, by contrast, can be decided in polynomial time.
94020.m: The Hamiltonian cycle problem is NP-complete, the Eulerian cycle problem is not.

94021.q: What form do all rules of a context-free grammar have?
a: Exactly one nonterminal on the left
Exactly two terminals on the left
Exactly one terminal on the right
94021.e: A rule A becomes α may be applied no matter what is to the left and right of A. Hence the name context-free.
94021.m: In context-free rules there is exactly one nonterminal on the left.

94022.q: Which language does the grammar with the rules S becomes aSb or ε generate?
a: a to the n, b to the n, with n at least 0
All words made of a and b
a to the n, b to the m, with any n and m
94022.e: Each use of aSb adds an a on the left and a b on the right. At the end S is replaced by the empty word, which gives a to the n, b to the n.
94022.m: The rule S becomes aSb produces as many a as b.

94023.q: What can a context-free grammar describe that a regular expression cannot?
a: Correctly nested brackets of any depth
All words made of lower-case letters
94023.e: For brackets of any depth, you have to keep count of how many are still open. This works with rules such as S becomes (S)S, but not with a finite number of states.

94024.q: What is a nonterminal in a grammar?
a: A helper symbol that is still replaced by rules
A symbol that appears in the finished word
A rule without a right-hand side
The last symbol of a word
94024.e: Nonterminals such as S are replaced during the derivation until only terminals are left. The terminals form the finished word.
94024.m: Nonterminals are replaced; terminals stay in the word.

94025.q: A grammar has the rules S becomes aSb or ab. Which word can it generate?
94025.e: Using aSb twice and then ab gives aaabbb. The grammar always produces as many a as b, and all the a come before all the b.
94025.m: The rule aSb creates as many a as b.

94026.q: What does a compiler need the grammar of a programming language for?
a: To check whether the code is built correctly
To predict runtime errors for certain
To check the spelling of comments
94026.e: Using the grammar, the compiler's parser checks whether the source code is syntactically correct and builds a syntax tree from it.
94026.m: With the grammar, the compiler checks the syntax of a program.

94027.q: When is a context-free grammar called ambiguous?
a: When a word has two different syntax trees
When it has two start symbols
When it generates infinitely many words
94027.e: A well-known example is the “dangling else”, where it is unclear which if an else belongs to. For compilers, such ambiguities are resolved with extra rules.
94027.m: An ambiguous grammar allows several syntax trees for one word.

94028.q: With which notation was the syntax of ALGOL 60 described by a context-free grammar in 1960?
94028.e: John Backus and Peter Naur used this notation for the ALGOL 60 report. Variants of it still describe the syntax of many programming languages today.
94028.m: Backus-Naur form describes programming languages with context-free rules.

94029.q: Who developed the lambda calculus in the 1930s?
94029.e: Alonzo Church created the lambda calculus as a formal system for functions and how they are applied. It is seen as the basis of functional programming.
94029.m: The lambda calculus comes from Alonzo Church.

94030.q: What does the expression (lambda x: x * 2)(5) give in Python?
94030.e: lambda x: x * 2 is a nameless function that doubles its argument. Here it is called directly with 5. Such lambda expressions go back to the lambda calculus.
94030.m: A lambda expression is a function without a name.

94031.q: Which programming style is mainly based on the lambda calculus?
94031.e: In the lambda calculus, everything consists of functions applied to arguments. Languages such as Haskell, Lisp or F# build on this idea.
94031.m: The lambda calculus is the basis of functional programming.

94032.q: What do expressions in the pure lambda calculus consist of?
a: Only variables, functions and function calls
94032.e: The pure lambda calculus has no built-in numbers. Even numbers and truth values are represented as functions.
94032.m: In the lambda calculus, everything is a function.

94033.q: With which other model of computation is the lambda calculus equally powerful?
94033.e: In 1936/37 Alonzo Church and Alan Turing showed that both models can compute exactly the same functions. The Church-Turing thesis is based on this.
94033.m: The lambda calculus and the Turing machine can compute the same things.

94034.q: What does the lambda function λx.x do?
94034.e: λx.x takes an x and gives back exactly this x. It is called the identity function.

94035.q: Which programming language from 1958 was directly influenced by the lambda calculus?
94035.e: John McCarthy developed Lisp at MIT and took over the keyword LAMBDA for anonymous functions. Lisp is considered one of the first functional languages.
94035.m: Lisp took ideas from the lambda calculus.

94036.q: In which language do you write a nameless function as, for example, x => x + 1?
94036.e: Arrow functions in JavaScript are lambda expressions. Python, Java and C# also have such nameless functions.
94036.m: Many modern languages have lambda expressions.

94037.q: What does the Church-Turing thesis state?
a: Everything intuitively computable can be computed by a Turing machine
Turing machines are faster than computers
94037.e: The thesis equates the intuitive idea of what is computable with the formal idea of Turing computability. All known models of computation have confirmed it so far.
94037.m: The Church-Turing thesis equates intuitive computability with Turing computability.

94038.q: Why can the Church-Turing thesis not be proved mathematically?
a: The term “intuitively computable” is not formally defined
Because Turing machines do not exist
Because Church and Turing contradicted each other
94038.e: A proof needs formally defined terms on both sides. But intuitive computability is exactly what the thesis sets out to formalise.
94038.m: The Church-Turing thesis is a working hypothesis that cannot be proved.

94039.q: Who, independently of Turing, developed an equally powerful model of computation with the lambda calculus?
94039.e: Alonzo Church presented the lambda calculus in the 1930s. In 1937 Turing showed that it can compute as much as Turing machines. That is why the thesis is named after both.
94039.m: Church and Turing independently found equally powerful models.

94040.q: Can quantum computers compute functions that Turing machines cannot compute?
a: No, they can only solve some problems faster
Yes, they solve the halting problem
Yes, they compute the busy beaver function
No, they cannot compute anything at all
94040.e: A quantum computer can be simulated on a Turing machine with exponential effort. At most, the extended thesis about efficient computation is called into question.
94040.m: Quantum computers are faster, but not more powerful, than Turing machines.

94041.q: What follows from the Church-Turing thesis for today's supercomputers?
a: They compute nothing that a Turing machine could not also compute
They are faster and therefore fundamentally more powerful
They can solve the halting problem
They no longer need a program
94041.e: Supercomputers are much faster, but not fundamentally more powerful than a Turing machine. What they compute, a Turing machine with enough time and tape could also compute.
94041.m: Faster computers are not more powerful than Turing machines.

94042.q: Which cellular game by John Conway has been proved Turing-complete?
94042.e: In the Game of Life, logic gates and memory can be built from patterns such as gliders. In principle, this lets you simulate any Turing machine.
94042.m: Conway's Game of Life is Turing-complete.

94043.q: What does the example of the very simple cellular automaton “Rule 110” show?
a: Even extremely simple rules can be Turing-complete
Simple rules always create simple patterns
94043.e: Rule 110 only sets how a cell decides its next state from itself and its two neighbours. Even so, Matthew Cook proved that it can simulate any Turing machine.
94043.m: Turing completeness does not need complicated rules.

94044.q: Is there a machine that has been built that can solve the halting problem in general?
a: No, such machines are purely hypothetical
Yes, but only with an internet connection
94044.e: Machines that could compute more than Turing machines are called hypercomputers. Whether they are physically possible is disputed, and none has been built. Quantum computers do not solve the halting problem either.
94044.m: No machine that has been built can solve the halting problem.

94045.q: Which herb is the main ingredient in green pesto?
94045.e: Green pesto is made from basil, pine nuts, cheese, garlic and olive oil. It comes from Italy.
94045.m: Green pesto is made from basil.

94046.q: Which vegetable is basil especially often eaten with?
94046.e: Basil goes very well with tomatoes. For example, people eat tomatoes with mozzarella and basil.

94047.q: Which country's cooking is hard to imagine without basil?
94047.e: In Italy basil goes into many dishes, for example pesto or tomato sauce.
94047.m: Basil is very popular in Italian cooking.

94048.q: What can basil not cope with at all?
94048.e: Basil is a plant from warm regions. Even a frost kills it.
94048.m: Basil likes warmth and cannot cope with frost.

94049.q: Basil is also called the “royal herb”. Where does this name come from?
94049.e: The name basil comes from the Greek word for royal. That is why it is also called the royal herb.
94049.m: Basil is also called the royal herb.

94050.q: Which country does basil probably originally come from?
94050.e: Basil probably comes from India and reached Europe through trade. It needs lots of warmth.

94051.q: Where does basil grow best in the garden or on the balcony?
a: In the water of the pond
94051.e: Basil needs lots of light and warmth. It is best in a sheltered spot in the sun.
94051.m: Basil needs a warm, sunny spot.

94052.q: Which pizza is traditionally topped with tomatoes, mozzarella and basil?
94052.e: Pizza Margherita has the colours red, white and green. The green comes from the basil.
94052.m: Basil belongs on a Pizza Margherita.

94053.q: Which part of basil do people usually eat?
94053.e: With basil, people mainly use the fresh green leaves. They pick them off the plant.
94053.m: We eat the leaves of basil.

94054.q: Which two kinds of parsley can you often buy?
94054.e: Curly parsley has crinkly leaves, flat-leaf parsley has flat leaves. Flat-leaf usually tastes stronger.
94054.m: There is curly and flat-leaf parsley.

94055.q: Which vegetable is parsley related to?
94055.e: Parsley and carrots belong to the same plant family, the carrot family (umbellifers). You can tell by the flowers.
94055.m: Parsley is related to the carrot.

94056.q: Which vitamin is found in especially large amounts in fresh parsley?
94056.e: Fresh parsley contains a lot of vitamin C. That is why it is especially healthy raw.
94056.m: Parsley contains lots of vitamin C.

94057.q: In which year does a parsley plant usually flower?
94057.e: Parsley is a biennial. In the first year it grows leaves, and in the second year it flowers.
94057.m: Parsley flowers in its second year.

94058.q: Which part of parsley is usually sprinkled over food?
94058.e: The fresh green leaves are finely chopped and sprinkled over soups, potatoes or salad.
94058.m: We usually eat the leaves of parsley.

94059.q: Which poisonous plant can be mistaken for flat-leaf parsley?
94059.e: Fool's parsley looks similar to flat-leaf parsley but is poisonous. That is why you should not just pick herbs in the wild.

94060.q: What are boiled potatoes sprinkled with chopped herbs called?
94060.e: Boiled potatoes with butter and chopped parsley are called parsley potatoes. They are a popular side dish.
94060.m: Parsley potatoes are sprinkled with parsley.

94061.q: Which region does parsley originally come from?
94061.e: Parsley comes from the area around the Mediterranean Sea. Today it grows in many gardens.

94062.q: What do the stalks of chives look like?
94062.e: Chives have thin, tube-shaped stalks. They are hollow inside.

94063.q: What is the right way to harvest chives?
a: Cut the stalks off above the ground
94063.e: You cut the stalks with scissors a few centimetres above the ground. New stalks then grow back.
94063.m: Cut chives off above the ground.

94064.e: The flowers are small balls in pink to purple. They look very pretty.
94064.m: Chives have pink to purple flowers.

94065.e: The flowers are edible and taste mildly of onion. You can use them to decorate a salad.

94067.q: What happens to the chives in the garden after the winter?
94067.e: Chives are perennial. In winter they die back and in spring they sprout again.

94068.q: Why are chives usually added to food only at the end?
a: They lose their flavour when cooked
94068.e: Chives taste best fresh. If you cook them, their flavour is lost.
94068.m: Chives go fresh on the finished food.

94069.q: Where do chives also grow wild in Switzerland?
94069.e: Wild chives grow in the Alps, for example in damp spots in mountain meadows.
94069.m: Chives grow wild in the Alps.

94070.q: Which popular drink is made from peppermint leaves?
94070.e: You pour hot water over the leaves. This makes peppermint tea, hot or cold.

94071.q: Which substance makes peppermint feel cool in your mouth?
94071.e: Peppermint contains menthol. It gives a cool, fresh feeling in your mouth.
94071.m: The menthol in peppermint has a cooling effect.

94072.q: What does toothpaste often taste of?
94072.e: Many toothpastes taste of mint. That gives you fresh breath.

94073.q: How does peppermint spread in the garden?
a: With long runners in the ground
It does not spread at all
94073.e: Peppermint forms long runners under the ground. This way it quickly grows in all directions.

94074.q: What does peppermint feel like in your mouth?
94074.e: Peppermint contains a substance that feels cool in your mouth. That is why peppermint tea and peppermint sweets taste so fresh.
94074.m: Peppermint feels fresh and cool in your mouth.

94075.q: What shape is the stem of peppermint?
94075.e: If you roll the stem between your fingers, you can feel four edges. That is typical of mints.
94075.m: The peppermint stem has four edges.

a: It tastes strong and a bit hot
It is red like chilli peppers
94076.e: Peppermint tastes strong and a little bit hot. That is why it got the name pepper.

94077.q: Which kind of soil does peppermint like best?
94077.e: Mints like to grow in damp places. In the garden you need to water them regularly.

94078.q: Which part of peppermint is used for tea?
94078.e: For tea you use the fresh or dried leaves. That is where the fresh flavour is.
94078.m: Peppermint tea is made from the leaves.

94079.e: Thyme has tiny leaves on thin twigs. You strip them off with your fingers.

94080.q: What happens to thyme stems as the plant gets older?
94080.e: Thyme is a small shrubby plant. At the bottom, its twigs become hard and woody over time.

94081.q: Which region does common thyme come from?
94081.e: Common thyme comes from the warm countries around the Mediterranean. There it grows on dry slopes.

94082.q: What is thyme tea often drunk for?
94082.e: Thyme is an old medicinal plant. Thyme tea is traditionally drunk for a cough.
94082.m: Thyme tea is often drunk for a cough.

94083.q: Which animals like to visit thyme flowers?
94083.e: Thyme has lots of small flowers full of nectar. Bees, bumblebees and butterflies love to fly there.

94084.q: What kind of spot does thyme like?
94084.e: Thyme loves lots of sun and dry soil. Too much water harms it.
94084.m: Thyme likes it sunny and dry.

94085.q: Which kind of thyme smells of a sour citrus fruit?
94085.e: Lemon thyme has a fresh lemony smell. People like to use it for fish or tea.

94086.q: Which food does thyme go well with?
94086.e: Thyme gives tomato sauce, meat and potatoes a strong flavour. It is a typical kitchen herb.
94086.m: Thyme goes well with savoury dishes.

94087.q: What colour are the flowers of common thyme usually?
94087.e: Thyme has lots of tiny flowers in pale purple, pink or white. They appear in early summer.
94087.m: Thyme usually has pale purple to pink flowers.

94088.q: What do rosemary leaves look like?
94088.e: Rosemary has narrow, leathery leaves. They look a bit like fir needles.

94089.q: Which region does rosemary come from?
94089.e: Rosemary grows wild on the coasts of the Mediterranean. It loves sun and warmth.

94090.q: What is often seasoned with rosemary before it goes in the oven?
94090.e: Roast potatoes with rosemary are very popular. The rosemary gives them a spicy smell.
94090.m: Rosemary goes well with roast potatoes.

94091.q: What happens to rosemary leaves in winter?
94091.e: Rosemary is evergreen. It keeps its leaves in winter too.

94092.q: What colour are rosemary flowers usually?
94092.e: Rosemary has small, usually light blue flowers. They appear as early as spring.
94092.m: Rosemary usually has light blue flowers.

94093.q: What does a rosemary plant in Switzerland often need in winter?
94093.e: Rosemary comes from warm countries. In hard frost you should protect it or keep it indoors somewhere bright and cool over winter.
94093.m: Rosemary must be protected from hard frost.

94094.q: What does the Latin name “ros marinus” mean?
94094.e: “Ros marinus” means dew of the sea. Rosemary often grows close to the sea.
94094.m: Rosemary means dew of the sea.

94095.q: What kind of plant is rosemary?
94095.e: Rosemary grows as a shrub with woody twigs. It can grow more than a metre tall.

94096.q: How much water does rosemary in a pot need?
a: It has to stand in water
94096.e: Rosemary comes from dry regions. Too much water makes its roots rot.

94097.q: What do the leaves of common sage feel like?
94097.e: Sage leaves have fine hairs. That is why they feel velvety and look grey-green.

94098.q: What is sage tea traditionally often used for?
a: For gargling when you have a sore throat
94098.e: Sage is an old medicinal plant. People traditionally gargle with sage tea when their throat is scratchy.
94098.m: Gargle with sage tea for a sore throat.

94099.q: What are sage leaves fried in batter called in Switzerland, because their stalk looks like a mouse's tail?
94099.e: For Müslichüechli, sage leaves are dipped in batter and fried in hot fat. The stalk looks like a mouse's tail.

94100.q: Which Italian meat dish is made with sage and cured ham?
94100.e: For saltimbocca, sage and cured ham are laid on a thin veal escalope. The name means “jump into the mouth”.

94101.q: The name sage comes from the Latin word “salvare”. What does it mean?
94101.e: “Salvare” means to heal or to save. Sage was known early on as a medicinal plant.

94102.q: Which plant family does sage belong to?
94102.e: Sage belongs to the mint family, also called the lipped flowers. Its flowers look like little open lips.
94102.m: Sage belongs to the mint family.

94103.q: What colour are the flowers of common sage usually?
94103.e: Common sage has bluish purple flowers in early summer. Lots of insects visit the flowers.
94103.m: Common sage has bluish purple flowers.

94104.q: With which sauce do people like to eat gnocchi together with sage?
94104.e: Sage leaves are fried in butter until it turns brown. This sage butter goes well with gnocchi or ravioli.
94104.m: Sage butter goes well with gnocchi.

94105.q: What do dill leaves look like?
94105.e: Dill has very fine, thread-like leaves. They look almost like feathers.
94105.m: Dill has leaves as fine as threads.

94107.q: Which food does dill go especially well with?
94107.e: Dill and fish go very well together. Salmon with dill, for example, is well known.

94108.e: Dill flowers in large, flat umbrella-like clusters with lots of small yellow flowers.

94109.q: Apart from the leaves, which part of dill is also used as a spice?
94109.e: Dill seeds are a spice. They are used, for example, in bread or pickled vegetables.
94109.m: Dill seeds are a spice too.

94110.q: How long does a dill plant live?
94110.e: Dill is an annual. You sow it again every year.
94110.m: Dill has to be sown again every year.

94111.q: In which part of Europe is dill especially popular in cooking?
94111.e: In Sweden, Norway and Finland, dill goes into many dishes. It is popular there with fish and potatoes.
94111.m: People eat a lot of dill in Scandinavia.

94112.q: When is the best time to add fresh dill to food?
a: Right at the start of cooking
94112.e: Fresh dill loses its flavour if it is cooked for a long time. That is why you sprinkle it over only at the end.
94112.m: Add fresh dill only at the end.

94113.q: What do the flowers of German chamomile look like?
94113.e: The flowers have white petals around a yellow centre. They look like little stars.
94113.m: Chamomile flowers are white with a yellow centre.

94114.q: What is chamomile tea traditionally often drunk for?
94114.e: Chamomile tea is an old home remedy. Many people traditionally drink it when they have a tummy ache.
94114.m: Chamomile tea is often drunk for a tummy ache.

94115.q: Which part of chamomile is used for tea?
94115.e: For chamomile tea you use the dried flower heads. That is where the typical scent is.

94116.q: How can you recognise German chamomile when you cut through the yellow centre?
94116.e: In German chamomile, the yellow flower base is hollow inside. In similar plants it is filled.
94116.m: German chamomile has a hollow flower centre.

94117.q: Where does German chamomile often grow wild?
94117.e: German chamomile likes to grow in fields and along the edges of paths. It likes sun.

94118.q: Which flower does chamomile look like?
94118.e: Chamomile and daisies both have white petals and a yellow centre. They belong to the same plant family.

94119.q: In which season does chamomile mainly flower?
94119.e: Chamomile mainly flowers from May into the summer. That is when people collect the flowers.

94120.q: What do people traditionally do with hot chamomile tea when they have a cold?
94120.e: You lean over a bowl of hot chamomile tea and breathe in the steam. This is called inhaling.
94120.m: With a cold, people inhale chamomile steam.

94121.q: What do the leaves of lemon balm smell of?
94121.e: When you rub the leaves, they smell fresh and lemony. That is why the plant has its name.

94122.q: The word “Melissa”, the scientific name of lemon balm, comes from Greek. What does it mean?
94122.e: In Greek, “mélissa” means honeybee. Bees love to fly to the flowers of this plant.
94122.m: Melissa is the Greek word for honeybee.

94123.q: When is lemon balm tea traditionally drunk?
a: In the morning to wake up
94123.e: Lemon balm tea has long been thought to be calming. That is why many people drink it in the evening.
94123.m: Lemon balm tea is popular in the evening.

94124.q: Which herb do lemon balm leaves look like?
94124.e: The leaves are egg-shaped with toothed edges, similar to mint. You can tell the difference by the smell.

94125.q: Is lemon balm related to the lemon tree?
a: No, only the smell is similar
Yes, it is a cutting of it
94125.e: Lemon balm is a herb from the mint family. It only happens to smell similar to lemons.
94125.m: Lemon balm is not related to the lemon.

94126.q: What happens to lemon balm in the garden after the winter?
94126.e: Lemon balm is perennial. The top dies back in winter and it grows again in spring.
94126.m: Lemon balm grows back every spring.

94127.q: What colour are the small flowers of lemon balm?
94127.e: Lemon balm has small white to pale pink flowers. They sit where the leaves grow from the stem.
94127.m: Lemon balm has small white flowers.

94128.q: What do people like to use fresh lemon balm for in summer?
94128.e: A few lemon balm leaves make water, iced tea or lemonade nice and fresh.
94128.m: Lemon balm goes well in cold drinks.

94129.q: What colour are lavender flowers usually?
94129.e: Lavender usually flowers purple to blue. That is why this colour is also called lavender.

94130.q: Which region of France has famous lavender fields?
94130.e: In Provence in the south of France, huge purple lavender fields bloom in summer.
94130.m: Provence is famous for its lavender.

94131.q: Why do people put little bags of lavender in the wardrobe?
94131.e: Moths do not like the smell of lavender. That is why people put lavender bags with their clothes.

94132.q: The name lavender may come from the Latin “lavare”. What does that mean?
94132.e: “Lavare” means to wash. People like to put lavender in bath water or in soap.

94133.q: What do lavender leaves look like?
94133.e: Lavender has narrow leaves with a grey sheen. Fine hairs protect them from the heat.

94134.q: Which insects like to collect nectar from lavender flowers?
94134.e: Lavender flowers have lots of sweet nectar. That is why lots of bees and bumblebees buzz around the plant.

94135.q: What is lavender oil made from?
94135.e: Lavender oil is made from the scented flowers. It is used, for example, in soap.
94135.m: Lavender oil comes from the flowers.

94136.q: What kind of spot does lavender like?
94136.e: Lavender needs lots of sun and fairly dry soil. It does not like wet feet.
94136.m: Lavender needs sun and dry soil.

94137.q: Which well-known dish do people often sprinkle oregano on?
94137.e: Oregano is a typical pizza herb. It goes well with tomatoes and cheese.
94137.m: Oregano is a typical pizza herb.

94138.q: What does oregano smell like when you rub a leaf between your fingers?
94138.e: Oregano has a strong, spicy smell. That is why it is used to season pizza and tomato sauce.

94139.q: Which other kitchen herb is oregano closely related to?
94139.e: Oregano and marjoram belong to the same genus. That is why they taste similar.

94140.q: How is oregano especially often used in cooking?
94140.e: Dried oregano has a very strong flavour. That is why it is often used dried.

94141.q: Where does oregano grow wild in Switzerland?
94141.e: Wild oregano grows on sunny slopes and in dry meadows. There it smells strongly in summer.
94141.m: Wild oregano grows in sunny meadows.

94142.q: What colour are oregano flowers usually?
94142.e: Oregano has small pink to pale purple flowers. Butterflies and bees like to visit them.

94143.q: Which sauce do people like to add oregano to?
94143.e: Oregano gives tomato sauce a spicy flavour. It goes into many Italian sauces.
94143.m: Oregano goes well in tomato sauce.

94144.q: How long does an oregano plant live?
94144.e: Oregano is perennial. It grows back every year from the same rootstock.

94145.e: The Swiss engineer Georges de Mestral developed the hook and loop fastener. He called his invention Velcro.

94146.q: Where did the burrs get caught after Georges de Mestral went for a walk?
94146.e: After walks, lots of burrs were stuck in his dog's fur. He wanted to know why they held on so well.
94146.m: The burrs were caught in his dog's fur.

94147.q: What did Georges de Mestral use to look very closely at the burrs?
94147.e: Under the microscope he saw how the burrs hold on to fur and fabric. That is how he got the idea.
94147.m: A microscope makes tiny things look big.

94148.q: What does one side of a Velcro strip have so that it holds?
94148.e: One side has lots of tiny, bendy hooks. They catch on the other side.
94148.m: Velcro holds with lots of tiny hooks.

94149.q: The name “Velcro” contains the French word “velours”. What does “velours” mean?
94149.e: “Velours” means velvet. The soft side of a Velcro strip is a bit like velvet.
94149.m: Velours is the French word for velvet.

94150.q: How did the Swiss Georges de Mestral get the idea for Velcro?
a: Small plant seed heads got caught in his dog's fur
He watched a spider building its web
He watched a woodpecker on a tree
He saw frost patterns on a window
94150.e: After a walk, burrs were stuck in his dog's fur. Under the microscope he saw tiny hooks and copied them. In 1951 he applied for a patent for Velcro.
94150.m: Velcro was copied from the burr.

94151.q: Why do many children's shoes have Velcro?
a: You can do them up quickly without laces
It makes them glow in the dark
94151.e: With Velcro you do not have to tie shoelaces. That is easier for small children.
94151.m: Velcro makes putting on shoes easy.

94152.q: What do astronauts in space need Velcro strips for?
a: So things do not float away
94152.e: In space everything floats around. With Velcro strips you can fix objects to walls or clothes.
94152.m: In space, Velcro strips hold things in place.

94153.q: What colour is the handle of a Swiss Army knife usually?
94153.e: Most everyday Swiss Army knives have a red handle. This makes them well known all over the world.
94153.m: The typical Swiss Army knife has a red handle.

94154.q: Which symbol can be seen on many Swiss Army knives?
94154.e: The white Swiss cross is often shown on the handle. It shows that the knife comes from Switzerland.
94154.m: The Swiss cross can be seen on many pocket knives.

94155.q: Who was the first Swiss Army knife made for?
94155.e: The Swiss Army wanted a practical knife for its soldiers. That is how the first soldier's knife came about in 1890.
94155.m: The first Swiss Army knife was a soldier's knife.

94156.q: Which well-known company grew out of Karl Elsener's knife workshop in Ibach?
94156.e: Karl Elsener made soldier's knives in Ibach from 1891. His workshop became the company Victorinox.
94156.m: Victorinox makes the Swiss Army knife.

94157.q: In which canton is Ibach, where pocket knives are still made today?
94157.e: Ibach is part of the municipality of Schwyz in the canton of Schwyz. Knives have been made there for over 130 years.
94157.m: Ibach is in the canton of Schwyz.

94158.q: The knife company Victorinox is named after Victoria. Who was Victoria?
94158.e: Victoria was the first name of Karl Elsener's mother. He named his brand after her.
94158.m: Victorinox is named after the founder's mother.

94159.q: What does “inox” mean in the name Victorinox?
94159.e: “Inox” is an international word for stainless steel. The blades are made of it.

94160.q: Which tool did the very first Swiss soldier's knife of 1890 already have?
94160.e: The first model had a blade, a tin opener, a screwdriver and an awl. A saw was only added much later.
94160.m: Even the first soldier's knife had a tin opener.

94161.q: Which tool on a pocket knife do you use to pull the cork out of a bottle?
94161.e: The corkscrew is a small spiral. You twist it into the cork and pull it out.
94161.m: You open bottles with corks using the corkscrew.

94162.q: Who invented milk chocolate in Switzerland?
94162.e: Daniel Peter mixed chocolate with milk. That is how Swiss milk chocolate came about.

94163.q: Which milk did Daniel Peter finally use for his chocolate?
94163.e: Fresh milk contains a lot of water, and that does not go well with chocolate. It worked with condensed milk.

94164.q: Which friend helped Daniel Peter with his first experiments with milk?
94164.e: Henri Nestlé was a friend of Daniel Peter. He helped him with his milk powder in the first experiments.
94164.m: Henri Nestlé helped Daniel Peter with his experiments.

94165.q: Which beans is chocolate made from?
94165.e: Chocolate is made from the seeds of the cocoa tree. They are called cocoa beans.
94165.m: Chocolate is made from cocoa beans.

94166.q: Daniel Peter married into a chocolate family. What was the family called?
94166.e: Daniel Peter married Fanny-Louise Cailler. Her father made chocolate.
94166.m: Daniel Peter married into the Cailler family.

94167.q: Which Swiss man invented milk chocolate in 1875?
94167.e: Daniel Peter from Vevey mixed cocoa with milk and, after many attempts, managed to make solid chocolate from it. Rudolf Lindt, on the other hand, invented conching for smooth chocolate.

94168.q: On which lake did Daniel Peter make his first milk chocolate?
94168.e: Daniel Peter came from the canton of Vaud and worked in Vevey on Lake Geneva. His milk chocolate was created there in 1875.
94168.m: Milk chocolate was created on Lake Geneva.

94169.q: What shape are the pieces of a Toblerone?
94169.e: A Toblerone is made of triangles lined up in a row. This shape has been protected since 1909.

94170.q: In which Swiss city was Toblerone invented?
94170.e: Toblerone was invented in the Swiss capital. The first factory is there too.

94171.q: In which year was Toblerone invented?
94171.e: Toblerone has existed since 1908. So it is more than 100 years old.

94172.q: Who invented Toblerone together with Emil Baumann?
94172.e: Theodor Tobler and Emil Baumann invented Toblerone. That is why the name begins with “Tobler”.

94173.q: The name Toblerone contains the Italian word “torrone”. What is torrone?
a: A nougat made of honey and almonds
94173.e: Torrone is a sweet nougat made of honey and almonds. There are little pieces of it in the chocolate.
94173.m: Torrone is a nougat made of honey and almonds.

94174.q: Which Swiss mountain could be seen on the Toblerone packaging for a long time?
94174.e: For a long time the packaging showed the Matterhorn. Since 2023 a different, made-up mountain has been shown there.
94174.m: For a long time the Matterhorn was on the Toblerone packaging.

94175.q: Which animal is hidden in the mountain on the Toblerone packaging?
94175.e: If you look closely, you will find the outline of a bear in the mountain. Many people only spot it after searching for a long time.
94175.m: A bear is hidden in the Toblerone mountain.

94176.q: In which country has Toblerone partly been made since 2023?
94176.e: Since 2023, some Toblerone has been made in Bratislava in Slovakia. That is why the packaging may no longer show a Swiss mountain.
94176.m: Toblerone is partly made in Slovakia.

94177.q: Which kinds of chocolate does Toblerone come in?
94177.e: Toblerone comes in milk chocolate, dark chocolate and white chocolate. All of them contain nougat.
94177.m: Toblerone comes in several kinds of chocolate.

94178.q: In which year did the first Swatch come onto the market?
94178.e: The first Swatch was presented on 1 March 1983. It helped the Swiss watch industry through a difficult time.

94179.q: What material is the case of a classic Swatch made of?
94179.e: The classic Swatch has a plastic case. That is why it is light and cheap.
94179.m: The classic Swatch is made of plastic.

94180.q: Which two English words did the name Swatch come from?
94180.e: Swatch is short for “Second Watch”. You were meant to be able to change it like a piece of clothing.

94181.q: Who is seen as the “father of the Swatch”?
94181.e: Nicolas G. Hayek made the Swatch big and famous. It was designed by engineers at the company ETA.
94181.m: Nicolas G. Hayek is seen as the father of the Swatch.

94182.q: Which country do Swatch watches come from?
94182.e: Swatch is a watch brand from Switzerland. The company has its headquarters in Biel.

94183.q: In which city was the Swatch presented for the first time?
94183.e: The Swatch was shown for the first time in Zurich in 1983. After that it quickly became very popular.
94183.m: The Swatch was presented in Zurich.

94184.q: What are Swatch watches especially known for?
94184.e: Swatch watches come in lots of cheerful colours and patterns. Some were designed by artists.

94185.q: What do you usually do with Ovomaltine powder?
94185.e: Ovomaltine is a powder that you stir into milk. This makes a sweet drink.

94186.q: In which year did Ovomaltine come onto the market?
94186.e: Ovomaltine has existed since 1904. At first it was sold as a strengthening drink.

94187.e: The chemist Albert Wander developed Ovomaltine. His father had founded the Wander company.

94188.q: Which ingredient makes up most of Swiss Ovomaltine?
94188.e: Swiss Ovomaltine is about two thirds barley malt extract (as of 2024). That is where the “malt” part of the name comes from.

94189.q: The “Ovo” in the name comes from the Latin word “ovum”. What does it mean?
94189.e: “Ovum” is Latin for egg. Ovomaltine used to contain eggs too.
94189.m: Ovum is the Latin word for egg.

94190.q: What is Ovomaltine called in England and the USA?
94190.e: In England, the USA and many other countries it is called Ovaltine. The recipe there is a little different.
94190.m: In English-speaking countries Ovomaltine is called Ovaltine.

94191.q: In which place in the canton of Bern is Ovomaltine made today?
94191.e: The Wander company makes Ovomaltine in Neuenegg in the canton of Bern (as of 2024).

94192.q: In which city did Georg Wander found the company that Ovomaltine came from?
94192.e: Georg Wander founded the company in the federal city of Bern. His son later developed Ovomaltine there.
94192.m: The Wander company was founded in Bern.

94193.e: The doctor Maximilian Bircher-Benner invented muesli around 1900. That is why it is called Bircher muesli.

94194.q: What job did the inventor of Bircher muesli have?
94194.e: Bircher-Benner was a doctor. He wanted his patients to eat healthily, with lots of fruit.
94194.m: The inventor of Bircher muesli was a doctor.

94195.q: Which fruit is the most important ingredient in the original Bircher muesli?
94195.e: In the original recipe, lots of sour apples were grated, skin and all. The apple was the main thing.
94195.m: Apple is the main ingredient in the original Bircher muesli.

94196.q: Which flakes belong in Bircher muesli?
94196.e: Bircher muesli contains soaked oat flakes. In the original there was only one spoonful of them.
94196.m: Oat flakes belong in Bircher muesli.

94197.q: What do you stir into the flakes so that Bircher muesli becomes nice and moist?
94197.e: For Bircher muesli you soak oat flakes and stir in milk or yoghurt. Then grated apples are added.
94197.m: Milk or yoghurt goes into Bircher muesli.

94198.q: What does the Swiss German word “Müesli” mean?
94198.e: “Müesli” is the diminutive of “Mues”. Mues is a soft mush, like a purée.

94199.q: In which city did Bircher-Benner serve muesli in his sanatorium?
94199.e: Bircher-Benner had his clinic in Zurich. From 1904 he ran a sanatorium on the Zürichberg.
94199.m: Bircher-Benner had his sanatorium in Zurich.

94200.q: What was sprinkled on top of the original Bircher muesli?
94200.e: To finish, a spoonful of grated hazelnuts, walnuts or almonds went on top.
94200.m: Grated nuts went on top of the original Bircher muesli.

94201.q: Which country does the well-known Rex peeler come from?
94201.e: The Rex was invented in Switzerland in 1947. It is still made in almost the same way today.
94201.m: The Rex peeler is a Swiss design classic.

94203.q: The well-known Swiss vegetable peeler is called Rex. How does its blade lie?
94203.e: On the Rex, the blade lies across the handle and can move. That way it adapts to the shape of potatoes and carrots.
94203.m: On the Rex, the blade lies across the handle.

94204.q: What was the Rex peeler pictured on in 2003?
94204.e: In 2003, Swiss Post issued a stamp showing the Rex. It was part of a series on Swiss design classics.
94204.m: The Rex was on a stamp in 2003.

94205.q: In which place in the canton of Zurich was the Rex made for decades by the company Zena?
94205.e: The company Zena from Affoltern am Albis made the Rex for decades. Since 2020, Zena has belonged to Victorinox.
94205.m: The Rex was made in Affoltern am Albis for a long time.

94206.q: Which country did Julius Maggi, who invented the stock cube, come from?
94206.e: Julius Maggi was a Swiss businessman. He invented soups, seasoning and the stock cube.

94207.q: In which canton was Julius Maggi's factory?
94207.e: In 1869 Julius Maggi took over a mill in Kemptthal near Winterthur in the canton of Zurich. His factory grew up there.
94207.m: The Maggi factory was in Kemptthal in the canton of Zurich.

94208.q: What do you need a stock cube for?
94208.e: A stock cube contains spices and salt in solid form. With it you can quickly make a stock.
94208.m: With a stock cube you can quickly make a soup.

94209.q: What do you add to a stock cube to make stock?
94209.e: The cube dissolves in hot water. That turns it into stock.
94209.m: A stock cube dissolves in hot water.

94210.q: What did Julius Maggi invent in 1886 to make his soups taste better?
94210.e: In 1886 Maggi brought out his liquid seasoning. It still comes in a brown bottle today.
94210.m: Julius Maggi invented a liquid seasoning in 1886.

94211.q: What did Julius Maggi make his first ready-made soups from?
94211.e: Maggi made cheap soups from the flour of pulses such as peas and beans. They were nourishing and cheap.
94211.m: The first Maggi soups were made from pulses.

94212.q: In which town was Julius Maggi born in 1846?
94212.e: Julius Maggi was born in 1846 in Frauenfeld in the canton of Thurgau.
94212.m: Julius Maggi was born in Frauenfeld.

94213.q: Roughly when did the Maggi stock cube come onto the market?
94213.e: The Maggi stock cube came onto the market shortly after 1900, around 1907 to 1908. So it is more than 100 years old.
94213.m: The Maggi cube has existed for over 100 years.

94214.e: Wim Ouboter from Zurich developed the folding Micro scooter. He founded his own company for it.
94214.m: Wim Ouboter invented the Micro scooter.

94215.q: Which journeys is a scooter especially handy for?
94215.e: On a scooter you are faster than on foot over short distances. It is not made for long journeys.
94215.m: A scooter is meant for short trips.

94216.q: In which country was the folding Micro scooter invented?
94216.e: The Micro scooter was invented in Zurich. Today children all over the world ride it.
94216.m: The Micro scooter comes from Switzerland.

94217.q: What is handy about the Micro scooter?
94217.e: You can fold up the Micro scooter. That way you can easily carry it or take it on the tram.
94217.m: A Micro scooter can be folded up.

94218.q: What material is the frame of a Micro scooter usually made of?
94218.e: The frame is usually made of aluminium. The metal is light but still strong.
94218.m: Micro scooters usually have an aluminium frame.

94219.q: What should you wear on your head when riding a scooter?
94219.e: A helmet protects your head if you fall. That is why you wear one on a scooter too.
94219.m: A helmet protects your head when you ride a scooter.

94220.q: How do you move forwards on a scooter?
a: You push off with one foot
94220.e: You stand with one foot on the board. With the other foot you push off from the ground.
94220.m: On a scooter you push off with your foot.

94221.q: Which country does the well-known Micro kick scooter come from?
94221.e: The Swiss Wim Ouboter invented the Micro scooter in the 1990s. Around the year 2000, lots of children all over the world wanted one.
94221.m: The Micro kick scooter is a Swiss invention.

a: The coffee powder dissolves in water
94222.e: Nescafé is instant coffee. You put the powder into hot water and have coffee straight away.

94223.e: Nescafé was developed by the company Nestlé in Vevey. Today it is one of the biggest food companies in the world.
94223.m: Nescafé comes from the company Nestlé.

94224.q: Which two words make up the name “Nescafé”?
94224.e: The name combines the company name with the French word “café” for coffee.
94224.m: Nescafé is a short word made from Nestlé and café.

94225.q: What is special about Nescafé from Nestlé?
a: It is coffee powder that dissolves in hot water
It is made from cocoa beans
94225.e: Nescafé is instant coffee. You put the powder into hot water and have a coffee straight away. It came onto the market in 1938.

94226.q: Which country asked Nestlé for help with its coffee in 1930?
94226.e: A great deal of coffee is grown in Brazil. The country was looking for a way to make coffee keep for a long time.
94226.m: Brazil asked Nestlé for help with its coffee.

94227.q: What problem did Brazil have with its coffee around 1930?
a: There was far too much coffee
A disease had destroyed almost all the plants
It had not rained for years
Nobody wanted to grow coffee any more
94227.e: There was so much coffee that the leftovers were burnt or dumped in the sea. People were looking for a way to make coffee keep for a long time.
94227.m: Around 1930 Brazil had too much coffee.

94228.q: In which town on Lake Geneva does the company Nestlé have its headquarters?
94228.e: Nestlé has its headquarters in Vevey on Lake Geneva. Nescafé was also developed there.
94228.m: Nestlé has its headquarters in Vevey.

94229.q: In which country was Nescafé sold for the very first time?
94229.e: The instant coffee first went on sale in shops in Switzerland. After that it was sold in many countries.
94229.m: Nescafé was first sold in Switzerland.

94230.q: What is a coffee creamer lid?
a: The lid of a small portion of cream
94230.e: Coffee cream comes in small pots for one cup of coffee. On top there is a thin lid.
94230.m: A coffee creamer lid seals a small portion of cream.

94231.q: What material is a coffee creamer lid made of?
94231.e: The lid is a very thin foil made of aluminium. It is only about 0.03 to 0.04 millimetres thick.
94231.m: Coffee creamer lids are made of aluminium.

94232.q: What do many people in Switzerland do with coffee creamer lids?
a: They stick them on letters as stamps
They hang them on the Christmas tree
They pay with them in shops
94232.e: The lids have nice pictures and are collected. At swap meets, collectors swap their lids.
94232.m: Many people collect coffee creamer lids.

94233.q: What is often pictured on coffee creamer lids?
94233.e: Every year hundreds of new series with pictures come out. There are, for example, animals, flowers, cars and sights.
94233.m: There are lots of different pictures on coffee creamer lids.

94235.q: Roughly how many coffee creamer lid collectors are there in Switzerland?
94235.e: According to estimates, there are around 30,000 collectors in Switzerland. Switzerland is the centre of this hobby.
94235.m: Many thousands of people in Switzerland collect lids.

94236.q: Since roughly when has coffee cream come in small portion pots?
94236.e: Around 1970, people started filling coffee cream into small pots with an aluminium lid. Soon afterwards, people began to collect them.
94236.m: Portion pots of coffee cream have existed since about 1970.

94237.q: Why does a coffee creamer lid have a small tab?
a: So you can pull it off easily
So it does not blow away
So you can hang it up
94237.e: You can hold the lid by the small tab. That way you can simply pull it off the pot.
94237.m: You pull the lid off by the tab.

94238.q: Where in the nose are the cells that recognise smells?
a: Right at the top of the nose
At the tip of the nose
94238.e: The smell cells are in the lining right at the top of the nasal cavity. That is why you sniff, to pull air upwards.
94238.m: The smell cells are at the top of the nose.

94239.q: Where do the smell cells send their message?
94239.e: The smell cells send signals along nerves to the brain. Only there do we notice what we smell.
94239.m: The brain recognises what the nose smells.

94240.q: Which animal can smell much better than a person?
94240.e: Dogs have many more smell cells than people. That is why they can sniff out trails.
94240.m: Dogs have a very fine nose.

94241.q: What do avalanche dogs in Switzerland search for with their noses?
94241.e: Avalanche dogs smell people lying under the snow. That way they help with rescues in the mountains.
94241.m: Avalanche dogs find buried people with their noses.

94242.q: What does a snake do with its forked tongue?
94242.e: The snake catches scent particles from the air with its tongue. A special organ in its mouth then recognises the smell.
94242.m: Snakes smell with the help of their tongue.

94243.q: What happens if you are around the same smell for a long time?
a: You hardly smell it any more
You smell it more and more strongly
94243.e: The nose gets used to a smell that stays for a long time. That is why you hardly notice the smell of your own home.
94243.m: The nose gets used to smells that stay the same.

94244.q: Which animal helps to find truffles in the ground?
94244.e: Truffles are mushrooms under the ground. Pigs and specially trained dogs can smell them through the soil.
94244.m: Pigs can smell truffles under the ground.

94245.q: What is the sense we use to notice smells called?
94245.e: With our sense of smell we notice scents and stinks. It is one of our five senses.
94245.m: We notice smells with our sense of smell.

94246.q: Why do homes need smoke alarms?
a: When asleep you hardly smell smoke
Smoke smells of nothing at all
Smoke alarms put out the fire
94246.e: Someone who is asleep is usually not woken by the smell of smoke. But the loud alarm of the smoke alarm wakes you up.
94246.m: When you are asleep, the smoke alarm warns you instead of your nose.

94247.q: What have you got when your nose is runny and blocked?
94247.e: With a cold, the inside of the nose is inflamed. It makes a lot of mucus and swells up.
94247.m: With a cold, your nose runs or gets blocked.

94248.q: What usually causes an ordinary cold?
94248.e: A cold is usually caused by viruses. They are passed on when people sneeze, for example.
94248.m: A cold is mostly caused by viruses.

94249.q: Where does a used tissue belong?
94249.e: There are germs in a used tissue. That is why you throw it away and wash your hands afterwards.
94249.m: A used tissue goes in the bin.

94250.q: How long does an ordinary cold usually last?
94250.e: A simple cold usually goes away by itself after about a week.
94250.m: A cold usually goes away after about a week.

94251.q: What helps so that you do not pass your cold on to others?
94251.e: Germs often stick to our hands. We wash them away with water and soap.
94251.m: Washing your hands protects against infection.

94252.q: Does an antibiotic help against an ordinary cold?
a: Yes, straight away after an hour
Yes, but only in the evening
Yes, if you rub it on your nose
94252.e: Antibiotics only work against bacteria. An ordinary cold goes away by itself without them.
94252.m: Antibiotics do not help against an ordinary cold.

a: A cold that only happens in winter
94253.e: With hay fever, the body reacts to the dust from flowers, which is called pollen. Your nose runs and your eyes itch.
94253.m: Hay fever is an allergy to pollen.

94254.q: What does you good when you have a cold?
a: Lots of ice cream and running
94254.e: With a cold, rest and plenty to drink help, for example warm tea. That way the body can recover.
94254.m: With a cold, rest and warm drinks help.

94255.q: What should you never put into a nostril?
94255.e: Small things like beads or peas can get stuck in the nose. Then a doctor often has to help.
94255.m: Small objects do not belong in the nose.

94256.q: What are the two openings in a horse's nose called?
94256.e: Horses and cattle breathe through their nostrils. They can open them very wide.
94256.m: Horses can open their nostrils wide.

94257.q: Which animal has its nostrils at the tip of a long trunk?
94257.e: An elephant's trunk is a very long nose. Right at the front are the two nostrils.
94257.m: The trunk is the elephant's nose.

94258.q: What is the space behind the nostrils called?
94258.e: Air flows through the nostrils into the nasal cavity. From there it goes on into the throat.
94258.m: Behind the nostrils is the nasal cavity.

94259.q: Why is a dog's nose usually damp around the nostrils?
a: So that it can see better
Because it always has a cold
So that it barks more quietly
94259.e: Scent particles stick well to the damp skin around the nostrils. That way the dog can notice smells even better.
94259.m: A damp dog's nose helps with smelling.

94260.q: Which bird has its nostrils right at the tip of its beak?
94260.e: The kiwi from New Zealand has its nostrils at the tip of its long beak. That way it smells worms in the ground.
94260.m: The kiwi smells with the tip of its beak.

94261.q: Which animal can close its nostrils when diving?
94261.e: Hippos spend a lot of time in water. When they go under, they close their nostrils so no water runs in.
94261.m: Hippos close their nostrils when they dive.

a: On top of the tip of the snout
94262.e: A crocodile's nostrils are on top of its snout. That way it can breathe while lying almost completely under water.
94262.m: Crocodiles breathe through nostrils on top of the snout.

94263.q: How many basic tastes are known today?
94263.e: The five basic tastes are sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. Everything else is a mixture or comes from smelling.

94264.q: Is it true that each part of the tongue only tastes one flavour?
a: No, all parts taste all the basic tastes
Yes, only sweet at the front and only bitter at the back
Yes, only the middle tastes anything
Yes, only the edges taste anything
94264.e: The old tongue map is wrong. All the basic tastes can be detected all over the tongue.
94264.m: The whole tongue tastes all the basic tastes.

94265.q: Is “spicy”, like chilli, a basic taste?
a: No, it is a feeling of pain and heat
Yes, it is the sixth basic taste
Yes, it is a kind of sweet
Yes, it is a kind of salty
94265.e: The substance in chilli irritates nerves that report heat and pain. That is why spicy food feels like burning.
94265.m: Spicy is a feeling of pain, not a taste.

94266.q: What does food need so that the tongue can taste it?
94266.e: Saliva dissolves the taste substances from the food. Only then can the taste buds recognise them.

94267.q: Which animal tastes with its feet?
94267.e: Butterflies have sensory cells on their feet. When they land on a flower, they can taste straight away whether there is food there.

94268.q: Which fish has taste cells over almost all of its skin?
94268.e: Catfish have taste cells all over their body. That way they find their food in murky water.
94268.m: The catfish tastes with almost all of its skin.

94269.q: Why does very cold ice cream taste less sweet than melted ice cream?
a: Cold makes the tongue less sensitive
94269.e: When it is very cold, the tongue senses sweetness less strongly. That is why melted ice cream often tastes much sweeter.

94270.e: Cats lack the sensory cell for sweet. They mainly eat meat and do not need sugar.

94271.e: Sugar tastes sweet. It is found in fruit, honey and sweets.

94272.q: Which taste do even babies especially like?
94272.e: Even babies like sweet things, and breast milk tastes slightly sweet too.
94272.m: Even babies like the sweet taste.

94273.q: What does a sweet taste tell the body?
94273.e: Sweet food contains sugar, and sugar provides energy. That is why our body likes sweet things.
94273.m: Sweet shows that there is energy in the food.

94274.q: Why should you brush your teeth after eating sweets?
a: So that your tongue gets sweeter
94274.e: Bacteria in the mouth turn sugar into acid. This acid can make holes in the teeth, called tooth decay.
94274.m: Brushing your teeth after sweet things protects against tooth decay.

94275.q: Which fruit tastes especially sweet when ripe?
94275.e: Ripe bananas contain a lot of sugar, so they taste sweet.

94276.q: How does the taste of a fruit change when it ripens?
94276.e: As it ripens, the fruit makes more sugar. Unripe fruit often tastes sour or tart.
94276.m: Ripe fruit tastes sweeter than unripe fruit.

94277.q: Which sweet syrup is made from the sap of a tree?
94277.e: Maple syrup is made from the sap of the sugar maple. The sap is boiled until a sweet syrup is left.
94277.m: Maple syrup comes from the sap of the maple tree.

94278.q: From which tall grass plant is sugar made in warm countries?
94278.e: Sugar cane is a tall grass with sweet juice. A lot of sugar is made from it in warm countries.
94278.m: Sugar cane is a sweet grass.

94279.q: Which liquid from the kitchen tastes sour?
94279.e: Vinegar contains acetic acid, which is why it tastes sour. It is used in salad dressing, for example.

94280.e: Sour food contains acid, such as citric acid or acetic acid. The tongue recognises this acid.

94281.q: What does milk that has gone off taste like?
94281.e: When milk gets old, bacteria turn the milk sugar into acid. That is why it tastes sour.
94281.m: Milk that has gone off tastes sour.

94282.q: Which dairy product tastes slightly sour?
94282.e: Yoghurt is made with bacteria that produce lactic acid. That is why yoghurt tastes slightly sour.
94282.m: Yoghurt tastes slightly sour because of lactic acid.

94283.q: Which vegetable is used for sauerkraut?
94283.e: Sauerkraut is made from finely cut white cabbage. As it ferments, lactic acid forms and makes it sour.
94283.m: Sauerkraut is made from white cabbage.

94284.q: What can a sour taste warn you about?
94284.e: Unripe fruit and spoiled food often taste sour. That way you notice that something is not good.
94284.m: Sour can warn of something unripe or spoiled.

94285.q: What face do many people pull when they bite into a lemon?
a: They screw up their eyes and mouth
94285.e: The strong sour taste makes many people pull a face. Their eyes and mouth get screwed up.
94285.m: Many people pull a face at sour things.

94286.q: Which green citrus fruit tastes very sour?
94286.e: The lime is related to the lemon. Its juice contains a lot of acid and tastes very sour.

94287.q: What do crisps usually taste like?
94287.e: Crisps are seasoned with salt. That is why they taste salty.

94288.q: Which seasoning do you sprinkle on a breakfast egg to make it taste salty?
94288.e: Table salt tastes salty. Many people sprinkle a pinch of it on a boiled egg.

94290.q: Why does our body need a little salt?
a: So that nerves and muscles work well
94290.e: Salt contains sodium, which nerves and muscles need. But too much salt is unhealthy.
94290.m: The body needs a little salt, but not too much.

94291.q: What tastes salty when it runs down your face?
94291.e: Tears contain a little salt. That is why they taste slightly salty.

94292.q: Why is salt spread on the roads in winter?
a: So that the road gets clean
So that the road gets warm
94292.e: Salt makes ice and snow melt. That way roads and pavements are less slippery.
94292.m: Road salt makes ice on the road melt.

94293.q: What does eating a lot of salty food often give you?
94293.e: Salt holds on to water in the body. That is why the body signals thirst after salty food.

94294.q: What does coffee without sugar taste like?
94294.e: Coffee contains bitter substances such as caffeine. Without sugar it therefore tastes bitter.

94295.q: What does a bitter taste often warn us about?
94295.e: Many poisonous plants taste bitter. That is why people often prefer to spit out bitter things.

94296.q: Which chocolate tastes the most bitter?
94296.e: Dark chocolate has a lot of cocoa and little sugar. Cocoa tastes bitter.
94296.m: Dark chocolate tastes more bitter than milk chocolate.

94297.q: Which vegetable often tastes a little bitter?
94297.e: Chicory contains bitter substances. That is why many children like it less.

94298.q: Why do children often like bitter things less than adults?
a: Children cannot taste bitterness at all
Bitter things are only poisonous for children
94298.e: Children react more strongly to bitterness than adults. As they get older, many get used to bitter food.

94299.q: What does the white pith under orange peel taste like?
94299.e: The white pith of an orange contains bitter substances. That is why people often pick it off.
94299.m: The white pith of an orange tastes bitter.

94300.q: Which drink made from leaves can turn bitter if it brews too long?
94300.e: If black tea brews for too long, a lot of tannins dissolve. Then it tastes bitter.
94300.m: Tea that brews too long turns bitter.

94301.q: Apart from sour, what does a grapefruit taste like?
94301.e: Grapefruits contain bitter substances. So they taste bitter and also a bit sour.

94302.q: Which red salad leaf tastes slightly bitter?
94302.e: Radicchio has red leaves with white veins. It contains bitter substances, so it tastes slightly bitter.

94303.q: Which basic taste has a name that roughly means “delicious”?
94303.e: Umami roughly means delicious. It describes a strong, savoury taste.

94304.q: Which country does the word “umami” come from?
94304.e: The Japanese scientist Kikunae Ikeda described the taste umami in 1908. He found it in a seaweed soup.
94304.m: The word umami comes from Japan.

94305.e: Stock tastes strong and savoury. This taste is called umami.

94306.q: Which cheese has a strong umami taste?
94306.e: Cheese that has matured for a long time, like Parmesan, tastes very savoury. It has a lot of umami.
94306.m: Mature cheese like Parmesan tastes umami.

94307.q: What is the substance that gives many foods their umami taste called?
94307.e: Glutamate is found naturally in many foods. The tongue has sensory cells that recognise it as umami.

94308.q: Which sauce from Asia tastes strongly umami?
94308.e: Soy sauce is made from soya beans and matured for a long time. It tastes salty and very umami.

94309.q: Which vegetable tastes especially umami when ripe and dried?
94309.e: Ripe and dried tomatoes contain a lot of the substance that tastes umami. That is why they flavour sauces so well.

94310.q: Which savoury spread from Switzerland tastes strongly umami?
94310.e: Cenovis is a savoury paste made from brewer's yeast that you spread on bread and butter. Yeast extract tastes strongly umami.
94310.m: Cenovis is a savoury Swiss yeast spread.

94311.q: Where are most of the taste buds?
94311.e: Most taste buds are on the tongue. Only a few are in other places in the mouth.
94311.m: Most taste buds are on the tongue.

94312.q: What are the little bumps on the tongue that contain taste buds called?
94312.e: The rough tongue is covered in little bumps called papillae. Many of them contain taste buds.
94312.m: Taste buds sit in the papillae of the tongue.

94313.q: Roughly how many taste buds does a person have?
94313.e: A person has several thousand taste buds. Each one is made up of many sensory cells.
94313.m: A person has a few thousand taste buds.

94314.q: What happens to the sensory cells in the taste buds after a while?
a: They are replaced by new ones
94314.e: The sensory cells only live a short time, about one to two weeks. Then new ones grow.
94314.m: Taste cells are renewed again and again.

94315.q: What often happens when you burn your tongue on hot tea?
a: You taste less for a while
You cannot smell anything any more
94315.e: Heat can injure the sensory cells on the tongue. Until new ones have grown, you taste less.
94315.m: A burnt tongue tastes less for a while.

94316.q: What does the surface of the tongue feel like?
94316.e: The many papillae make the tongue rough. The taste buds are in them too.
94316.m: The tongue is rough because of the papillae.

94317.q: What connects the taste buds to the brain?
94317.e: The sensory cells send their message along nerves to the brain. There the feeling of sweet or bitter is created.
94317.m: Nerves carry taste to the brain.

94318.q: Apart from the tongue, where else are there some taste buds?
a: On the roof of the mouth and in the throat
94318.e: Some taste buds are on the roof of the mouth and in the throat. But most are on the tongue.
94318.m: There are taste buds on the roof of the mouth too.

94319.e: A scent is a smell that we find pleasant. One example is the smell of flowers.
94319.m: A scent is a pleasant smell.

94320.q: Which purple plant smells strongly and is often put into scented bags?
94320.e: Lavender has purple flowers and a strong scent. Dried, it is put in little bags in the wardrobe.

94321.q: Why do many flowers have a scent?
94321.e: The scent attracts bees and other insects. As they visit, they carry pollen from flower to flower.

94322.q: What can you often smell in the morning at the baker's?
94322.e: Baking produces lots of scents. That is why the baker's smells of fresh bread.

94323.q: What is a scented liquid you spray on your skin called?
94323.e: Perfume contains scents from flowers, woods or the laboratory. You spray it on to smell nice.

94324.q: Where do scent particles have to go for us to smell them?
94324.e: Scent particles float in the air. We breathe them in, and the smell cells in the nose recognise them.
94324.m: Scent particles travel through the air into the nose.

94325.q: What can scents easily bring back?
94325.e: In the brain, smells quickly reach the areas for feelings and memories. That is why a scent often reminds you of the past.

94326.q: Which flower is famous for its scent and often has thorns on its stem?
94326.e: Many roses smell strongly and have thorns on the stem. Rose oil is also made from their petals.
94326.m: Roses are known for their scent.

94327.q: Why do you smell less outside in winter than in summer?
a: The nose is smaller in winter
There is no air in winter
The smell cells sleep in winter
94327.e: When it is warm, scents evaporate faster and drift through the air. In the cold there are fewer scent particles.
94327.m: Warmth spreads scents better than cold.

94328.e: A stink is a smell that we find disgusting. It often warns us about something bad.
94328.m: A stink is an unpleasant smell.

94329.q: Which animal sprays a smelly liquid when in danger?
94329.e: The skunk lives in America. When in danger, it sprays a very foul-smelling liquid at its enemies.
94329.m: The skunk defends itself with a stink.

94330.q: What does the stink of spoiled food warn us about?
a: That it is about to rain
94330.e: Spoiled food smells bad because bacteria are growing in it. Anyone who eats it can get ill.
94330.m: You should not eat food that stinks.

94331.q: What does natural gas smell of, so that a leak is noticed straight away?
a: A smelly substance that is added
94331.e: Natural gas itself hardly smells. That is why a strong-smelling substance is added, so that you smell a leak straight away.
94331.m: Natural gas is given a smell so that leaks are noticed.

94332.q: What do rotten eggs smell of?
94332.e: Rotten eggs give off a gas that contains sulphur. It smells very unpleasant.

94333.q: Which insect gives off a foul smell when disturbed?
94333.e: Stink bugs release a foul-smelling liquid when in danger. That way they scare off enemies.
94333.m: Stink bugs protect themselves with a stink.

94334.q: What should you do if your home smells of gas?
a: Open the windows and go outside
94334.e: Gas can burn or explode. That is why you let in air, leave the home and call for help outside.
94334.m: If you smell gas, let in air and go outside.

94335.q: Which giant flower stinks of rotting meat?
94335.e: The titan arum has one of the largest flower heads in the world. Its stink attracts flies and beetles that pollinate it.
94335.m: The titan arum attracts insects with its stink.

94336.q: What flows through a cable so that a lamp lights up?
94336.e: Electric current flows through the wire in the cable. It makes lamps light up and motors turn.

94337.q: Can you see the electricity in a cable?
94337.e: Electricity flows inside the wire and is invisible. You can only tell it is there from what it does, for example from the light of a lamp.
94337.m: Electricity in a cable is invisible.

94338.q: Which fish can give strong electric shocks itself?
94338.e: The electric eel lives in South America. With special organs it produces electric shocks to stun prey and fight off enemies.
94338.m: The electric eel can produce electricity.

94339.q: Which sea fish senses the weak electric signals of its prey?
94339.e: Sharks have special sense organs on their snout. With them they sense the weak electric signals of animals, even when they are hidden in the sand.
94339.m: Sharks sense the electric signals of their prey.

94340.q: Where do most trains in Switzerland get their energy from?
a: From the line above the track
94340.e: Almost the whole Swiss railway network is electrified. The trains take electricity from the overhead line above the tracks.
94340.m: Swiss trains mostly run on electricity from the overhead line.

94341.q: What is the arm on the roof of a locomotive that takes electricity from the line called?
94341.e: The pantograph presses against the overhead line from below. That way electricity flows into the locomotive and drives the motors.
94341.m: The pantograph collects electricity for the locomotive.

94342.q: What happens in a flat during a power cut?
a: The lights and appliances go off
94342.e: Without electricity, lamps, the fridge and other appliances can't work. That is why it suddenly goes dark during a power cut.
94342.m: Without electricity, lamps and appliances go off.

94343.q: Why does it sometimes crackle when you take off a woolly jumper?
94343.e: Rubbing gives the fabric an electric charge. The charge jumps across in tiny sparks, and you hear that as crackling.
94343.m: Rubbing can make tiny electric sparks.

94344.q: Who built the first battery around the year 1800?
94344.e: The Italian Alessandro Volta stacked metal discs with soaked pieces of card. This voltaic pile was the first battery.
94344.m: Alessandro Volta built the first battery.

94345.q: How many volts does an ordinary small round AA battery have?
94345.e: An ordinary AA battery gives a voltage of 1.5 volts. That is harmless to your hands.

94346.q: Which battery has two snap connectors next to each other on top?
94346.e: The 9-volt battery is a small rectangular block. On top it has two connectors that snap into place.
94346.m: The 9-volt battery has two connectors on top.

94347.q: What is a small, flat, round battery like the ones in watches called?
94347.e: Button cells are small and flat like a button. They are found in watches, scales and small toys.
94347.m: Small flat batteries are called button cells.

94348.q: Why are button cells dangerous for small children?
a: If swallowed they can cause serious injury
94348.e: A swallowed button cell can get stuck in the food pipe and injure it. That is why button cells must be kept out of reach of small children.
94348.m: Keep button cells away from small children.

94349.q: Where does a battery get its electricity from?
a: From the air in the room
94349.e: Inside the battery, chemical substances react with each other. This produces electric current until the substances are used up.
94349.m: A battery makes electricity from substances inside it.

94350.q: Why must you never throw batteries into a fire?
94350.e: In the heat, batteries can burst or explode. Poisonous substances are released.
94350.m: Batteries never go in a fire.

94351.q: What can leak out of an old battery in a device?
94351.e: Old batteries can start to leak. The liquid that comes out is corrosive and can damage the device.
94351.m: Old batteries can leak corrosive liquid.

94352.q: What happens to the lamp if a wire in the circuit comes loose?
94352.e: If a wire comes loose, the path for the electricity is broken. Then no more current can flow to the lamp.
94352.m: A loose wire breaks the circuit.

94353.q: What is a circuit that is broken somewhere called?
94353.e: If the circuit is broken at one point, it is called open. No current flows in an open circuit.
94353.m: No current flows in an open circuit.

94354.q: Why is an electric circuit called a “circuit”?
a: The current flows all the way round from terminal to terminal
The wires are always bent round
The lamp is always perfectly round
The battery turns in a circle
94354.e: The current flows from one terminal of the battery through the wires and the lamp back to the other terminal. So its path is a closed loop.
94354.m: In a circuit, the current flows all the way round back to the battery.

94355.q: What is a device in a circuit that uses electricity, like a lamp or a motor, called?
94355.e: Lamps, motors or bells need electricity to work. That is why they are called loads or consumers.

94356.q: What does a small electric motor do in a closed circuit?
94356.e: An electric motor turns electricity into a turning movement. You can use it, for example, to drive a small propeller.
94356.m: An electric motor turns when current flows.

94357.q: What do you draw in a circuit diagram instead of real pictures of the parts?
94357.e: In a circuit diagram, each component has a simple symbol. That way you can draw a circuit quickly.
94357.m: A circuit diagram shows components as simple symbols.

94358.q: How does a lamp shine with an almost flat battery?
94358.e: An almost flat battery only supplies a little energy. That is why the lamp shines more faintly.
94358.m: With an almost flat battery, the lamp shines faintly.

94359.q: What does an electric bell do when the circuit is closed?
94359.e: When current flows through the bell, a small hammer strikes a bell. That makes the ringing sound.
94359.m: A bell rings when current flows.

94360.q: What is a cable called that you use to connect a device to a socket further away?
94360.e: An extension cable has a plug at one end and a socket at the other. That way the electricity reaches further.
94360.m: An extension cable takes electricity further away.

94361.q: Why shouldn't you lay a cable under a carpet?
a: It can be damaged and get hot
94361.e: Under the carpet the cable gets stepped on and can break. Also, the heat can't escape, which is dangerous.

94362.q: What do you do with a cable reel before you plug in a powerful device?
a: You put it in the sun
You tie it in a knot
94362.e: In a cable reel that is still wound up, the cable can get very hot. That is why you unroll it completely.
94362.m: Unroll a cable reel completely before using it.

94363.q: What are the thick lines that run across the country high up on big pylons called?
94363.e: High-voltage power lines carry electricity from the power stations over long distances. They hang high up on pylons.
94363.m: High-voltage lines carry electricity over long distances.

94364.q: Where are many power cables in towns and cities?
94364.e: In towns, power cables are usually laid in the ground. There they are protected and don't get in the way.
94364.m: In towns, power cables are often in the ground.

94365.q: Why do the wires in a power cable have different coloured coverings?
a: So that you can tell them apart
So that they shine more nicely
So that animals don't eat them
94365.e: Each colour shows what a wire is for. That way the electrician can connect the wires correctly.
94365.m: The colours of the wires help to connect them correctly.

94366.q: What colour is the covering of the protective earth wire?
