94726.q: In terms of the law of constant proportions, how does salt water differ from the compound sodium chloride?
a: Salt water varies, sodium chloride has a fixed composition
Salt water has fixed mass ratios, sodium chloride varying ones
Both always have the same fixed mass ratio
94726.e: A mixture like salt water can contain more or less salt; in pure sodium chloride, on the other hand, sodium and chlorine are always in the same mass ratio.
94726.m: Mixtures have a variable composition, compounds a fixed one.

94727.q: What is the empirical formula of glucose C₆H₁₂O₆?
94727.e: The subscripts 6, 12 and 6 can be divided by 6; the smallest whole-number ratio of atoms is 1 to 2 to 1.
94727.m: The empirical formula gives the smallest whole-number ratio of atoms.

94728.q: What is the empirical formula of benzene C₆H₆?
94728.e: Carbon and hydrogen are in the ratio 6 to 6, so 1 to 1; ethyne C₂H₂ also has the same empirical formula.
94728.m: Different substances can have the same empirical formula.

94729.q: What is the empirical formula of hydrogen peroxide H₂O₂?
94729.e: The ratio 2 to 2 can be reduced to 1 to 1; the molecular formula H₂O₂, on the other hand, gives the atoms in one molecule.
94729.m: The molecular formula and the empirical formula are not always the same.

94730.q: By mass, a compound consists of 40.0 % carbon, 6.7 % hydrogen and 53.3 % oxygen. What is its empirical formula?
94730.m: From the mass percentages you first work out the amounts of substance and then their ratio.

94731.q: By mass, a hydrocarbon consists of 75 % carbon and 25 % hydrogen. What is its empirical formula?
94731.e: In 100 g: 75 / 12 = 6.25 mol C and 25 / 1.008 ≈ 24.8 mol H; the ratio is about 1 to 4.
94731.m: For the empirical formula, you round the ratio of amounts to small whole numbers.

94732.q: By mass, an iron oxide contains 70 % iron (M about 56 g/mol) and 30 % oxygen (M about 16 g/mol). What is its empirical formula?
94732.e: 70 / 56 = 1.25 mol Fe and 30 / 16 = 1.875 mol O; the ratio 1 to 1.5 gives 2 to 3 in whole numbers.
94732.m: If you get a ratio with 0.5, you double both numbers.

94733.q: A compound has the empirical formula CH₂ and a molar mass of 56 g/mol. What is its molecular formula?
94733.e: The CH₂ unit has about 14 g/mol; 56 / 14 = 4, so C₄H₈.
94733.m: With the molar mass, you can find the molecular formula from the empirical formula.

94734.q: Why is only an empirical formula and no molecular formula given for salts such as sodium chloride?
a: An ionic lattice does not consist of individual molecules
Sodium chloride is a gas at room temperature
Salts have no definite molar mass
The ions are too small to count
94734.e: In the crystal, each ion is surrounded by several ions of opposite charge; the formula NaCl only gives the 1 to 1 ratio of the ions.
94734.m: For ionic compounds, the formula only describes the ratio of the ions.

94835.q: Which logic gate only gives a 1 when all inputs are 1?
94835.e: The AND gate only outputs 1 when all inputs are 1. Otherwise the output is 0.
94835.m: An AND gate needs all ones to output a one.

94836.q: Which gate outputs 0 for the inputs 1 and 1, but 1 for 1 and 0?
94836.e: XOR (exclusive or) gives 1 when exactly one input is 1. If both are 1, the output is 0.
94836.m: XOR is true when the two inputs differ.

94837.q: With which gates alone can every Boolean function be built?
94837.e: NAND and NOR are functionally complete: from them alone you can build NOT, AND and OR and therefore any switching function.
94837.m: NAND and NOR are called universal gates.

94838.q: How many rows does the truth table of a gate with three inputs have?
94838.e: Each input can be 0 or 1, so there are 2 to the power of 3, that is 8, combinations.
94838.m: With n inputs, a truth table has 2 to the power of n rows.

94839.q: What does a NOR gate output when both inputs are 0?
94839.e: NOR is a negated OR. 0 OR 0 gives 0, and its negation is 1.
94839.m: A NOR gate only outputs 1 when all inputs are 0.

94840.q: According to De Morgan's laws, which expression is equivalent to NOT(A AND B)?
94840.e: De Morgan states that the negation of a conjunction equals the disjunction of the negations.
94840.m: When negating, AND becomes OR and each part is negated.

94841.q: What are the logic gates in today's computer chips made of?
94841.e: Modern chips contain billions of tiny transistors in CMOS technology. Early computers still built their gates from relays or valves.
94841.m: Logic gates today are made of transistors.

94842.q: When does an XNOR gate with two inputs give a 1?
a: When both inputs are the same
94842.e: XNOR is the negated XOR. It therefore reports equality: 0 and 0 as well as 1 and 1 give 1.
94842.m: The XNOR gate works like an equality checker for two bits.

94843.q: Which two outputs does a half adder have?
94843.e: A half adder adds two bits and outputs the sum bit and the carry bit.
94843.m: The half adder gives a sum bit and a carry bit.

94844.q: Which gate produces the sum bit in a half adder?
94844.e: The sum bit is 1 when exactly one of the two bits is 1. That matches the XOR function exactly.
94844.m: The sum of a half adder comes from an XOR.

94845.q: Which gate produces the carry bit in a half adder?
94845.e: A carry only happens with 1 plus 1. That is exactly the AND of the two inputs.
94845.m: The carry of a half adder comes from an AND.

94846.q: What does a half adder lack compared with a full adder?
a: An input for the carry from the previous digit
An output for the sum bit
An input for the sign bit
94846.e: The full adder has three inputs: two bits and the incoming carry. The half adder lacks this carry input.
94846.m: Only the full adder can process a carry from the previous digit.

94847.q: Which components are enough to build a full adder?
a: Two half adders and an OR gate
One half adder and a NOT gate
Three half adders without other gates
94847.e: The first half adder adds the two bits and the second adds the incoming carry. An OR combines the two partial carries.
94847.m: Two half adders and an OR together make a full adder.

94848.q: What does a half adder output when both inputs are 1?
94848.e: 1 plus 1 is 10 in binary. So the sum bit is 0 and the carry is 1.

94849.q: An adder passes the carry on from digit to digit. Why does it become slow with many bits?
a: Each digit has to wait for the carry from the previous one
Each digit needs its own clock
The sum bits are calculated twice
It can only add even numbers
94849.e: The carry runs through all the digits like a wave. The more bits, the longer it takes until the last sum bit is fixed.
94849.m: A carry that is passed along slows down wide adders.

94850.q: What does the binary addition 0111 + 0001 give?
94850.e: 1 + 1 gives 0 with a carry of 1. The carry runs on through all three ones until it creates a 1 in the fourth place: 1000.
94850.m: A carry can run on over several digits.

94851.q: What is a register in a processor?
a: A very fast storage place directly in the processor
An area on the hard disk for file names
A list of all installed programs
A part of main memory for graphics data
94851.e: Registers are small memory cells in the processor that the arithmetic logic unit can access without delay.
94851.m: Registers are a computer's fastest memory.

94852.q: What does the program counter store?
a: The address of the next instruction
The number of instructions already carried out
The result of the last calculation
The number of the running process
94852.e: The program counter points to the memory address from which the next machine instruction is fetched. A jump changes its value.
94852.m: The program counter always knows where the program goes next.

94853.q: What does the instruction register contain?
a: The list of all instructions in a program
94853.e: After fetching, the instruction is loaded into the instruction register, where the control unit decodes it.
94853.m: The instruction register holds the instruction currently being decoded.

94854.q: In simple processors, what is the register called where the results of the arithmetic logic unit end up?
94854.e: In accumulator machines, the accumulator is an operand and also the target of most arithmetic operations.
94854.m: The accumulator collects the results of calculations.

94855.q: What does the stack pointer point to?
a: The current end of the stack
The start of the program code
94855.e: The stack pointer holds the address of the top of the stack. PUSH and POP change it automatically.
94855.m: The stack pointer marks the top of the stack.

94856.q: When is the zero flag set in the status register?
a: When the result of an operation is zero
When a division by zero is attempted
94856.e: The zero flag shows that the last result was 0. Conditional jumps such as “jump if equal” use it.
94856.m: The zero flag reports a result of zero.

94857.q: What does 64 bit mean for a processor?
a: It has 64 GB of main memory
94857.e: In a 64-bit processor, the general registers hold 64 bits. This lets it handle large numbers and a great deal of main memory directly.
94857.m: A processor's bit width is the width of its registers.

94858.q: What does the carry flag show after an addition?
a: A carry out of the most significant bit
94858.e: The carry flag is set when, with unsigned numbers, a carry goes beyond the width of the register.
94858.m: The carry flag reports a carry beyond the top bit.

94859.q: What does the abbreviation RISC stand for?
94859.e: RISC processors use a reduced set of simple instructions of equal length that can be carried out quickly.
94859.m: RISC relies on a few simple instructions.

94860.q: Which class of instruction sets does the x86 architecture belong to?
94860.e: x86 has many, partly complex instructions of different lengths and is therefore considered CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computer).
94860.m: x86 is the best-known example of CISC.

94861.q: Which instruction set architecture is open and can be used without a licence?
94861.e: RISC-V is an open standard: any company may build processors with it without paying licence fees.
94861.m: RISC-V is an open instruction set without licence fees.

94862.q: Why are many companies and universities interested in the RISC-V instruction set?
a: They can build their own processors with it without licence fees
RISC-V chips are always faster than all others
94862.e: RISC-V is an open standard. Anyone who designs a processor with it does not have to pay licence fees to any company, unlike with ARM or x86, for example.
94862.m: RISC-V is open and costs no licence fees.

94863.q: Which instruction set architecture is in the vast majority of smartphones?
94863.e: Almost all smartphone processors use the energy-saving ARM architecture.
94863.m: Smartphones almost always run on ARM processors.

94864.q: What is typical of a load-store architecture?
a: Only load and store instructions access main memory
Every instruction may calculate directly in main memory
Programs are only loaded from the hard disk
There are no registers, only a stack
94864.e: In load-store architectures, typical of RISC, instructions only calculate with registers. Memory access happens separately with load and store.
94864.m: In a load-store architecture, you only calculate in registers.

94865.q: What is the part of a machine instruction called that sets the operation to be carried out?
94865.e: The opcode (operation code) decides what the instruction does; the operands decide what it works with.
94865.m: The opcode tells the processor which operation to carry out.

94866.q: Which Intel processor from 1978 founded the x86 architecture?
94866.e: The Intel 8086 came on the market in 1978. Its successors 80186, 80286 and 80386 gave the family the name x86.
94866.m: The x86 family began with the Intel 8086 in 1978.

94867.q: Which company developed the 64-bit extension x86-64?
94867.e: AMD introduced x86-64 (also called AMD64). Intel later adopted the extension for its processors.
94867.m: The 64-bit extension of x86 comes from AMD.

94868.q: What is a cache in a processor for?
a: It keeps frequently used data ready quickly
It cools the processor under heavy load
It stores data permanently after switching off
It connects the processor to the internet
94868.e: The cache is a small, fast buffer memory. It bridges the difference in speed between the processor and main memory.
94868.m: A cache makes frequent accesses faster.

94869.q: What is it called when the data you are looking for are not found in the cache?
94869.e: With a cache miss, the data must be fetched from slower memory. A successful find is called a cache hit.
94869.m: A cache miss costs time because slow memory has to be asked.

94870.q: Which cache level is usually the smallest and fastest?
94870.e: The L1 cache sits right next to the processor core. It is only a few dozen kilobytes in size but the fastest.
94870.m: The closer a cache is to the core, the smaller and faster it is.

94871.q: How are data transferred between main memory and the cache?
94871.e: Data are not transferred byte by byte but in blocks, usually 64 bytes in today's processors. That way neighbouring data are in the cache too.
94871.m: A cache always loads data in blocks as cache lines.

94872.q: Which entry does the LRU replacement strategy push out?
a: The one not used for the longest time
94872.e: LRU means “Least Recently Used”. The entry whose last use was longest ago is replaced.
94872.m: LRU throws out whatever has gone unused the longest.

94873.q: What is it called that after a memory access, neighbouring addresses are often read?
94873.e: Spatial locality occurs, for example, when going through an array. That is why the cache loads whole blocks.
94873.m: Spatial locality means that neighbouring addresses will soon be needed.

94874.q: What does a cache with the write-back strategy do?
a: It only writes changed data to main memory when they are pushed out
It writes every change straight to main memory as well
It only writes data to the hard disk
94874.e: Write-back marks changed lines as “dirty” and only writes them back when they are pushed out. Write-through writes immediately.
94874.m: Write-back saves memory accesses by putting off writing back.

94875.q: With which memory technology are processor caches usually built?
94875.e: SRAM is faster than DRAM and does not need constant refreshing, but it needs more transistors per bit.
94875.m: Caches are made of fast SRAM.

94876.q: A cache has a 90 per cent hit rate, 1 ns access time and 100 ns extra time per miss. What is the average access time?
94876.e: Average access time is hit time plus miss rate times penalty: 1 ns plus 0.1 times 100 ns gives 11 ns.
94876.m: Even a few cache misses make the average access time much longer.

94877.q: What is the basic idea of a processor pipeline?
a: Several instructions are processed at the same time in different stages
Each instruction is carried out twice as a check
Instructions are compressed before they run
The processor only works every second clock cycle
94877.e: As on an assembly line, each instruction is split into stages. While one instruction is being carried out, the next is already being decoded.
94877.m: A pipeline works like an assembly line for instructions.

94878.q: Why does a pipeline increase a processor's performance even though a single instruction is not finished any faster?
a: Because an instruction can be finished in every clock cycle
Because each instruction needs fewer stages
Because the processor uses less power
94878.e: As on an assembly line, each item takes the same time, but many more come out per hour. The classic RISC pipeline has five stages for this.
94878.m: A pipeline increases throughput, not the speed of a single instruction.

94879.q: What happens in the first stage of the classic RISC pipeline?
94879.e: The first stage is called instruction fetch: the instruction is loaded from the address in the program counter.
94879.m: In the pipeline, every instruction starts by being fetched.

94880.q: What is a conflict called in which an instruction needs the result of the previous instruction, which is not yet finished?
94880.e: A data hazard arises from dependencies between instructions that are close together in the pipeline.
94880.m: Data hazards arise when a result is needed too early.

94881.q: With which technique are results passed directly to the next stage without waiting for them to be written back?
94881.e: With forwarding (bypassing), the processor passes a result straight to the following instruction and so avoids waiting cycles.
94881.m: Forwarding sends results on by the shortest route.

94882.q: What helps against waiting times caused by conditional jumps in a pipeline?
94882.e: With jumps, it is unclear which instruction comes next. Branch prediction guesses the target and keeps filling the pipeline speculatively.
94882.m: Good branch prediction keeps the pipeline full.

94883.q: What is an empty clock cycle called that is inserted into the pipeline to wait for a result?
94883.e: A bubble (or stall) is a cycle without useful work, so that a dependent instruction can calculate correctly.
94883.m: Pipeline bubbles cost cycles without a result.

94884.q: How many clock cycles does an ideal 5-stage pipeline without conflicts need for 100 instructions?
94884.e: The first instruction needs 5 cycles, after which another one finishes every cycle: 5 plus 99 gives 104 cycles.
94884.m: A full pipeline finishes one instruction per cycle.

a: A low-level language with short codes for machine instructions
94885.e: In assembly, each statement basically matches one machine instruction, written as a readable short code.
94885.m: Assembly is machine language in readable form.

94886.q: What are the readable short codes for machine instructions such as MOV or ADD called?
94886.e: Mnemonics are memory aids: ADD stands for adding, MOV for moving.
94886.m: Mnemonics make machine instructions easy to remember.

94887.q: What does the x86 instruction MOV do?
a: It copies a value to a destination
94887.e: Despite the name “move”, the value is copied: the source stays as it is.
94887.m: MOV copies data from a source to a destination.

94888.q: Which x86 instruction always jumps to another address, without any condition?
94888.e: JMP is the unconditional jump. JE only jumps if the zero flag is set, and CALL also stores a return address.
94888.m: JMP always jumps; conditional jumps only under conditions.

94889.q: Which x86 instruction puts a value on the stack?
94889.e: PUSH reduces the stack pointer and stores the value at the new top. POP takes it off again.
94889.m: PUSH puts on the stack, POP takes off.

94890.q: Why can an assembly program hardly be moved to other processors?
a: It is tied to a particular instruction set
It always needs an internet connection
It only runs under one operating system
It is too big for other processors
94890.e: Assembly instructions match the machine instructions of a particular architecture. An ARM processor does not understand an x86 program.
94890.m: Assembly is tied to one processor architecture.

94891.q: What is a label in an assembly program?
a: A symbolic name for an address
An error message from the assembler
94891.e: Labels mark places in the code, such as jump targets. The assembler replaces them with the real addresses.
94891.m: Labels save you from calculating with fixed addresses.

94892.q: Which tool translates machine code back into assembly notation?
94892.e: A disassembler turns bytes of machine code back into mnemonics, for example for debugging or analysis.
94892.m: The disassembler makes machine code readable again.

94893.q: What is the first phase of a compiler, which breaks the source code into tokens, called?
94893.e: The lexer (scanner) recognises keywords, names, numbers and symbols and turns them into tokens.
94893.m: The lexer breaks source code into tokens.

94894.q: What does a compiler's parser create from the tokens?
a: A list of errors in memory
94894.e: The parser checks the grammar and builds a syntax tree from it, which shows the structure of the program.
94894.m: The parser turns tokens into a syntax tree.

94895.q: Who developed one of the first compilers, the A-0 system, in 1952?
94895.e: Grace Hopper created the A-0 system for the UNIVAC I and later promoted the language COBOL.
94895.m: Grace Hopper is considered a pioneer of compilers.

94896.q: For which programming language did IBM deliver one of the first optimising compilers in 1957?
94896.e: John Backus's team presented the Fortran compiler in 1957. It produced surprisingly efficient machine code.
94896.m: Fortran was the first widely used high-level language with a compiler.

a: A compiler that produces code for a different platform
A compiler that mixes two languages
A compiler that only looks for errors
94897.e: A cross-compiler runs, for example, on a PC but produces code for a microcontroller or a smartphone.
94897.m: A cross-compiler translates for a different target system.

94898.q: What does GCC stand for today?
94898.e: GCC began in 1987 as the GNU C Compiler and today supports several languages, hence the new name.
94898.m: GCC is a collection of compilers from the GNU project.

94899.q: What does a just-in-time compiler do?
a: It only translates parts of the program while it is running
It only translates at fixed times of day
It translates the program before installation
It translates machine code into source code
94899.e: A JIT compiler translates frequently run parts into machine code at runtime, as in the Java Virtual Machine.
94899.m: A JIT compiler translates exactly when code is needed.

a: It reads the program and runs it directly step by step
It translates the program once and saves an EXE file
It only checks the spelling in the code
94900.e: An interpreter analyses the statements at runtime and carries them out at once, without first creating a separate program file.
94900.m: An interpreter translates and runs in one go.

94901.q: What is a typical disadvantage of interpreted programs?
a: They only run on one computer
94901.e: Because the analysis has to be done again every time it runs, interpreted programs are often slower than compiled ones.

94902.q: Which language is usually run by an interpreter in its standard implementation?
94902.e: The reference implementation CPython runs Python programs with an interpreter. C, Rust and Fortran are compiled.
94902.m: Python is a typical interpreted language.

94903.q: Into which intermediate form does CPython translate the source code before running it?
94903.e: CPython produces bytecode for a virtual machine. This is then worked through by the interpreter loop.
94903.m: CPython runs bytecode, not the source code directly.

94904.q: What does the abbreviation REPL stand for in interactive interpreters?
94904.e: A REPL reads an input, evaluates it, prints the result and waits again.
94904.m: In a REPL you try out code line by line.

94905.e: The Java compiler produces bytecode. The JVM interprets it or translates it into machine code with a JIT.
94905.m: Java bytecode runs on the Java Virtual Machine.

94906.q: Which language was built into home computers such as the Commodore 64 as an interpreter?
94906.e: The Commodore 64 started straight into a BASIC interpreter stored in ROM.
94906.m: Many home computers of the 1980s started straight into BASIC.

94907.q: What is an advantage of an interpreter when programming?
a: You can test code straight away without a separate translation step
You no longer need source code
94907.e: Changes can be tried out at once, which makes learning and experimenting easier.
94907.m: With an interpreter you see changes straight away.

94908.q: What is a process in an operating system?
a: A file on the hard disk
An entry in the start menu
94908.e: A process includes the program code, its data, registers and its state while it runs.
94908.m: A process is a running program.

94909.q: Which three basic states can a process have in the simple state model?
94909.e: A running process has the CPU, a ready one is waiting for it, and a blocked one is waiting for something such as input.
94909.m: A process is ready, running or blocked.

94910.q: What is the data structure called in which the operating system manages the state of a process?
94910.e: The process control block (PCB) holds things such as the process ID, register contents, state and memory information.
94910.m: The process control block is the profile of a process.

94911.q: Which system call does a process use under Unix to create a copy of itself?
94911.e: fork creates a child process as a copy of the parent process. The child can then load a different program with exec.
94911.m: Under Unix, new processes are created with fork.

94912.q: What distinguishes the threads of a process from separate processes?
a: Threads share the same address space
Threads never run at the same time
Threads need their own hard disk
94912.e: The threads of a process share code, data and open files. Separate processes have their own address spaces.
94912.m: Threads share the memory of their process.

94913.q: What is a zombie process under Unix?
a: A finished process whose return value has not yet been collected
A process that secretly steals data
A process that keeps restarting itself
A process with no program assigned to it
94913.e: The process has finished, but its entry stays in the process table until the parent process collects the exit status with wait.
94913.m: A zombie is waiting for its parent process to collect it.

94914.q: What is the procedure called in which the CPU is switched from one process to another?
94914.e: In a context switch, the registers and state of the old process are saved and those of the new one are loaded.
94914.m: Every context switch costs a little computing time.

94915.q: Which process has process ID 1 under Unix and Linux?
94915.e: The init process, on many Linux systems today systemd, is started first and is the ancestor of all other user processes.
94915.m: The init process with ID 1 starts all other processes.

94916.q: What is the job of a process scheduler?
a: It decides which process gets the CPU and when
It measures the temperature of the CPU
It translates programs into machine code
94916.e: The scheduler shares out computing time among the ready processes according to a particular strategy.
94916.m: The scheduler shares out computing time.

94917.q: How does the round robin method work?
a: Each process gets a fixed time slice in turn
The shortest process always runs first
The most important process runs without interruption
94917.e: When its time slice is up, the process goes to the back of the queue and the next one has its turn.
94917.m: Round robin hands out time slices in a circle.

94918.q: What rule does the First Come First Served method follow?
94918.e: FCFS serves processes like a queue at a counter and does not interrupt running processes.
94918.m: With FCFS, whoever comes first is processed first.

94919.q: Which method minimises the average waiting time if all run times are known?
94919.e: If you deal with the short jobs first, the fewest processes have to wait a long time overall.
94919.m: Short jobs first lowers the average waiting time.

a: The operating system can take the CPU away from a running process
A process always gives up the CPU voluntarily
Processes are deleted before they start
Only one process may ever run
94920.e: With preemptive scheduling, the operating system interrupts, for example with a timer interrupt. With cooperative scheduling, the process has to give up the CPU itself.
94920.m: Preemptive means the operating system may interrupt.

94921.q: What is it called when a low-priority process never gets its turn?
94921.e: In starvation, higher-priority processes are always given preference.
94921.m: A starving process never gets its turn.

94922.q: Which technique prevents starvation by slowly raising the priority of waiting processes?
94922.e: With aging, the priority grows with the waiting time until even a process that has waited a long time gets its turn.
94922.m: Thanks to aging, every process gets its turn eventually.

94923.q: Three processes with run times of 6, 3 and 1 ms arrive at the same time in this order. What is the average waiting time with FCFS?
94923.e: The waiting times are 0, 6 and 9 ms. Their sum of 15 ms divided by 3 gives 5 ms.
94923.m: With FCFS, short processes often wait behind long ones.

94924.q: Which scheduling method gives each process a fixed time slice in turn?
94924.e: With round robin, each process runs for a short time slice and then has to join the back of the queue again. That way everyone gets a turn regularly.
94924.m: Round robin shares out the CPU in turn in fixed time slices.

94925.q: What does each process get with virtual memory management?
94925.e: Each process sees its own address space and is thus kept separate from other processes.
94925.m: Virtual memory shields processes from one another.

94926.q: Which hardware unit translates virtual addresses into physical ones?
94926.e: With every memory access, the MMU converts the virtual address into a physical one using the page tables.
94926.m: The MMU translates addresses with every access.

94927.q: Why does the operating system divide main memory into pages of equal size with virtual memory management?
a: So that memory can be managed and swapped out in fixed blocks
So that the processor calculates faster
So that the screen becomes sharper
94927.e: Pages of equal size are easy to allocate, load and swap out. On x86, a normal page is 4 KiB.
94927.m: Virtual memory is managed in pages of equal size.

94928.q: What is the event called when a required page is not in main memory?
94928.e: In a page fault, the MMU raises an interrupt and the operating system loads the page.
94928.m: A page fault brings missing pages into main memory.

94929.q: What is the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) for?
a: It stores recently used address translations
It buffers data for the printer
94929.e: The TLB is a small cache for page table entries, so that not every translation has to be looked up in main memory.
94929.m: The TLB speeds up address translation.

94930.q: What is the table called that shows which virtual page lies in which physical frame?
94930.e: For each virtual page, the page table contains the page frame and bits such as “present” or “writable”.
94930.m: The page table maps pages to frames.

94931.q: What is the state called in which the system does almost nothing but swap pages in and out?
94931.e: In thrashing, main memory is too scarce. Performance collapses because the system is constantly swapping.
94931.m: When thrashing, the computer is busy almost only with swapping.

94932.q: With 4 KiB pages, how many bits of an address form the offset within the page?
94932.e: 4 KiB is 4096 bytes, and 4096 is 2 to the power of 12. So 12 bits are needed for the offset.
94932.m: The page size determines the number of bits for the offset.

94933.q: Where are rarely used pages swapped out to when main memory runs low?
a: To a swap area on mass storage
94933.e: The operating system writes pages to a swap file or swap partition and brings them back when needed.
94933.m: Virtual memory uses mass storage as a reserve.

94934.q: What colour are the ripe berries of deadly nightshade?
94934.e: The ripe berries of deadly nightshade are black and shiny. They look like small cherries but are very poisonous.
94934.m: Never eat black, shiny berries in the forest.

94935.q: Why is deadly nightshade especially dangerous for children?
94935.e: The berries look like sweet cherries and even taste a little sweet. Just a few berries can seriously poison a child.
94935.m: What looks tasty is not always edible.

94936.q: Where does deadly nightshade often grow?
a: In the middle of a lake
94936.e: Deadly nightshade likes to grow in bright spots in the forest, for example in clearings and along forest paths.
94936.m: Deadly nightshade can grow in forest clearings.

94937.q: What does the fruit of deadly nightshade look like?
94937.e: The fruit is a round berry the size of a cherry. That is why its German name means “mad cherry”.
94937.m: Deadly nightshade has berries that look like cherries.

94938.q: What happens to the eyes when someone has eaten deadly nightshade?
94938.e: The poison of deadly nightshade makes the pupils, the black dots in the eye, very wide. Everything then looks blurred.
94938.m: Huge pupils can be a sign of deadly nightshade poisoning.

94939.q: Which parts of deadly nightshade are poisonous?
94939.e: With deadly nightshade, all parts are poisonous, including the leaves, root and berries.
94939.m: No part of deadly nightshade is safe.

94940.q: What colour are the flowers of deadly nightshade?
94940.e: The bell-shaped flowers of deadly nightshade are brownish to purple. They hang singly on the plant.
94940.m: Deadly nightshade has brownish purple bell flowers.

94941.q: How tall can deadly nightshade grow?
a: Up to about as tall as a person
94941.e: Deadly nightshade is a large perennial plant. It usually grows 50 to 150 centimetres tall, sometimes even 2 metres.
94941.m: Deadly nightshade is a large plant.

94942.q: What colour are the flowers of monkshood?
94942.e: Monkshood has dark blue to purple flowers.

94943.q: What does the shape of the monkshood flower remind you of?
94943.e: The top petal arches over the flower like a helmet or a hood.
94943.m: The monkshood flower looks like a knight's helmet.

94944.e: Monkshood is thought to be the most poisonous plant in Europe. Even small amounts can be life-threatening.
94944.m: Always leave monkshood where it is.

94945.q: Why should you not even pick monkshood with bare hands?
a: The poison goes through the skin
94945.e: The poison of monkshood can work through the skin and make it burn and tingle. That is why you should not touch it.

94946.q: Where does monkshood often grow in Switzerland?
94946.e: Monkshood likes to grow in damp meadows and near alpine huts in the mountains. But you can also find it in gardens.
94946.m: When hiking in the mountains you may see monkshood.

94947.q: Which animals like to visit monkshood flowers?
94947.e: Bumblebees are strong enough to crawl into the helmet-shaped flower to get nectar. While doing so, they pollinate the flower.

94948.q: What should you do if a friend wants to pick monkshood flowers?
a: Warn them and fetch an adult
Pick some too and smell them
Put the flowers in your mouth
94948.e: Monkshood is very poisonous. You warn your friend and tell an adult.
94948.m: With poisonous plants, warn others and get help.

94949.q: Roughly how tall does monkshood grow?
a: Only as tall as a finger
Only as tall as a shoe
94949.e: Monkshood usually grows 50 to 150 centimetres tall. It often reaches a child's hip or higher.

94951.q: What colour are the flowers of the common foxglove usually?
94951.e: The flowers are usually purple-red to pink. Inside they have dark spots with a pale edge.
94951.m: The common foxglove has purple-red flowers.

94952.q: How are the flowers arranged on the stem of the foxglove?
a: One below the other on one side
As a single flower at the top
94952.e: Lots of flowers hang one below the other on one side of the tall stem, like bells on a pole.
94952.m: On the foxglove, lots of flowers hang on a long stem.

94953.q: Which organ does foxglove poison especially affect?
94953.e: Foxglove poison affects the heart. That is why all parts of the plant are dangerous.
94953.m: Foxglove is a poison for the heart.

94954.q: What are substances from the foxglove used for in medicine?
94954.e: Doctors use carefully measured active substances from the foxglove to strengthen weak hearts. You must never take the plant yourself.
94954.m: Only doctors may give foxglove substances as medicine.

94955.q: Which insect likes to crawl into foxglove flowers?
94955.e: Bumblebees crawl right into the big flower tubes. The spots inside show them the way to the nectar.
94955.m: The spots inside the foxglove show the bumblebee the way.

94956.q: Where does the common foxglove often grow?
a: At the edge of the forest
94956.e: The common foxglove likes to grow at forest edges and in forest clearings. Many people also plant it in their gardens.
94956.m: Foxgloves can glow at the edge of the forest.

94957.q: Which parts of the common foxglove are poisonous?
94957.e: With the foxglove, the leaves, flowers, stem and seeds are poisonous.
94957.m: Every part of the foxglove is poisonous.

94958.q: In which month does lily of the valley usually flower?
94958.e: Lily of the valley mainly flowers in May. Its German name even means “little May bell”.
94958.m: Lily of the valley flowers in May.

94959.q: What colour are the berries of lily of the valley?
94959.e: After flowering, lily of the valley forms small red berries. They are poisonous too.
94959.m: The red berries of lily of the valley are poisonous.

94960.q: What do lily of the valley flowers smell like?
94960.e: Lily of the valley has a strong, sweet scent. That is why some people put it in a vase.
94960.m: Lily of the valley smells sweet but is poisonous.

94961.q: What should you do after picking lily of the valley?
94961.e: Some of the poison can stick to your hands. That is why you wash them well after touching it.
94961.m: Wash your hands after touching poisonous plants.

94962.q: Why should you not drink the water from a vase of lily of the valley?
94962.e: The poison of lily of the valley can get into the vase water. That is why the water should be poured away.
94962.m: Vase water from lily of the valley is not for drinking.

94963.q: In which season does the autumn crocus flower?
94963.e: The autumn crocus flowers in September and October, so in autumn. That is where its name comes from.
94963.m: The autumn crocus flowers in autumn.

94964.q: What colour are the flowers of the autumn crocus?
94964.e: The flowers are delicate lilac to pale purple and stand straight up out of the meadow.
94964.m: The autumn crocus has pale purple flowers.

94965.q: Which spring flower does the flower of the autumn crocus look like?
94965.e: The flower looks like a crocus. But the crocus flowers in spring.
94965.m: A lilac crocus in autumn is often an autumn crocus.

94966.q: What is special about the flower of the autumn crocus?
a: It only flowers once in ten years
94966.e: In autumn you only see the flower. The leaves only grow the following spring.
94966.m: In autumn the autumn crocus shows only its flower.

94967.q: When do the leaves of the autumn crocus grow?
94967.e: The leaves appear in spring together with the seed capsule, but without a flower. Then they can be mistaken for edible wild herbs.
94967.m: The leaves of the autumn crocus come in spring.

94968.q: Where does the autumn crocus often grow?
94968.e: The autumn crocus likes to grow in damp meadows and pastures, in Switzerland too.
94968.m: The autumn crocus can grow in autumn meadows.

94969.q: Why do farmers not let their cows eat the autumn crocus?
94969.e: The autumn crocus is very poisonous, for people and for cows, horses and sheep. That is why farmers watch out for it.
94969.m: The autumn crocus is poisonous for grazing animals too.

94970.q: What does the autumn crocus grow back from every year?
a: From a corm in the ground
94970.e: The autumn crocus has a corm in the ground. New flowers and leaves grow from it every year.
94970.m: The autumn crocus survives the winter as a corm.

94971.e: Mezereon flowers from February or March, often while there is still snow on the ground.
94971.m: Mezereon is one of the first plants to flower each year.

94972.q: What colour are the flowers of mezereon usually?
94972.e: The small flowers are pink to purple-red. Occasionally there are white ones too.

94973.q: Where are the flowers on mezereon?
a: At the top of long stalks
94973.e: The flowers sit closely together directly on the bare twigs. The leaves only grow after flowering.
94973.m: On mezereon, the bare twigs flower.

94974.q: What kind of plant is mezereon?
94974.e: Mezereon is a small shrub, usually only about a metre tall.

94975.q: What colour are the berries of mezereon?
94975.e: In late summer mezereon has bright red berries. They are very poisonous.
94975.m: The red berries of mezereon are poisonous.

94976.q: What do mezereon flowers smell like?
94976.e: The flowers have a strong, sweet scent. This attracts insects in early spring.
94976.m: Mezereon smells strongly, but you do not pick it.

94977.q: What happens if mezereon sap gets on your skin?
a: Your skin can go red and burn
Your skin goes as hard as wood
94977.e: The bark and sap contain a harsh poison. On the skin it can cause redness and blisters.

94978.q: Where does mezereon grow in the wild?
94978.e: Mezereon grows in deciduous forests and mountain forests, in Switzerland too.
94978.m: You can discover mezereon in the forest.

94979.e: The flowers are bright yellow like gold. That is why laburnum is also called golden rain.

94980.q: How do laburnum flowers hang on the tree?
a: One by one on the ground
Not at all, it never flowers
94980.e: The flowers hang down in long clusters. It looks like golden rain.
94980.m: Laburnum looks like falling golden rain.

94981.q: Where do you find laburnum especially often?
94981.e: Laburnum is a popular ornamental tree. That is why it is often found in gardens and parks.
94981.m: Poisonous plants can grow in gardens too.

94982.q: What do the fruits of laburnum look like?
94982.e: After flowering, laburnum forms pods similar to beans or peas. The seeds are inside.

94983.q: Why are laburnum pods dangerous for children?
a: They look like beans to play with
94983.e: Children like to play at cooking with the bean-like pods and seeds. But the seeds are especially poisonous.
94983.m: Do not play at cooking with laburnum pods.

94984.q: Which parts of laburnum are poisonous?
94984.e: All parts of laburnum are poisonous, the seeds most of all.

94985.q: What kind of plant is laburnum?
94985.e: Laburnum is a small tree or large shrub and grows several metres tall.
94985.m: Laburnum is a tree with yellow flowers.

94986.q: In which season does laburnum flower?
94986.e: Laburnum flowers in spring, from about April to June.
94986.m: In May, yellow flowers hang from the laburnum.

94987.q: What colour are the ripe berries of lords-and-ladies?
94987.e: In summer, lots of bright red berries sit close together on a spike. They are poisonous.
94987.m: Leave red berries on a spike in the forest alone.

94988.q: How are the berries of lords-and-ladies arranged?
94988.e: The berries sit close together on an upright spike. It looks like a small corn cob.
94988.m: Lords-and-ladies has its berries on a spike.

94989.q: What wraps around the flower of lords-and-ladies?
94989.e: The flower sits inside a large, greenish leaf wrapped around it like a paper cone.
94989.m: The flower of lords-and-ladies sits in a cone-shaped leaf.

94990.q: How does lords-and-ladies hold small insects in its flower for a short time?
a: In a trap made of hairs
94990.e: Small midges slide into the chamber at the bottom of the flower. Hairs hold them there until the next morning. By then they are covered in pollen and are allowed out again.
94990.m: Lords-and-ladies traps insects for a short time so they pollinate it.

94991.e: Lords-and-ladies likes damp, shady deciduous forests.

94992.q: Which edible plant can young lords-and-ladies leaves be mistaken for?
94992.e: Young lords-and-ladies leaves often grow among wild garlic. That is why you must check every leaf carefully when picking.
94992.m: Watch out for lords-and-ladies when picking wild garlic.

94993.q: What shape are the leaves of lords-and-ladies?
94993.e: The leaves are large and arrow-shaped, often with dark spots. That is why it is also called spotted arum.

94994.q: What happens if you bite into a piece of lords-and-ladies?
94994.e: The plant contains harsh substances. They burn in your mouth and throat.
94994.m: Lords-and-ladies burns in your mouth and is poisonous.

94995.q: How can you recognise hemlock by its stem?
94995.e: The stem has reddish-brown to purple spots. That is why it is called spotted hemlock.
94995.m: Red spots on the stem warn you of hemlock.

94996.q: What does hemlock smell of when you crush it?
94996.e: Crushed leaves have a nasty smell of mouse wee. But it is better not to crush it at all.

94997.e: Hemlock has lots of small white flowers in clusters that look like umbrellas.
94997.m: Hemlock has small white umbrella-shaped flower clusters.

94998.q: What do the flower clusters of hemlock look like?
94998.e: The flowers form umbels. They look like open umbrellas.
94998.m: Many poisonous meadow plants have flowers like umbrellas.

94999.q: Which kitchen herb can young hemlock leaves be mistaken for?
94999.e: The finely feathered leaves of hemlock look similar to parsley.
94999.m: Only pick wild herbs with an expert.

95000.e: Hemlock is one of the most poisonous plants here. Even a little of it is dangerous.

95001.e: You find it along paths, hedges, waste ground and riverbanks.
95001.m: Poisonous plants can grow along paths too.

a: Only as tall as a fingernail
95002.e: Hemlock often grows 1 to 2 metres tall, sometimes even taller.

95003.q: What happens if the sap of giant hogweed gets on your skin and then the sun shines?
a: Your skin turns yellow and never itches
95003.e: The sap makes the skin sensitive to sunlight. Then painful blisters appear, like burns.
95003.m: Giant hogweed and sun together burn the skin.

95004.q: How tall can giant hogweed grow?
95004.e: Giant hogweed grows up to about 3 metres tall, so much taller than an adult.
95004.m: Giant hogweed is taller than a person.

95005.q: What colour are the flowers of giant hogweed?
95005.e: Giant hogweed has white flowers in huge umbrella-shaped clusters.

95006.q: How big can the flower umbrellas of giant hogweed get?
a: As big as a bike wheel
95006.e: The flower umbrellas are often 30 to 50 centimetres wide. That is about as big as a small bike wheel.
95006.m: The flower umbrellas of giant hogweed are huge.

95007.q: Where does giant hogweed often grow here?
a: In the middle of a deep lake
95007.e: Giant hogweed likes damp places, by streams, forest edges and paths. You need to watch out for it there.
95007.m: Giant hogweed often grows by streams and paths.

95008.q: What should you do if sap from giant hogweed has got on your skin?
a: Wash it and keep out of the sun
95008.e: Wash the spot well with water straight away and protect it from the sun. Then tell an adult.
95008.m: After touching hogweed, wash your skin and keep out of the sun.

95009.q: Why should you not make blowpipes out of giant hogweed stems?
a: The sap burns the skin in sunlight
The stems are made of glass
95009.e: The hollow stems are tempting for making things. But sap on your mouth can cause bad burns in the sun.
95009.m: Never make things or play with giant hogweed.

95010.e: Giant hogweed flowers in summer, around June and July.
95010.m: In summer you see the giant white umbrellas.

95011.q: What do you often see on your skin after touching a stinging nettle?
95011.e: Small white or red bumps appear on the skin. They sting and itch for a while.

95012.q: Does the sting of a nettle usually go away again?
95012.e: The stinging is unpleasant, but usually goes away by itself after a few hours.
95012.m: Nettle stings hurt, but they pass.

95013.q: Which animals like to eat nettle leaves?
95013.e: The caterpillars of the peacock butterfly and the small tortoiseshell eat nettle leaves.
95013.m: Without nettles, some caterpillars would have no food.

95014.q: What can you make from nettle leaves?
95014.e: Dried or cooked nettle leaves no longer sting. You can make tea or soup from them.
95014.m: Dried or cooked nettles no longer sting.

95015.q: Where do stinging nettles often grow?
95015.e: Nettles like to grow on nutrient-rich soil, for example along paths, fences and streams.
95015.m: Nettles like to grow along paths.

95016.q: What is the best way to protect yourself from stinging nettles?
95016.e: Long trousers and sleeves protect your skin from the stinging hairs.
95016.m: Long trousers protect you from nettles.

95017.q: What helps when your skin stings after touching nettles?
95017.e: Rinsing the spot with cool water calms the skin. Scratching usually makes it worse.

95018.q: When can you call the poisons helpline 145?
95018.e: Tox Info Suisse can be reached day and night, on every day of the year.
95018.m: You can always reach the poisons helpline 145.

95019.q: Which number do you dial if a poisoned child is unconscious?
95019.e: If someone is unconscious, the ambulance service is needed immediately. You call it on 144.
95019.m: If someone is unconscious, call the ambulance on 144.

95020.q: Should you make someone sick after they have eaten a poisonous plant?
95020.e: Tox Info Suisse advises not to make someone vomit. It is better to call 145 straight away.
95020.m: In a poisoning, do not make someone vomit.

95021.q: What do you take to the doctor if someone has eaten part of a plant?
95021.e: A piece of the plant or a photo helps the experts identify the plant.
95021.m: A piece of the plant helps to identify it.

95022.q: In which city is Tox Info Suisse based?
95022.e: Tox Info Suisse, the Swiss poisons information centre, is based in Zurich.
95022.m: The Swiss poisons information centre is in Zurich.

95023.q: What is the first thing you do if a little brother or sister has eaten a poisonous berry?
95023.e: Tell an adult straight away. They will then call 145.
95023.m: In a poisoning, fetch an adult straight away.

95024.q: What is the rule for unknown berries in the forest?
a: Never eat them without an adult
95024.e: Many poisonous berries look tasty. Only eat berries that an adult knows for sure.

95025.q: What should you do if plant sap has got into your eye?
95025.e: Tox Info Suisse advises rinsing the eye with lukewarm water for 10 to 15 minutes while keeping it open.
95025.m: Rinse anything that splashed into your eye with water for a long time.

95026.q: How do the flowers of lily of the valley hang on the stalk?
a: As a single flower at the top
95026.e: On lily of the valley, 5 to 10 little bell flowers hang in a row, all on the same side.
95026.m: The little bells of lily of the valley hang in a row.

95027.q: How many large leaves does lily of the valley usually have?
95027.e: Lily of the valley usually has two, occasionally three, broad leaves. The flower stalk grows between them.
95027.m: Lily of the valley usually has two leaves.

95028.q: Where does lily of the valley grow in the wild?
95028.e: Lily of the valley grows wild in bright deciduous forests, where it often forms large carpets.
95028.m: You can see carpets of lily of the valley in deciduous forests.

95029.q: Which plant looks similar to the stinging nettle but does not sting?
95029.e: The dead-nettle has similar leaves but no stinging hairs. It is called “dead” because it does not sting.

95030.q: What will the expert on the poisons helpline want to know from you?
a: What was eaten, how much and when
95030.e: So that the experts can help, they need to know exactly what someone ate, how much and when. The person's age is important too.
95030.m: On the poisons helpline, say what was eaten, how much and when.

95031.q: The scientific name of deadly nightshade contains the word “belladonna”. What does that mean in Italian?
95031.e: “Bella donna” means beautiful woman in Italian. In the past, women used the plant for beauty, which was very dangerous.

95032.q: How long does a common foxglove plant usually live?
95032.e: In the first year, only a clump of leaves grows on the ground. The foxglove only flowers in its second year, and then it usually dies.
95032.m: The foxglove only flowers in its second year.

95033.q: Which parts of monkshood are poisonous?
95033.e: With monkshood, all parts are poisonous. The most poison is in the root tuber.

95034.q: Which English doctor vaccinated a boy with cowpox against smallpox in 1796?
95034.e: Edward Jenner showed that harmless cowpox protects against dangerous smallpox. His method then spread all over the world.
95034.m: Edward Jenner is seen as the father of the smallpox vaccination.

95035.q: Which animal does the word “vaccine” come from?
95035.e: “Vacca” is Latin for cow. The first vaccination was done with cowpox.
95035.m: The word vaccine comes from the Latin word for cow.

95036.q: How do you usually get a vaccination?
95036.e: Most vaccines are given with a small injection in the upper arm. It only stings for a moment.
95036.m: Most vaccinations are given with an injection.

95037.q: What does the body learn from a vaccination?
95037.e: The vaccine shows the body a harmless part of a germ. Later, the body's defences quickly recognise the real germ.
95037.m: With a vaccination, the body practises fighting germs.

95038.q: Which disease no longer exists anywhere in the world thanks to vaccinations?
95038.e: The World Health Organization declared smallpox wiped out in 1980. This was achieved through worldwide vaccination.
95038.m: Smallpox was wiped out by vaccinations.

95039.q: Where are the vaccinations you have had recorded in Switzerland?
95039.e: The vaccination record lists all your vaccinations with their dates. That way the doctor knows which vaccination is still missing.
95039.m: All your vaccinations are in your vaccination record.

95040.q: What are the defence substances that the body makes after a vaccination called?
95040.e: Antibodies are defence substances in the blood. They recognise certain germs and help to make them harmless.
95040.m: Antibodies help the body fight germs.

95041.q: Why do you put a plaster on a small wound?
a: So the skin does not go brown
95041.e: The plaster covers the wound. That way less dirt and fewer germs get in.
95041.m: A plaster protects a wound from dirt.

95042.q: What should you do before putting a plaster on a graze?
95042.e: Dirt in a wound can cause an infection. That is why you clean the wound first, for example with clean water.
95042.m: The wound is cleaned before the plaster goes on.

95043.q: Which part of a plaster lies directly on the wound?
a: The soft pad in the middle
The sticky strip at the edge
95043.e: The pad in the middle is called the wound pad. It does not stick to the wound and soaks up a little blood.
95043.m: The soft pad of the plaster lies on the wound.

95044.q: What do the thin strips of film on a new plaster protect?
95044.e: The strips cover the glue and the pad. You only pull them off just before you stick the plaster on.
95044.m: The film keeps a new plaster clean and sticky.

95045.q: What does a blister plaster help with?
95045.e: A blister plaster cushions a blister on the skin. It protects it from rubbing in your shoe, for example when hiking.
95045.m: A blister plaster protects blisters from rubbing.

95046.q: How can you tell that a wound under a plaster might be infected?
95046.e: Redness, warmth, swelling and more pain are signs of infection. Then you should show the wound to a doctor.
95046.m: A red and hot wound may be infected.

95047.q: What is the outer layer of many waterproof plasters made of?
95047.e: A thin plastic film does not let any water through. That is why you can even shower with it.
95047.m: Waterproof plasters have a plastic outer layer.

95048.q: What does a clinical thermometer measure?
95048.e: With a clinical thermometer you can see how warm the body is. That way you can tell whether someone has a fever.
95048.m: A clinical thermometer measures body temperature.

95049.q: Roughly how warm is the body of a healthy person?
95049.e: Normal body temperature is around 37 degrees Celsius. It changes a little during the day.
95049.m: A healthy person's body is about 37 degrees.

95050.q: What should a child with a fever do a lot of?
95050.e: With a fever, the body sweats and loses water. Rest helps it fight the illness.
95050.m: With a fever, you should drink plenty and rest.

95051.q: Why do you clean a clinical thermometer after using it?
a: So no germs are passed on
95051.e: Germs from the sick person can stick to the thermometer. If you clean it, the next person is less likely to catch something.
95051.m: A clinical thermometer is cleaned after use.

95052.q: How can you often tell, even without a thermometer, that someone might have a fever?
95052.e: With a fever, the whole body is warmer than usual. You can often feel this on a hot forehead. But you can only measure it exactly with a thermometer.
95052.m: A hot forehead can be a sign of fever.

95053.q: Which poisonous metal used to be in many clinical thermometers?
95053.e: Mercury is a liquid metal that expands when it gets warm. Because it is poisonous, digital thermometers are used today.
95053.m: Clinical thermometers used to contain poisonous mercury.

95054.q: Where can you quickly take someone's temperature with a special thermometer?
95054.e: An ear thermometer measures the warmth in the ear using invisible heat rays. It only takes a few seconds.
95054.m: An ear thermometer measures fever in the ear.

95055.q: How does a digital clinical thermometer usually show that it has finished measuring?
95055.e: A digital clinical thermometer usually beeps. Then you can read the number on the display.
95055.m: A digital clinical thermometer beeps when it has finished.

95056.q: What does the doctor listen to with a stethoscope?
95056.e: With a stethoscope you can hear sounds inside the body. The heart and the breathing in the lungs can be heard especially well.
95056.m: With a stethoscope you listen to the heart and lungs.

95057.q: Where does the doctor put the two ends of the stethoscope?
95057.e: The arms with the earpieces go into the ears. The doctor places the round end on the chest or back.
95057.m: The ends of the stethoscope go into the ears.

95058.e: The doctor René Laënnec built the first stethoscope. It was a simple wooden tube.

95059.q: What did René Laënnec first use to listen to a heart, before he built a real stethoscope?
95059.e: Laënnec rolled paper into a tube and held it against the chest. With it he heard the heart better than with his ear alone.
95059.m: The first stethoscope was a roll of paper.

95060.q: What does the Greek word “stethos” in stethoscope mean?
95060.e: “Stethos” is Greek and means chest. “Skopein” means to look at or examine.
95060.m: Stethos is the Greek word for chest.

95061.q: In which country did the inventor of the stethoscope live?
95061.e: René Laënnec worked as a doctor in a hospital in Paris. That is where he developed the stethoscope.
95061.m: The stethoscope was invented in France.

95062.q: Why should you breathe deeply when the doctor listens to your back?
a: So the doctor can hear the lungs well
So the heart beats more slowly
95062.e: When you breathe deeply, a lot of air flows through the lungs. The doctor can then hear whether the breathing sounds healthy.
95062.m: When the doctor listens to your lungs, you breathe deeply in and out.

95063.q: In which century was the stethoscope invented?
95063.e: The stethoscope was invented in 1816. The years from 1801 to 1900 make up the 19th century.
95063.m: The stethoscope is around 200 years old.

95064.q: What can you see inside the body with X-rays?
95064.e: X-rays pass through the soft parts of the body, but bones stop them. That is why you see the bones on the picture.
95064.m: With X-rays you can see the bones.

95065.q: What do you feel while an X-ray is being taken?
95065.e: You can neither see nor feel X-rays. You just have to keep completely still for a moment.
95065.m: You feel nothing during an X-ray.

95066.q: What is often put over other parts of the body during an X-ray to protect them?
95066.e: Lead is good at stopping X-rays. The heavy apron protects the parts of the body that are not being X-rayed.
95066.m: A lead apron protects you during an X-ray.

95067.q: What colour are bones on a normal X-ray picture?
95067.e: Where the rays are stopped, the picture stays light. That is why bones are white and soft tissue is darker.
95067.m: Bones are white on an X-ray picture.

95068.q: What did Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen himself call his new rays?
95068.e: At first Röntgen did not know what the rays were. So he called them X-rays, like an unknown number x. In English they are still called that today.

95069.q: Whose hand is shown in one of the first famous X-ray pictures?
a: The hand of the German emperor
95069.e: Shortly after his discovery, Röntgen X-rayed the hand of his wife Anna Bertha. In the picture you can see the bones and her ring.
95069.m: An early X-ray picture shows the hand of Röntgen's wife.

95070.q: Where are X-ray machines used at the airport?
95070.e: At the check, suitcases and bags go through an X-ray machine. That way you can see what is inside without opening them.
95070.m: Luggage is X-rayed at the airport.

95071.q: Who makes glasses and adjusts them to fit?
95071.e: Opticians make glasses and adjust them to fit the face. They also test how well you can see.

95072.q: What does a short-sighted person see badly without glasses?
95072.e: Short-sighted people see things close up clearly. But things far away, like the board at school, look blurry.
95072.m: Short-sighted people see things far away blurrily.

95073.q: What does a long-sighted person see badly without glasses?
95073.e: Long-sighted people see distant things well. But when they read a book very close up, the writing becomes blurry.
95073.m: Long-sighted people see things close up blurrily.

95074.q: In which country were the first glasses made around the year 1300?
95074.e: The first reading glasses were probably made towards the end of the 13th century in northern Italy. They had lenses made of quartz or glass.
95074.m: The first glasses came from Italy.

95075.q: Which glasses do you wear in craft lessons when drilling?
95075.e: When drilling and sawing, small chips can fly around. Safety goggles keep them away from your eyes.
95075.m: Safety goggles protect your eyes during craft work.

95076.q: Why do people wear a brace on their teeth?
a: So you no longer have to brush
95076.e: A brace slowly pushes the teeth into the right position. This often takes several months or years.

95077.q: What is the doctor who looks after braces called?
95077.e: Orthodontists are experts in the position of the teeth and jaw. They plan the brace.

95078.q: What is a brace that you can take out yourself called?
95078.e: You can take a removable brace out to eat and to brush your teeth. A fixed brace stays in your mouth the whole time.
95078.m: A removable brace can be taken out.

95079.q: What is a fixed brace made of?
95079.e: A small bracket is glued onto each tooth. A wire connects them and slowly pulls the teeth into place.
95079.m: A fixed brace has brackets and a wire.

95080.q: What is especially important with a fixed brace?
95080.e: Bits of food easily get stuck on the wires and brackets. That is why you have to brush especially carefully.
95080.m: With a brace, you brush your teeth especially well.

95081.q: At what age do many children get a brace?
95081.e: At this age the permanent teeth and the jaw are still growing. Then the teeth can be moved easily.
95081.m: Many children wear a brace between the ages of 9 and 14.

95082.q: Which foods do you have to be careful with when you have a fixed brace?
95082.e: Toffee or hard nuts can loosen brackets or bend the wire. Soft foods are no problem.
95082.m: With a fixed brace you avoid sticky and hard foods.

95083.q: When do you usually get a plaster cast?
95083.e: When a bone is broken, the doctor often puts on a plaster cast. It holds the broken part of the body still.
95083.m: When you break a bone, you often get a cast.

95084.q: Why does a cast keep the broken bone still?
a: So it does not get cold
95084.e: A bone can heal by itself. But it has to stay still so that the broken pieces grow back together straight.
95084.m: A cast helps the bone grow back together straight.

95085.q: Roughly how long does a child with a broken arm wear a cast?
95085.e: A bone needs time to heal. In children this often takes about three to six weeks.
95085.m: A cast usually stays on for a few weeks.

95086.q: What do friends like to write on a cast?
95086.e: Many children let their friends sign their cast. It cheers you up and is a nice memory.
95086.m: Many people let their friends sign their cast.

95087.q: What do you usually walk with when your leg is in a cast?
95087.e: Crutches support your body as you walk. That way you do not have to put weight on the injured leg.
95087.m: With a leg in a cast you walk on crutches.

95088.q: What are many modern casts made of today?
95088.e: A cast made of plastic is lighter and stronger than real plaster. But it is often still just called a plaster cast.
95088.m: Many casts are made of plastic today.

95089.q: What do you often feel under a cast that you have been wearing for a long time?
95089.e: Under the cast the skin sweats and cannot be washed. That is why it often itches. Even so, you should not poke anything inside.
95089.m: The skin under a cast often itches.

95090.q: Which germs does an antibiotic help against?
95090.e: Antibiotics kill bacteria or stop them growing. They do not help against viruses, for example with a cold.

95091.q: How do children often take an antibiotic?
95091.e: Many antibiotics are swallowed as tablets. For children they often also come as a syrup.
95091.m: An antibiotic is often swallowed as a tablet or syrup.

95092.q: In which year was penicillin discovered?
95092.e: In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould was killing bacteria in his dish. Later it was turned into a medicine.

95093.q: Which living thing was the first penicillin obtained from?
95093.e: Penicillin is made by a green mould. The mould uses it to fight off bacteria.

95094.q: Who prescribes an antibiotic in Switzerland?
95094.e: In Switzerland, antibiotics you swallow are only available on prescription. The doctor decides whether you need one.
95094.m: An antibiotic is prescribed by a doctor.

95095.q: How long should you take an antibiotic for?
a: As long as the doctor says
95095.e: You take an antibiotic exactly as it was prescribed. Otherwise some bacteria may survive.
95095.m: You take an antibiotic exactly as instructed.

95096.q: What can happen if antibiotics are used too often?
95096.e: Some bacteria get used to antibiotics. Then the medicines no longer work well. This is called resistance.
95096.m: Too many antibiotics make bacteria resistant.

95097.q: Where do you collect an antibiotic with a prescription?
95097.e: You get medicines at the chemist's. For an antibiotic, you show the doctor's prescription there.
95097.m: Prescription medicines are collected at the chemist's.

95098.q: Besides water, what do you need to wash germs off your hands properly?
95098.e: Soap loosens grease and dirt from the skin. The germs are then rinsed away with the water.
95098.m: Soap gets your hands really clean.

95099.q: When should you definitely wash your hands?
a: After getting up from a chair
95099.e: Lots of germs get onto your hands in the toilet. Washing your hands stops them being passed on.
95099.m: Always wash your hands after using the toilet.

95100.q: Why do doctors disinfect their hands before treating someone?
a: So they don't pass on germs that cause illness
95100.e: Bacteria and viruses can travel from one person to the next on hands. Disinfecting kills most germs.
95100.m: Clean hands stop illnesses being passed on.

a: Tiny living things that can make you ill
95101.e: Germs are so small that you can only see them under a microscope. Some of them can make you ill.
95101.m: Germs are tiny and can make you ill.

95102.q: What is the best thing to dry your hands with after washing them?
95102.e: A clean towel has few germs on it. Clothes and hair, on the other hand, can put dirt back on your hands.
95102.m: Dry your hands on a clean towel after washing.

95103.q: Which parts are easy to forget when washing your hands?
95103.e: People often don't wash enough between their fingers and around their thumbs. That is why you should rub your fingers together.
95103.m: When washing your hands, rub between your fingers too.

95104.q: What can you use for clean hands when you are out and there is no water?
95104.e: Hand sanitiser kills many germs without water. You rub it in until your hands are dry.

95105.q: Which number do you dial in Switzerland for an ambulance?
95105.e: In Switzerland, 144 connects you to the ambulance service. 117 is the police and 118 is the fire brigade.
95105.m: The ambulance number in Switzerland is 144.

95106.q: What is the number of Rega, the Swiss air rescue service?
95106.e: You can reach Rega on 1414. It helps with helicopters, for example in the mountains.

95107.q: Which emergency number works all over Europe, including Switzerland?
95107.e: 112 is the European emergency number. It also works in Switzerland, even from a mobile phone.
95107.m: 112 is the emergency number all over Europe.

95108.q: What do you do first for a small burn on your hand?
95108.e: Cool running water eases the pain of small burns. Butter or flour should never go on a burn.
95108.m: Cool a small burn with water.

95109.q: How do you position an unconscious person who is breathing normally?
95109.e: In the recovery position the airway stays clear. Vomit can run out of the mouth instead of getting into the lungs.
95109.m: Put an unconscious person who is breathing in the recovery position.

95110.q: How do you hold your head when you have a nosebleed?
95110.e: With your head forward, the blood runs out of your nose and not down your throat. A cool cloth on the back of the neck can help.
95110.m: With a nosebleed, tilt your head forward.

95111.q: At an accident, what do you check first before you help?
95111.e: Anyone who helps should not put themselves in danger. First look around, then think and then act.
95111.m: When helping, check your own safety first.

95112.q: Which number do you call in Switzerland if someone has swallowed something poisonous?
95112.e: On 145 you reach Tox Info Suisse. Experts there help with poisoning, day and night.

95113.q: Which flag looks like the Red Cross flag with the colours swapped?
95113.e: The Red Cross has a red cross on a white background. It was chosen in honour of Switzerland, whose flag has the colours the other way round.
95113.m: The Red Cross emblem is the Swiss flag reversed.

95114.q: In which Swiss city does the International Committee of the Red Cross have its headquarters?
95114.e: The International Committee of the Red Cross, ICRC for short, has its headquarters in Geneva. From there it helps in many countries.
95114.m: The ICRC has its headquarters in Geneva.

95115.q: Which emblem does the Red Cross movement use in many Muslim countries?
95115.e: Besides the Red Cross there is the Red Crescent. Both belong to the same aid movement.
95115.m: In many countries the aid movement is called the Red Crescent.

95116.q: Who does the Red Cross help especially in wars?
95116.e: The Red Cross helps everyone in need, no matter which side they are on. It also visits prisoners of war.
95116.m: The Red Cross helps the wounded and prisoners.

95117.q: What do many adults donate through the Swiss Red Cross to help sick people?
95117.e: Blood donations are important for operations and accidents. In Switzerland the Red Cross blood donation service organises the donations.
95117.m: Giving blood can help sick people.

95118.q: What is the abbreviation for the Swiss Red Cross?
95118.e: SRK stands for Schweizerisches Rotes Kreuz, the Swiss Red Cross. It helps in Switzerland, for example with transport services and courses.
95118.m: The Swiss Red Cross is called SRK for short.

95119.q: What does the Red Cross emblem on a vehicle mean in a war?
95119.e: The Red Cross emblem is a protective sign. Anyone using it to help the wounded must not be attacked in a war.
95119.m: The Red Cross emblem protects helpers in war.

95120.q: At which battle in Italy did Henry Dunant see thousands of wounded in 1859?
95120.e: After the Battle of Solferino, many wounded lay there with no help. Dunant helped care for them together with women from the village.
95120.m: Henry Dunant witnessed the Battle of Solferino in 1859.

95121.q: Which prize did Henry Dunant receive in 1901 as one of the first winners?
95121.e: The Nobel Peace Prize was awarded for the first time in 1901. Henry Dunant shared it with the Frenchman Frédéric Passy.
95121.m: Henry Dunant received the first Nobel Peace Prize.

95122.q: What did Henry Dunant write after the war of 1859 to shake people up?
95122.e: In his book Dunant described the suffering of the wounded. He suggested setting up aid groups in every country.
95122.m: Henry Dunant wrote a book about the suffering in war.

95123.q: Which aid organisation did Henry Dunant help to found?
95123.e: In 1863 Dunant and others founded the committee in Geneva that became the International Red Cross.
95123.m: Henry Dunant helped to found the Red Cross.

95124.q: What was Henry Dunant's original job?
95124.e: Dunant was a merchant and travelled to see Emperor Napoleon III about a business deal. That is how he came to the battlefield.
95124.m: Henry Dunant was originally a businessman.

95125.q: Which aid organisation was founded by the Swiss Henry Dunant?
95125.e: Henry Dunant saw many wounded soldiers after a battle. So he founded the Red Cross, which helps the injured.
95125.m: Henry Dunant founded the Red Cross.

95126.q: Which sense tells you whether something is rough or smooth?
95126.e: With the sense of touch you feel what a surface is like. You need neither eyes nor ears for it.
95126.m: With the sense of touch you feel rough and smooth.

95127.q: Where on the hand are there especially many touch receptors?
a: On the back of the hand
95127.e: There are a great many tiny sensors in the fingertips. That is why you can feel things especially finely with them.

95128.q: What do ants use to feel their way?
95128.e: Ants touch the ground and other ants with their movable antennae. They can also smell with them.

95129.q: Which part of its body does an elephant use to feel things especially finely?
95129.e: The tip of an elephant's trunk is very sensitive. With it, the elephant can even feel and grab small things like a peanut.
95129.m: An elephant feels things with its trunk.

95130.q: What do you say about someone who does a difficult thing very carefully and skilfully?
95130.e: Having a delicate touch means being sensitive and skilful. The phrase comes from the fine sense of touch in the fingers.
95130.m: Someone who is skilful and sensitive has a delicate touch.

95131.q: Where do the nerves report what the fingers feel?
95131.e: The nerves carry the messages from the skin to the brain in a flash. Only there do you notice what you are touching.
95131.m: The brain processes what the skin feels.

95132.q: What do babies very often use to feel objects?
95132.e: Lips and tongue can feel very finely. That is why babies put lots of things in their mouth to explore them.
95132.m: Babies often explore things with their mouth.

95133.q: What can you find out by touch with your eyes closed?
a: Whether something is soft or hard
95133.e: When you touch something, you feel whether it gives way or is firm. Colours and brightness, on the other hand, can only be seen.
95133.m: By touch you feel whether something is soft or hard.

95134.q: What do cats use to feel their surroundings in the dark?
95134.e: A cat's whiskers are very sensitive. They can feel even tiny movements of air and narrow gaps.

95135.q: What does a glowing sign on a switched-off hob mean?
95135.e: Even after it is switched off, a hob stays hot for a long time. The display warns you not to touch it.
95135.m: A heat warning light warns of a hot hob.

95136.q: What do you call a lightning-fast movement of the body that happens without thinking?
95136.e: In a reflex, the body reacts by itself and very quickly. This protects us from injuries.
95136.m: A reflex is a movement without thinking.

95137.q: What do you use to hold a hot pan?
95137.e: A thick oven glove only lets the heat through slowly. That way you do not burn your hands.
95137.m: You hold hot pans with an oven glove.

95138.q: What does the body do in great heat to cool down?
95138.e: Sweat comes out of the skin and evaporates. This makes the skin cooler.
95138.m: In the heat, the body cools down by sweating.

95139.q: Which part of the body do parents often use to check that a baby's bath water is not too hot?
95139.e: The skin on the elbow is thinner and less used to heat than the palm of the hand. So you can easily tell whether the water feels pleasant.
95139.m: You check the warmth of bath water with your elbow.

95140.q: What does your skin get if you stay in the sun too long without protection?
95140.e: The sun's rays damage the skin. It turns red, hot and painful. Sun cream and shade protect you.
95140.m: Too much sun gives you sunburn.

95141.q: What can form on the skin when you burn yourself?
95141.e: With a burn, fluid collects under the skin. This forms a blister, which you should not burst.
95141.m: A burn can cause a blister.

95142.q: Why should you not walk barefoot over hot tarmac in summer?
a: You can burn the soles of your feet
It makes you tired straight away
95142.e: Dark tarmac gets very hot in the sun. The skin on the soles of your feet can get burnt.
95142.m: Hot tarmac can burn the soles of your feet.

95143.q: What do you get on your skin when you are cold?
95143.e: In the cold, the tiny hairs stand up and the skin forms little bumps. In Switzerland people call this “chicken skin”.
95143.m: When you are cold, you get goose bumps.

95144.q: What does the body do to make heat when it is very cold?
95144.e: When you shiver, your muscles move very fast. This makes heat.
95144.m: Shivering warms the body in the cold.

95145.q: Which parts of the body usually get cold first?
95145.e: In the cold, the body sends warm blood mainly to the important organs. That is why fingers and toes get cold quickly.
95145.m: Fingers and toes get cold first.

95146.q: What is an injury to the skin caused by extreme cold called?
95146.e: In extreme cold, the skin on fingers, toes, ears or nose can be damaged. This is called frostbite.

95147.q: What protects your hands from the cold in winter?
95147.e: Gloves hold the warm air around your hands. That way your fingers do not cool down so quickly.
95147.m: Gloves keep your hands warm in winter.

95148.q: What happens to your hand if you hold an ice cube for a long time?
95148.e: The cold slows down the nerves in the skin. Then you feel almost nothing and your hand goes numb.
95148.m: Great cold makes the skin numb.

95149.q: What do you put on a fresh bump on the head?
95149.e: Cold makes the swelling less bad and eases the pain. Never put ice directly on the skin.

95150.q: Why does a metal railing feel colder in winter than a wooden one?
a: Wood is always in the sun
95150.e: Metal takes the warmth from your hand very quickly. That is why it feels colder, even when it is just as cold as the wood.
95150.m: Metal feels cold because it carries heat away quickly.

95151.q: Why is pain useful for the body?
95151.e: Pain is a warning signal. It shows that something is hurting the body or that something is wrong.

95152.q: What is a medicine that eases pain called?
95152.e: A painkiller dulls the pain. Children should only take it when an adult allows it.

95153.q: What does the number 0 mean on a pain scale from 0 to 10?
